subject: Pharmacology I
question: Define pharmacovigilance. Classify adverse drug reactions with examples. Describe the role of the nurse in monitoring and reporting adverse drug reactions.

diagram.caption: Flow of ADR reporting under the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India

answer_html:
Introduction Every drug that can cure can also harm. Clinical trials study a drug in a few thousand carefully selected people for a short time; rare and long-term harms are discovered only when the drug is used by millions in real life. Hence every country needs a system to watch for drug-related harm after a medicine reaches the market. This is pharmacovigilance. Nurses, who give medicines and observe patients round the clock, are often the first to notice an adverse reaction.

A. Definitions

  1. Pharmacovigilance (WHO) – "the science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse effects or any other drug-related problem."
  2. Adverse drug reaction (ADR) (WHO) – "a response to a drug which is noxious and unintended, and which occurs at doses normally used in man for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy of disease, or for modification of physiological function."
  3. Adverse drug event (ADE) – any harm occurring during drug therapy, whether or not caused by the drug (includes medication errors).
  4. Serious ADR – one that results in death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs hospitalisation, causes persistent disability, or produces a congenital anomaly.

B. Classification of adverse drug reactions 1. Based on mechanism (Rawlins and Thompson, extended) – "A to F" | Type | Meaning | Features | Examples | |---|---|---|---| | A – Augmented | Exaggerated normal effect | Dose-related, predictable, common (about 80%), low mortality | Hypoglycaemia with insulin, bleeding with warfarin, bradycardia with beta-blockers, sedation with antihistamines, postural hypotension with prazosin | | B – Bizarre | Unrelated to the known action | Not dose-related, unpredictable, uncommon, often serious | Anaphylaxis to penicillin, Stevens–Johnson syndrome with sulphonamides/nevirapine, haemolysis with primaquine in G6PD deficiency (idiosyncrasy), malignant hyperthermia with halothane | | C – Chronic (continuing) | Due to long-term use | Time- and dose-related | Adrenal suppression and Cushing's syndrome with long-term steroids, analgesic nephropathy, tardive dyskinesia | | D – Delayed | Appear long after use | Often after years | Teratogenicity (thalidomide – phocomelia), carcinogenicity, secondary leukaemia after alkylating agents | | E – End of use (withdrawal) | On sudden stopping | Rebound effects | Rebound hypertension after clonidine, angina after stopping beta-blockers, adrenal crisis after stopping steroids, seizures after stopping antiepileptics | | F – Failure of therapy | Unexpected lack of effect | Often due to interactions | Contraceptive failure with rifampicin, resistance to antibiotics |

2. Based on severity (Hartwig scale)

  • Mild – no change in treatment needed (e.g., mild nausea).
  • Moderate – change in treatment or longer hospital stay needed.
  • Severe – life-threatening, causes disability, or needs intensive care.

3. Common terms describing ADRs

  • Side effect – unwanted but predictable effect at therapeutic dose (dry mouth with atropine).
  • Toxic effect – due to overdose or accumulation (digoxin toxicity).
  • Intolerance – a toxic effect at a usual dose in a particular person (tinnitus with small dose of quinine).
  • Idiosyncrasy – genetically determined abnormal reaction (haemolysis with primaquine in G6PD deficiency).
  • Drug allergy (hypersensitivity) – immune-mediated reaction (penicillin rash, anaphylaxis).
  • Photosensitivity – skin reaction on exposure to sunlight (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones).
  • Drug dependence – compulsion to take a drug (opioids, benzodiazepines).
  • Iatrogenic disease – disease caused by drug treatment (drug-induced parkinsonism, peptic ulcer from NSAIDs).
  • Teratogenicity, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity.

C. Pharmacovigilance in India

  • Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI) – started in 2010 by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO); the National Coordination Centre is the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), Ghaziabad.
  • ADR Monitoring Centres (AMCs) in medical colleges and hospitals collect reports.
  • Reports are assessed for causality (WHO-UMC scale: certain, probable, possible, unlikely; or Naranjo algorithm) and sent to the WHO Uppsala Monitoring Centre global database.
  • Signals lead to regulatory action – label changes, warnings, restrictions or banning of drugs (e.g., many irrational fixed-dose combinations).
  • Any health professional – including nurses – and even patients can report through the Suspected ADR Reporting Form, the PvPI toll-free helpline (1800-180-3024) or the ADR PvPI mobile app.
  • A separate Materiovigilance Programme monitors adverse events from medical devices, and haemovigilance covers blood transfusion reactions.

D. Role of the nurse in monitoring and reporting ADRs 1. Prevention

  • Take a careful drug and allergy history before giving any medicine; document allergies clearly and use allergy wristbands.
  • Follow the "rights" of medication administration; double-check high-alert drugs.
  • Know the common ADRs, contraindications and interactions of drugs she gives.
  • Give test doses where hospital policy requires and keep anaphylaxis kits ready.

2. Detection and monitoring

  • Observe patients after drug administration – especially after the first dose of antibiotics, IV iron, antisera, contrast media and vaccines (watch for 15–30 minutes).
  • Monitor vital signs, skin, urine output, blood sugar, bleeding, mental status as relevant to the drug.
  • Check laboratory values (potassium, creatinine, INR, drug levels).
  • Listen to patients' complaints – a new symptom after starting a drug may be an ADR.

3. Immediate management

  • Stop the suspected drug (if safe) and inform the doctor at once.
  • Give emergency care (e.g., adrenaline in anaphylaxis) as per protocol.
  • Preserve the drug sample/batch number where relevant.

4. Reporting and documentation

  • Record the reaction in the nurse's notes and medication chart (time, drug, dose, reaction, action taken, outcome).
  • Fill the PvPI Suspected ADR Reporting Form (patient initials, age, sex; description of reaction; suspected drug with dose, route, batch, start and stop dates; concomitant drugs; outcome; reporter details) and send it to the ADR Monitoring Centre/pharmacovigilance cell.
  • Report even known or doubtful reactions – the system needs numbers to detect signals.

5. Patient education

  • Explain likely side effects and warning signs to watch for; advise patients to report reactions, carry allergy cards, avoid self-medication.

6. Participation

  • Attend training on pharmacovigilance; help in ADR audits; promote a culture of reporting without fear.

Conclusion Pharmacovigilance makes medicines safer for everyone after they reach the market. By preventing, detecting, managing and reporting adverse drug reactions, the nurse becomes an essential link in the drug-safety chain from the bedside to national and global databases.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the factors modifying drug action and dosage.
answer_html:
Introduction The same dose of the same drug does not produce the same effect in every person. A dose of morphine that relieves pain in one adult may stop breathing in an elderly patient with liver failure; a usual dose of primaquine may destroy the red cells of a G6PD-deficient child. Factors that modify drug action explain these differences and guide individualised dosing – a vital part of safe nursing practice.

1. Age (a) Neonates and infants

  • Immature liver enzymes and kidneys, more body water, less plasma protein, immature blood–brain barrier.

  • Examples: chloramphenicol causes "grey baby syndrome" (inability to conjugate); sulphonamides displace bilirubin causing kernicterus; greater sensitivity to opioids. (b) Children

  • Doses are calculated by body weight (mg/kg) or body surface area; tetracyclines stain developing teeth; fluoroquinolones may damage growing cartilage; aspirin can cause Reye's syndrome. (c) Elderly

  • Reduced kidney and liver function, less muscle and more fat, reduced homeostatic reserve, increased sensitivity of brain and heart.

  • More ADRs with sedatives, antihypertensives (falls), digoxin, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides; polypharmacy increases interactions.
  • "Start low, go slow."

2. Body weight and body surface area

  • Standard doses are for an average adult (about 60–70 kg); obese and very thin persons need adjustment.
  • Anticancer drugs are dosed by body surface area (mg/m²); many antibiotics by mg/kg.

3. Sex

  • Women have a higher proportion of body fat and lower body weight on average.
  • Pregnancy – altered absorption, increased volume of distribution and renal clearance; risk of teratogenicity (avoid unnecessary drugs, especially in the first trimester).
  • Lactation – drugs pass into milk (e.g., lithium, antithyroid drugs, tetracyclines).
  • Menstruation and menopause also influence some drugs.

4. Pathological (disease) states

  • Liver disease – reduced metabolism → accumulation of morphine, diazepam, chlorpromazine; low albumin increases free drug.
  • Kidney disease – accumulation of renally excreted drugs: aminoglycosides, digoxin, metformin, vancomycin – doses must be reduced according to creatinine clearance.
  • Heart failure – reduced liver and kidney blood flow.
  • Gastrointestinal disease – vomiting, diarrhoea, malabsorption reduce oral absorption.
  • Thyroid disease – hypothyroid patients are very sensitive to morphine and sedatives.
  • Malnutrition – low albumin increases free phenytoin and warfarin.
  • Fever, shock, burns alter absorption and distribution.

5. Genetic factors (pharmacogenetics)

  • G6PD deficiency – haemolysis with primaquine, dapsone, sulphonamides, nitrofurantoin.
  • Slow acetylators – isoniazid peripheral neuropathy; fast acetylators – reduced response.
  • Pseudocholinesterase deficiency – prolonged apnoea after succinylcholine.
  • Malignant hyperthermia – with halothane and succinylcholine.
  • HLA-B*1502 – carbamazepine-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome (common in some Asian groups).

6. Route, time and formulation

  • The same drug acts faster and more strongly IV than orally (bypasses absorption and first-pass metabolism).
  • Food reduces absorption of some drugs (ampicillin, rifampicin – give on an empty stomach) and increases others (griseofulvin with fatty meals).
  • Chronopharmacology – steroids given in the morning; simvastatin at night.
  • Formulation – sustained-release tablets must not be crushed.

7. Psychological factors

  • Faith in the doctor and nurse, anxiety and expectations influence responses – placebo (beneficial) and nocebo (harmful) effects.

8. Environmental factors and habits

  • Smoking induces liver enzymes (reduces theophylline levels).
  • Alcohol – acute use inhibits and chronic use induces enzymes; adds to sedation.
  • Altitude, temperature and exposure to pesticides.

9. Repeated administration – cumulation and tolerance

  • Cumulation – drugs eliminated slowly accumulate (digoxin, phenobarbitone).
  • Tolerance – larger doses needed for the same effect (opioids, nitrates); cross-tolerance between related drugs; tachyphylaxis – rapidly developing tolerance (ephedrine).

10. Drug interactions and other drugs

  • Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) reduce effects of oral contraceptives and warfarin; enzyme inhibitors (erythromycin, fluconazole, ciprofloxacin) increase toxicity.
  • Synergism and antagonism between drugs.

11. Dose and individual variation

  • Response increases with dose up to a limit; some drugs have a narrow therapeutic index (digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, warfarin, aminoglycosides) and need monitoring of blood levels.
  • Idiosyncrasy and drug allergy are unpredictable individual factors.

Summary table | Factor | Example | |---|---| | Neonate | Grey baby syndrome with chloramphenicol | | Elderly | Falls with sedatives/antihypertensives | | Pregnancy | Thalidomide phocomelia | | Liver disease | Prolonged action of morphine | | Kidney disease | Aminoglycoside toxicity | | Genetics | Primaquine haemolysis in G6PD deficiency | | Food | Reduced absorption of rifampicin | | Smoking | Reduced theophylline levels | | Tolerance | Increasing doses of opioids | | Interaction | Rifampicin making oral contraceptives fail |

Nursing implications

  1. Check age, weight, pregnancy/lactation status, allergies, liver and kidney function before giving drugs; calculate paediatric doses carefully and double-check.
  2. Observe the elderly closely for confusion, falls and hypotension.
  3. Give drugs at the right time in relation to food.
  4. Monitor drug levels and laboratory values for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs.
  5. Ask about smoking, alcohol, herbal products and other medicines.
  6. Educate patients about adherence, interactions and warning signs.

Conclusion Drug response varies with the patient's age, weight, sex, disease, genes, habits and other drugs. Considering these factors allows the dose to be tailored to the individual – the essence of safe and effective drug therapy.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain teratogenicity and iatrogenic disease with an example of each. List two disadvantages of the sublingual route.
answer_html:
A. Teratogenicity (2 marks) Definition: Teratogenicity is the capacity of a drug to cause fetal abnormalities (birth defects) when taken by the mother during pregnancy. Key points

  • Greatest risk during organogenesis – the 3rd to 8th week after conception (often before the woman knows she is pregnant). Drugs taken in the first two weeks usually cause "all-or-none" effects (abortion or no effect); later drugs affect growth and function.
  • Examples
    • Thalidomide – phocomelia (seal-like limbs) – the classic tragedy of 1960.
    • Warfarin – fetal warfarin syndrome (nasal hypoplasia, bone defects).
    • Sodium valproate – neural tube defects; phenytoin – fetal hydantoin syndrome.
    • Isotretinoin – severe craniofacial and heart defects.
    • ACE inhibitors – fetal kidney damage; tetracyclines – discoloured teeth; streptomycin – deafness; alcohol – fetal alcohol syndrome.
  • Prevention: avoid all unnecessary drugs in pregnancy (especially first trimester); use drugs with proven safety (paracetamol, penicillins); pregnancy test before prescribing known teratogens; folic acid supplementation; counsel women of child-bearing age.

B. Iatrogenic disease (2 marks) Definition: Iatrogenic disease (Greek iatros = physician) is a disease or harm caused by medical treatment – by drugs, procedures or advice – rather than by the patient's original illness. Examples

  • Drug-induced parkinsonism with phenothiazines or metoclopramide.
  • Peptic ulcer and GI bleeding with NSAIDs and corticosteroids.
  • Cushing's syndrome with long-term steroid therapy.
  • Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity with aminoglycosides.
  • Pseudomembranous colitis after broad-spectrum antibiotics; hypoglycaemia due to insulin overdose. Prevention: rational prescribing, correct dosing, monitoring, avoiding unnecessary drugs and procedures.

C. Disadvantages of the sublingual route (1 mark)

  1. Only small doses of potent, lipid-soluble drugs can be given (e.g., nitroglycerin, buprenorphine).
  2. Bitter or irritant drugs cannot be given; may irritate or ulcerate the oral mucosa.
  3. If the tablet is swallowed with saliva, the advantage of bypassing the liver is lost.
  4. The patient cannot eat, drink, talk or smoke while the tablet dissolves.
  5. Not suitable for unconscious, uncooperative or very young patients; frequent dosing is inconvenient.

Nursing points Ask every woman of child-bearing age about pregnancy before giving drugs; watch for iatrogenic effects; teach patients to keep sublingual tablets under the tongue until fully dissolved and not to swallow saliva immediately.

Conclusion Teratogenicity and iatrogenic disease remind us that drugs must always be used with caution, and the sublingual route, though rapid, has definite limitations.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain drug interactions with examples and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Definition A drug interaction is a modification of the effect of one drug by another drug (or by food, alcohol or herbal products) given before, together with or after it. The result may be increased effect (toxicity), decreased effect (therapeutic failure) or occasionally a beneficial effect.

1. Pharmaceutical (in vitro) interactions – incompatibility

  • Physical or chemical reactions outside the body, when drugs are mixed in a syringe or infusion.
  • Examples: phenytoin precipitates in dextrose; penicillin and aminoglycosides inactivate each other in the same infusion; calcium and sodium bicarbonate form a precipitate; diazepam precipitates in IV fluids; no drugs should be added to blood.

2. Pharmacokinetic interactions – one drug alters the absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion of another.

  • Absorption: antacids, iron, calcium and milk chelate tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones; metoclopramide speeds absorption of paracetamol.
  • Distribution (protein-binding displacement): aspirin and sulphonamides displace warfarin (bleeding); sulphonamides displace bilirubin in neonates.
  • Metabolism:
    • Enzyme inducers – rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, chronic alcohol, smoking – speed metabolism of other drugs → oral contraceptive failure, reduced warfarin effect.
    • Enzyme inhibitors – erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole/fluconazole, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, grapefruit juice – slow metabolism → toxicity of warfarin, theophylline, statins.
  • Excretion: probenecid reduces renal excretion of penicillin (prolongs action – used beneficially); thiazides reduce lithium excretion (lithium toxicity); NSAIDs reduce methotrexate excretion.

3. Pharmacodynamic interactions – drugs act on the same receptor or system.

  • Synergism
    • Additive – effect equals the sum (aspirin + paracetamol for pain).
    • Potentiation (supra-additive) – sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim (cotrimoxazole); levodopa + carbidopa; alcohol + benzodiazepines (dangerous sedation).
  • Antagonism
    • Receptor – naloxone reverses morphine; atropine blocks organophosphate effects.
    • Chemical – protamine neutralises heparin.
    • Physiological – adrenaline counteracts histamine in anaphylaxis.

4. Food–drug interactions

  • MAO inhibitors + tyramine-rich foods (cheese, wine) → hypertensive crisis ("cheese reaction").
  • Warfarin + vitamin K-rich green leafy vegetables → reduced effect.
  • Tetracycline + milk → reduced absorption; alcohol + metronidazole → disulfiram-like reaction.

5. Clinical significance

  • Most dangerous with narrow-therapeutic-index drugs – warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, aminoglycosides.
  • Elderly patients on many drugs (polypharmacy) are at greatest risk.

6. Nursing implications

  1. Take a complete medication history including over-the-counter, herbal and Ayurvedic products.
  2. Never mix drugs in one syringe or infusion unless compatibility is known; flush lines between drugs.
  3. Space doses – give antacids/iron/calcium at least 2 hours apart from tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
  4. Monitor INR, drug levels, blood sugar and BP when interacting drugs are added or stopped.
  5. Advise women on rifampicin to use additional or alternative contraception.
  6. Educate patients about alcohol and food interactions.

Conclusion Drug interactions are common and often preventable; awareness and careful administration by the nurse prevent toxicity and treatment failure.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the drug laws and schedules in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Drugs are powerful substances that can heal or harm; therefore their manufacture, import, sale, storage and use are controlled by law. In India the central regulator is the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), headed by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), along with state drug controllers.

1. Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945

  • Regulates the import, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs and cosmetics to ensure their quality, safety and efficacy.
  • Prohibits sale of spurious, adulterated and misbranded drugs; provides for licensing and inspection.
  • Important schedules under the Rules: | Schedule | Content | |---|---| | Schedule C and C1 | Biological products – vaccines, sera, insulin, blood products; special storage and labelling | | Schedule G | Drugs to be used under medical supervision (label: "It is dangerous to take this preparation except under medical supervision") | | Schedule H | Prescription-only drugs – label "Rx" and "Schedule H drug – to be sold by retail on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner only" (antibiotics, antihypertensives, etc.) | | Schedule H1 (2013) | Third/fourth-generation antibiotics, carbapenems, anti-TB drugs and certain habit-forming drugs; red-bordered warning label; pharmacist must keep a register of prescriber, patient and quantity for 3 years – to curb antimicrobial resistance and misuse | | Schedule X | Narcotic and psychotropic drugs liable to abuse – label "XRx"; prescription in duplicate, one copy retained by the pharmacist; stored under lock and key | | Schedule M | Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) | | Schedule F | Requirements for blood banks and blood products | | Schedule J | Diseases for which no drug may claim to prevent or cure (e.g., cancer, AIDS, diabetes) | | Schedule P | Life period (shelf life) of drugs |
  • New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 now govern approval of new drugs and clinical trials.

2. Pharmacy Act, 1948

  • Regulates the profession of pharmacy; only registered pharmacists may compound and dispense medicines; establishes the Pharmacy Council of India.

3. Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985

  • Controls opium, morphine, codeine, pethidine, cannabis, cocaine and psychotropic substances.
  • Strict penalties for illegal production, possession and trafficking.
  • The 2014 amendment made "essential narcotic drugs" (morphine, fentanyl, methadone) easier to obtain for pain relief and palliative care.

4. Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954

  • Prohibits advertisements claiming magical cures for specified diseases.

5. Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013

  • The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) fixes ceiling prices of essential medicines (NLEM).

Nursing implications

  • Nurses administer drugs only on the written order of a registered medical practitioner; they do not prescribe or sell drugs.
  • Narcotic and controlled drugs must be kept in a double-locked cupboard, with a narcotic register; counts are checked and signed at every shift handover; empty ampoules are returned to pharmacy; wastage is witnessed and recorded.
  • Check labels, expiry dates and storage conditions (Schedule C drugs like vaccines and insulin in the refrigerator).
  • Report spurious or substandard drugs.

Conclusion Drug laws protect patients from unsafe medicines and misuse; nurses must know and follow them, especially for controlled drugs.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the concept of rational use of drugs and essential medicines.
answer_html:
A. Rational use of drugs Definition (WHO, 1985): Rational use of medicines requires that "patients receive medications appropriate to their clinical needs, in doses that meet their own individual requirements, for an adequate period of time, and at the lowest cost to them and their community."

1. Elements of rational use – "right" Right diagnosis → right drug (effective, safe, suitable, cheap) → right dose, route, frequency and duration → right patient information → right monitoring.

2. Examples of irrational drug use

  • Polypharmacy – too many drugs per patient.
  • Overuse of antibiotics for viral fevers, colds and diarrhoea (major cause of antimicrobial resistance).
  • Unnecessary injections when oral drugs would work (risk of infection and abscess).
  • Irrational fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) – India has banned hundreds of such combinations.
  • Use of tonics and vitamins without need; brand-name prescribing of costly drugs.
  • Self-medication and over-the-counter sale of prescription drugs; incomplete courses.
  • Not following standard treatment guidelines.

3. Steps to promote rational use

  • Standard treatment guidelines (e.g., ICMR, national programmes).
  • Essential medicines lists and hospital formularies.
  • Drug and therapeutics committees; antimicrobial stewardship.
  • Education of prescribers, nurses and the public; independent drug information.
  • Prescription audits and feedback; regulation of promotion.

B. Essential medicines Definition (WHO): Essential medicines are those that satisfy the priority health-care needs of the population; they are selected considering disease prevalence, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness, and should be available at all times, in adequate amounts, appropriate dosage forms, assured quality and at a price the individual and community can afford.

1. Lists

  • WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – first published in 1977, revised every two years.
  • National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), India – first in 1996; the NLEM 2022 contains 384 medicines, categorised for primary (P), secondary (S) and tertiary (T) levels of care.

2. Benefits

  • Better access and quality; lower cost through bulk purchase and price control (NPPA).
  • Easier training, supply and stock management; promotes rational prescribing.

3. Related initiatives in India

  • Free Drugs Service Initiative under the National Health Mission.
  • Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana – quality generic medicines at low prices through Jan Aushadhi Kendras.

Role of the nurse Give medicines exactly as prescribed, avoid unnecessary injections, educate patients about completing courses and avoiding self-medication, and report irrational or unsafe practices.

Conclusion Rational use of essential medicines delivers the greatest health benefit at the lowest cost and risk.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Define pharmacology. Explain its branches and the sources of drugs.
answer_html:
Definitions

  • Pharmacology (Greek pharmakon = drug, logos = study) is the science of drugs – their sources, properties, actions on the body, fate in the body, uses and adverse effects.
  • Drug (WHO) – "any substance or product that is used or intended to be used to modify or explore physiological systems or pathological states for the benefit of the recipient."

A. Branches of pharmacology

  1. Pharmacokinetics – what the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion).
  2. Pharmacodynamics – what the drug does to the body (actions and mechanisms).
  3. Pharmacotherapeutics – use of drugs in the prevention and treatment of disease.
  4. Chemotherapy – drugs against microbes, parasites and cancer cells.
  5. Toxicology – poisonous effects of drugs and chemicals, their diagnosis and treatment.
  6. Clinical pharmacology – study of drugs in humans (clinical trials, rational use).
  7. Pharmacy – preparation, compounding and dispensing of medicines.
  8. Pharmacognosy – study of drugs from natural (plant and animal) sources.
  9. Pharmacogenetics/pharmacogenomics – genetic basis of variation in drug response.
  10. Pharmacoepidemiology and pharmacoeconomics – drug use and costs in populations.
  11. Posology – study of doses.

B. Sources of drugs 1. Plants (most ancient source) | Drug | Plant | |---|---| | Morphine, codeine | Opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) | | Digoxin | Foxglove (Digitalis lanata) | | Atropine | Belladonna (Atropa belladonna) | | Quinine | Cinchona bark | | Reserpine | Rauwolfia serpentina (Indian snakeroot) | | Vincristine | Periwinkle (Vinca rosea) | | Artemisinin | Artemisia annua | | Ephedrine | Ephedra |

2. Animals

  • Insulin (earlier from pig and cattle pancreas), heparin (pig intestine), thyroid extract, antisera and antivenom (horse serum), cod-liver oil (vitamins A and D), gonadotrophins.

3. Minerals

  • Iron, calcium, magnesium sulphate, potassium chloride, zinc, iodine, kaolin, liquid paraffin.

4. Microorganisms

  • Antibiotics – penicillin (Penicillium), streptomycin (Streptomyces griseus); vaccines.

5. Synthetic and semi-synthetic

  • Synthetic – most modern drugs: aspirin, paracetamol, sulphonamides, fluoroquinolones, antihypertensives.
  • Semi-synthetic – natural compounds chemically modified: ampicillin and amoxicillin (from penicillin nucleus).

6. Biotechnology (genetic engineering)

  • Recombinant human insulin, hepatitis B vaccine, erythropoietin, interferons, growth hormone, monoclonal antibodies.

7. Human sources

  • Immunoglobulins, albumin, clotting factors from donated blood.

C. Nursing relevance

  • Knowledge of the source warns about allergy (horse-serum antivenom and antisera – test dose; pork-derived heparin and religious concerns).
  • Recombinant products (insulin, vaccines) need refrigeration; plant alkaloids like atropine and digoxin have a narrow margin of safety.

Conclusion Drugs come from plants, animals, minerals, microbes, laboratories and genetic engineering; pharmacology and its branches study them so that they can be used safely and effectively.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: What are orphan drugs? Give examples.
answer_html:
Orphan drugs are drugs developed to diagnose, prevent or treat rare diseases – conditions affecting so few people that companies have little commercial interest in making them. In India, the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 define an orphan drug as one intended for a condition affecting not more than five lakh persons in the country; governments give incentives (fee waivers, faster approval) to encourage their development.

Examples

  • Enzyme replacement therapies – imiglucerase (Gaucher's disease), agalsidase (Fabry disease), alglucosidase alfa (Pompe disease).
  • Antidotes – fomepizole (methanol poisoning), digoxin immune Fab (digoxin toxicity).
  • Nusinersen (spinal muscular atrophy).

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Define prodrug. Give examples.
answer_html:
A prodrug is an inactive (or much less active) drug that is converted into its active form inside the body, usually by metabolism in the liver or tissues.

Examples | Prodrug | Active form | |---|---| | Levodopa | Dopamine (in brain) | | Enalapril | Enalaprilat | | Prednisone | Prednisolone | | Codeine | Morphine | | Clopidogrel | Active thiol metabolite | | Valacyclovir | Acyclovir | | Omeprazole | Active sulphenamide (in acidic parietal cell) |

Advantages: better absorption (valacyclovir), crossing the blood–brain barrier (levodopa), longer action, reduced toxicity or better taste.

Nursing point: prodrugs need normal liver function for activation – e.g., clopidogrel may be less effective in poor metabolisers and with interacting drugs.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: What is tachyphylaxis? Give examples.
answer_html:
Tachyphylaxis (acute tolerance) is the rapid reduction in response to a drug on repeated administration at short intervals, which cannot be overcome by increasing the dose.

Examples

  • Ephedrine, tyramine and amphetamine – indirectly acting sympathomimetics that deplete noradrenaline stores.
  • Nitrates (nitroglycerin) on continuous use – hence a nitrate-free interval is advised.
  • Nicotine, desmopressin.

Difference from tolerance: tolerance develops slowly (days to weeks) and can be overcome by increasing the dose (e.g., opioids, alcohol).

Nursing point: remove nitrate patches for 8–12 hours (usually at night) to prevent loss of effect.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Classify antiseptics and disinfectants according to their chemical nature. Explain their mechanisms of action and the factors that influence their activity.
answer_html:
Introduction Antiseptics and disinfectants are chemical agents used to destroy or inhibit microorganisms. They are among the oldest drugs in medicine – Lister's carbolic acid (1867) made surgery safe. Nurses use them every day for skin preparation, wound care, hand hygiene and cleaning equipment and surfaces, so they must understand which agent to use, how it acts and what reduces its effect.

Definitions

  • Antiseptic – a chemical that inhibits or kills microorganisms on living tissues (skin, mucosa, wounds) without significant harm to tissues – e.g., povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine.
  • Disinfectant – a chemical used on inanimate objects to destroy pathogenic microorganisms (usually not spores) – e.g., sodium hypochlorite, glutaraldehyde.
  • Sterilant – kills all forms including spores (ethylene oxide).
  • -cidal (kills) versus -static (inhibits growth).
  • The same chemical may act as an antiseptic at low concentration and a disinfectant at high concentration.

A. Classification according to chemical nature | Group | Examples | Main uses | |---|---|---| | 1. Alcohols | Ethyl alcohol 70%, isopropyl alcohol 60–70% | Skin antisepsis, hand rubs, thermometers | | 2. Aldehydes | Formaldehyde (formalin), glutaraldehyde 2%, ortho-phthalaldehyde | High-level disinfection of endoscopes; tissue preservation | | 3. Phenols and derivatives | Phenol (carbolic acid), cresol, lysol, chloroxylenol (Dettol), triclosan, hexachlorophene | Floors, toilets, drains; household antiseptic | | 4. Halogens | Chlorine compounds – sodium hypochlorite, bleaching powder, chloramine; iodine compounds – tincture iodine, povidone-iodine | Blood spills, water disinfection; skin and wound antisepsis | | 5. Oxidising agents | Hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate, peracetic acid, benzoyl peroxide | Wound cleaning, high-level disinfection | | 6. Biguanides | Chlorhexidine, polyhexanide | Hand scrub, skin prep, mouthwash | | 7. Surface-active agents (detergents) | Cationic – cetrimide, benzalkonium chloride (quaternary ammonium compounds); anionic – soaps | Cleaning, wound washing, surfaces | | 8. Acids | Boric acid, acetic acid, benzoic acid, salicylic acid | Ear infections, Pseudomonas wounds (acetic acid), fungal infections (Whitfield's ointment) | | 9. Heavy metals | Silver nitrate, silver sulphadiazine, mercurochrome (obsolete) | Burns; neonatal eye prophylaxis (historically) | | 10. Dyes | Gentian violet (crystal violet), brilliant green, acriflavine | Skin and mucosal fungal infections (thrush), wounds | | 11. Gases | Ethylene oxide, formaldehyde vapour | Sterilisation of heat-sensitive items; fumigation |

B. Mechanisms of action

  1. Coagulation and denaturation of microbial proteins
    • Alcohols, phenols, acids, heavy metals and heat.
    • Alcohol works best at 70% – water is needed for protein denaturation and penetration; absolute alcohol only dehydrates the surface.
  2. Oxidation of cell components
    • Halogens (chlorine, iodine), hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate oxidise enzymes and proteins (–SH groups).
    • Hydrogen peroxide releases nascent oxygen, which is toxic especially to anaerobes.
  3. Damage to the cell membrane (increased permeability)
    • Chlorhexidine, cationic detergents (quaternary ammonium compounds) and phenols disrupt the lipid membrane → leakage of cell contents.
  4. Alkylation of proteins and nucleic acids
    • Aldehydes (glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde) and ethylene oxide alkylate amino, carboxyl and sulphydryl groups → kill spores too.
  5. Halogenation
    • Iodine combines with tyrosine residues; chlorine forms hypochlorous acid.
  6. Precipitation of proteins and binding to enzymes
    • Heavy metals (silver ions) bind sulphydryl groups of enzymes and DNA.
  7. Interference with metabolism
    • Dyes interfere with nucleic acids and cell division.

C. Factors that influence the activity of antiseptics and disinfectants

  1. Concentration – activity increases with concentration up to an optimum (except alcohol, best at 70%); too dilute solutions are ineffective and may allow bacterial growth (Pseudomonas in weak cetrimide).
  2. Contact time – each agent needs a minimum time (e.g., 2% glutaraldehyde 20 minutes for high-level disinfection; povidone-iodine about 2 minutes on skin).
  3. Presence of organic matter – blood, pus, faeces and mucus inactivate many agents (especially chlorine and quaternary compounds) – hence cleaning before disinfection.
  4. Type and number of microorganisms – spores > mycobacteria > non-enveloped viruses > fungi > vegetative bacteria > enveloped viruses (most to least resistant); heavy contamination needs longer time.
  5. Temperature – activity increases with temperature.
  6. pH – glutaraldehyde is active in alkaline pH; hypochlorite better in slightly acidic pH; phenols in acidic pH.
  7. Nature of the surface – crevices, porous materials and biofilms protect microbes.
  8. Interfering substances – soaps inactivate cationic detergents and chlorhexidine; hard water reduces activity.
  9. Stability and age of solution – hypochlorite loses strength quickly (prepare daily); activated glutaraldehyde lasts about 14 days.

D. Evaluation of disinfectants

  • Phenol coefficient (Rideal–Walker and Chick–Martin tests) compares the killing power of a disinfectant with phenol.
  • In-use tests check whether disinfectants in use in wards are still effective.

Nursing responsibilities

  1. Use the right agent at the right dilution; label containers with name, strength and date of preparation; never top up old solutions.
  2. Clean before disinfecting; ensure adequate contact time.
  3. Avoid mixing agents (e.g., hypochlorite with acids releases chlorine gas).
  4. Protect skin and eyes (gloves, goggles); ensure ventilation with glutaraldehyde and formalin.
  5. Do not use irritant agents on mucosa or open wounds unnecessarily; observe for allergy (iodine, chlorhexidine).
  6. Store in cool, dark places in closed containers.

Conclusion Antiseptics and disinfectants belong to many chemical groups and act mainly by denaturing proteins, oxidising cell components, damaging membranes or alkylating nucleic acids. Their effect depends on concentration, time, organic matter, organism type, temperature and pH – knowledge that ensures their correct and safe use.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Describe the qualities of an ideal antiseptic and the role of the nurse in the use of antiseptics.
answer_html:
Introduction An antiseptic is a chemical applied on living tissues to kill or inhibit microorganisms. No single antiseptic is perfect, but the closer an agent comes to the "ideal", the safer and more useful it is in practice.

A. Qualities of an ideal antiseptic

  1. Broad spectrum – active against bacteria (Gram-positive and Gram-negative), fungi, viruses, mycobacteria and ideally spores.
  2. Rapid action with sustained (residual) effect on the skin.
  3. Active in the presence of organic matter – blood, pus, serum, soap.
  4. Non-toxic and non-irritant to skin and tissues; should not delay wound healing.
  5. Non-allergenic (no sensitisation).
  6. Not absorbed into the body in significant amounts (no systemic toxicity).
  7. Chemically stable, long shelf life.
  8. Good penetration into crevices and hair follicles.
  9. Does not stain skin or clothes; pleasant or no odour.
  10. Compatible with soaps and other agents; does not corrode instruments.
  11. No development of resistance by microorganisms.
  12. Cheap and easily available; soluble in water.

B. Commonly used antiseptics (examples)

  • Povidone-iodine 5–10% – skin preparation, wounds.
  • Chlorhexidine 2–4% (with or without alcohol) – hand scrub, skin prep, mouthwash.
  • 70% alcohol – skin before injections.
  • Hydrogen peroxide 3% – wound cleaning.
  • Cetrimide–chlorhexidine (Savlon) – wound washing.

C. Role of the nurse in the use of antiseptics

  1. Select the appropriate antiseptic for the purpose (skin prep, wound, mucosa) as per hospital policy.
  2. Prepare correct dilutions with clean/sterile water; label with name, strength, date and time; discard as per policy.
  3. Use aseptic technique – sterile containers, forceps and swabs; never dip used swabs back into the solution.
  4. Allow the antiseptic adequate contact time and drying (e.g., chlorhexidine–alcohol before cannulation and surgery).
  5. Clean before applying – remove blood and debris, as organic matter reduces activity.
  6. Check for allergies (iodine, chlorhexidine) and observe for irritation or burns; avoid strong antiseptics on granulating wounds and mucous membranes.
  7. Avoid pooling of alcohol-based preparations under the patient (fire risk with diathermy).
  8. Store in tightly closed containers away from heat and light; never top up partially used bottles.
  9. Educate patients and families on simple home wound care and hand hygiene.

Conclusion Knowing the qualities of an ideal antiseptic helps the nurse choose wisely, and correct use ensures maximum benefit with minimum harm.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the pharmacology of hydrogen peroxide and potassium permanganate.
answer_html:
Introduction Hydrogen peroxide and potassium permanganate are oxidising agents. They release oxygen which oxidises essential components of microorganisms. They are inexpensive and widely used in Indian hospitals and homes.

A. Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)

  1. Preparations – 3% solution ("10 volumes" – releases 10 times its volume of oxygen); 6% and higher strengths for disinfection.
  2. Mechanism – the enzyme catalase in tissues breaks H₂O₂ into water and nascent oxygen, which oxidises microbial proteins and lipids; the effervescence (frothing) mechanically lifts debris, pus and clots.
  3. Spectrum – active especially against anaerobes; short-lived action.
  4. Uses
    • Cleaning of wounds, ulcers and abscess cavities (especially foul, anaerobic wounds).
    • Removal of ear wax (diluted) and cleaning of the mouth (1.5% mouthwash) in Vincent's infection.
    • 6–7.5% for high-level disinfection of equipment; vaporised hydrogen peroxide for room fumigation.
  5. Adverse effects and precautions
    • May damage new granulation tissue and delay healing if used repeatedly.
    • Do not use in closed body cavities or deep sinuses under pressure – risk of gas (oxygen) embolism.
    • Store in dark, cool place (decomposes with light and heat); concentrated solutions burn skin.

B. Potassium permanganate (KMnO₄)

  1. Preparation – purple crystals; used as a dilute solution 1:10,000 (light pink colour) to 1:4,000.
  2. Mechanism – releases oxygen and manganese dioxide; oxidises organic matter and microbes; also astringent (dries weeping lesions).
  3. Uses
    • Wet dressings and soaks for weeping eczema, infected ulcers, fungal infections of feet, pemphigus and other oozing skin lesions (dries exudate).
    • Sitz baths for perineal wounds (in some practices).
    • Gastric lavage in some poisonings (alkaloids, phosphorus) – historical use.
    • Disinfection of water/fruits (old practice).
  4. Adverse effects and precautions
    • Stains skin, nails and clothes brown.
    • Crystals or strong solutions are corrosive – always dissolve fully and check that the solution is light pink before use; never apply crystals directly.
    • Ingestion of concentrated solution causes burns of mouth and stomach.

Nursing responsibilities Prepare correct dilutions freshly, check colour/strength, protect eyes, use only on intended areas, document and observe for irritation.

Conclusion Both agents act by releasing oxygen; H₂O₂ is useful for cleaning dirty wounds and KMnO₄ for drying weeping skin lesions – when used at the right strength.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Write four uses of povidone-iodine.
answer_html:
Povidone-iodine is an iodophor (iodine complexed with polyvinylpyrrolidone) that slowly releases free iodine; broad-spectrum (bacteria, fungi, viruses, some spores).

Uses

  1. Pre-operative skin preparation and before invasive procedures (cannulation, catheterisation, lumbar puncture).
  2. Surgical hand scrub (7.5% scrub solution).
  3. Wound and burn antisepsis; treatment of minor cuts and infected ulcers (5–10% solution, ointment).
  4. Vaginal and perineal preparation before delivery/procedures; mouthwash/gargle (1%) in oral infections.
  5. Disinfection of vial tops and cord care in some settings.

Precautions: iodine allergy, thyroid disorders, large burns, neonates (absorption); stains skin.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: What is phenol coefficient?
answer_html:
Phenol coefficient is a measure of the germicidal efficiency of a disinfectant compared with that of phenol under standard laboratory conditions.

Method (Rideal–Walker test)

  • Different dilutions of the test disinfectant and of phenol are allowed to act on a standard culture (Salmonella Typhi) for fixed times; subcultures show which dilution kills the organism.
  • Phenol coefficient = highest dilution of the test disinfectant that kills the organism ÷ highest dilution of phenol that kills it in the same time.
  • A coefficient greater than 1 means the disinfectant is more effective than phenol.

Limitation: tested without organic matter; the Chick–Martin test adds organic matter (yeast) to imitate real conditions.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: Classify the drugs used in peptic ulcer disease. Describe the mechanism of action, uses, adverse effects and nursing responsibilities of proton pump inhibitors, H2-receptor blockers and antacids.

diagram.caption: Gastric parietal cell showing sites of action of anti-ulcer drugs
labels: H2 receptor (histamine) – H2 blockers; M3 receptor (acetylcholine); gastrin receptor; H+/K+ ATPase proton pump – PPIs; antacids neutralising acid in lumen; sucralfate coating ulcer base

answer_html:
Introduction Peptic ulcer disease (gastric and duodenal ulcers) and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) are very common in India. They result from an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs, smoking, stress) and protective factors (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow). Drugs either reduce acid, neutralise acid, protect the mucosa or eradicate H. pylori.

A. Classification of drugs used in peptic ulcer

  1. Drugs that reduce gastric acid secretion
    • Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs): omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole.
    • Potassium-competitive acid blocker: vonoprazan (newer).
    • H2-receptor antagonists: famotidine, cimetidine, nizatidine (ranitidine has been withdrawn in many countries because of an impurity concern).
    • Anticholinergics: pirenzepine (rarely used).
    • Prostaglandin analogue: misoprostol (prevents NSAID ulcers).
  2. Drugs that neutralise gastric acid – antacids
    • Systemic: sodium bicarbonate.
    • Non-systemic: aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, magnesium trisilicate, calcium carbonate (often Al + Mg combinations).
  3. Ulcer-protective (cytoprotective) drugs
    • Sucralfate, colloidal bismuth subcitrate.
  4. Anti-H. pylori drugs
    • Amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole/tinidazole, tetracycline, bismuth – always given with a PPI.

B. Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole, pantoprazole) 1. Mechanism of action

  • PPIs are prodrugs; they are absorbed and reach the acidic canaliculi of parietal cells, where they are converted into an active form (sulphenamide).
  • This binds irreversibly (covalently) to the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) – the final common step of acid secretion.

  • Both basal and food-stimulated acid secretion fall by more than 90%; the effect of one dose lasts 24–48 hours until new pumps are made. 2. Uses

  • Peptic ulcer (duodenal and gastric) – 4–8 weeks.

  • GERD and reflux oesophagitis – most effective drugs.
  • Eradication of H. pylori – e.g., PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 14 days (triple therapy) or bismuth-based quadruple therapy.
  • Prevention of NSAID-induced ulcers; stress ulcer prophylaxis in ICU patients.
  • Zollinger–Ellison syndrome; upper GI bleeding from ulcers (IV pantoprazole after endoscopy).

  • Aspiration prophylaxis before general anaesthesia/caesarean section. 3. Adverse effects

  • Generally well tolerated: headache, nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain.

  • Long-term use: vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, osteoporosis and fractures, increased risk of pneumonia and C. difficile diarrhoea, rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping.
  • Interaction: omeprazole may reduce the effect of clopidogrel (pantoprazole preferred).

C. H2-receptor antagonists (e.g., famotidine) 1. Mechanism – competitively block histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells → reduce acid secretion, especially nocturnal acid; less potent than PPIs. 2. Uses – mild GERD, peptic ulcer (alternative to PPIs), pre-anaesthetic medication, urticaria (with H1 blockers). 3. Adverse effects – headache, dizziness, diarrhoea, confusion in the elderly.

  • Cimetidine – enzyme inhibitor (raises warfarin, theophylline levels), anti-androgenic effects (gynaecomastia, impotence).
  • Dose reduction in kidney disease.

D. Antacids 1. Mechanism – weak bases that neutralise gastric HCl, raise gastric pH and reduce pepsin activity; give quick symptom relief. 2. Uses – dyspepsia, heartburn, adjunct for ulcer pain relief, GERD (symptomatic). 3. Adverse effects

  • Aluminium hydroxide – constipation, hypophosphataemia.
  • Magnesium salts – diarrhoea; hypermagnesaemia in kidney failure.
  • Combination (Al + Mg) balances bowel effects.
  • Sodium bicarbonate – systemic alkalosis, sodium load (avoid in heart failure, hypertension), CO₂ belching, rebound acidity.
  • Calcium carbonate – constipation, hypercalcaemia, milk–alkali syndrome, rebound acidity. 4. Interactions – reduce absorption of iron, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, digoxin, levothyroxine – separate doses by at least 2 hours.

E. Ulcer protectives (in brief)

  • Sucralfate – forms a sticky protective coat over the ulcer base in acid; give on an empty stomach 1 hour before meals; causes constipation; avoid giving with antacids within 30 minutes.

F. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Timing
    • PPIs – 30–60 minutes before breakfast (pumps are activated by food); swallow whole – do not crush enteric-coated tablets/capsules.
    • H2 blockers – at bedtime or twice daily as ordered.
    • Antacids – 1 and 3 hours after meals and at bedtime; shake suspensions well; follow with water.
  2. Give IV pantoprazole as a slow injection or infusion as ordered; check compatibility.
  3. Monitor for relief of pain, signs of GI bleeding (malaena, haematemesis, falling Hb), bowel habits (constipation/diarrhoea), electrolytes (Mg, Ca) in long-term therapy.
  4. Space other drugs from antacids and sucralfate.
  5. Ensure completion of H. pylori eradication therapy (14 days) and counsel about side effects (metallic taste, dark stools with bismuth).
  6. Health education
    • Avoid NSAIDs, smoking and alcohol; eat regular small meals; avoid late-night heavy meals and lying down after meals (GERD); elevate head end of bed.
    • Do not use PPIs long-term without medical review; report black stools, vomiting of blood, weight loss or difficulty swallowing immediately.

Conclusion PPIs are the most powerful acid suppressants, H2 blockers are useful alternatives, and antacids give quick symptomatic relief. With correct timing, monitoring, H. pylori eradication and lifestyle advice, most peptic ulcers heal completely.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: Classify antiemetic drugs. Describe the pharmacology of commonly used antiemetics and the nurse's responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Pathways of vomiting and sites of action of antiemetics
labels: higher centres; drugs acting at each site

answer_html:
Introduction Nausea and vomiting are distressing symptoms caused by many conditions – pregnancy, motion sickness, gastroenteritis, surgery and anaesthesia, cancer chemotherapy, radiotherapy, drugs (opioids), migraine and raised intracranial pressure. Persistent vomiting leads to dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, aspiration and malnutrition. Antiemetics are drugs that prevent or relieve nausea and vomiting.

A. Physiology of vomiting (basis of drug action)

  • The vomiting centre in the medulla coordinates vomiting.
  • It receives impulses from:
    1. Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) in the area postrema – outside the blood–brain barrier; responds to drugs and toxins in blood; rich in dopamine D2, serotonin 5-HT3 and neurokinin NK1 receptors.
    2. Gastrointestinal tract – irritation releases serotonin → vagal afferents (5-HT3).
    3. Vestibular apparatus – motion sickness (histamine H1 and muscarinic receptors).
    4. Higher centres – sights, smells, fear, anticipation.

B. Classification of antiemetics | Class | Examples | Main uses | |---|---|---| | 1. 5-HT3 antagonists | Ondansetron, granisetron, palonosetron | Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, post-operative vomiting | | 2. Dopamine D2 antagonists | Metoclopramide, domperidone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol | Gastritis, post-operative, drug-induced vomiting, gastroparesis | | 3. H1 antihistamines | Promethazine, dimenhydrinate, cyclizine, meclizine, doxylamine (with pyridoxine) | Motion sickness, vomiting of pregnancy | | 4. Anticholinergics | Hyoscine (scopolamine) – tablets, transdermal patch | Motion sickness | | 5. NK1 receptor antagonists | Aprepitant, fosaprepitant | Highly emetogenic chemotherapy (delayed vomiting) | | 6. Corticosteroids | Dexamethasone | Chemotherapy (with ondansetron), post-operative | | 7. Benzodiazepines | Lorazepam | Anticipatory vomiting of chemotherapy | | 8. Cannabinoids | Dronabinol, nabilone | Refractory chemotherapy vomiting |

C. Commonly used antiemetics 1. Ondansetron

  • Mechanism: blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the CTZ and on vagal afferents in the gut.
  • Uses: chemotherapy-induced (given 30 minutes before chemotherapy, often with dexamethasone), radiotherapy and post-operative nausea and vomiting, gastroenteritis vomiting in children (single dose), hyperemesis gravidarum (as advised).
  • Dose: 4–8 mg orally/IV (0.1–0.15 mg/kg in children).
  • Adverse effects: headache, constipation, dizziness, QT prolongation (caution with other QT-prolonging drugs), rarely serotonin syndrome.
  • Not effective in motion sickness.

2. Metoclopramide

  • Mechanism: D2 antagonist in the CTZ; also a prokinetic – increases lower oesophageal sphincter tone and gastric emptying.
  • Uses: vomiting due to gastritis, drugs, post-operative, migraine; GERD and diabetic gastroparesis; before emergency anaesthesia to empty the stomach; to aid passage of tubes into the duodenum.
  • Dose: 10 mg orally/IM/IV three times daily (use for short periods).
  • Adverse effects: drowsiness, diarrhoea, extrapyramidal reactions – acute dystonia (spasm of face, neck, eyes – oculogyric crisis), especially in children and young women; tardive dyskinesia with long use; raised prolactin (galactorrhoea).
  • Contraindicated in GI obstruction or perforation, phaeochromocytoma, epilepsy, infants.

3. Domperidone

  • D2 antagonist that does not cross the blood–brain barrier → fewer extrapyramidal effects; prokinetic.
  • Uses: nausea and vomiting, dyspepsia, levodopa-induced vomiting in Parkinson's disease.
  • Adverse effects: QT prolongation and arrhythmias (avoid high doses and in heart disease), raised prolactin.

4. Promethazine and other H1 antihistamines

  • Block H1 and muscarinic receptors in the vestibular pathway; sedative.
  • Uses: motion sickness (take 30–60 minutes before travel), vomiting of pregnancy (doxylamine + pyridoxine is commonly used), post-operative vomiting, pre-anaesthetic sedation.
  • Adverse effects: drowsiness (warn against driving), dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention; avoid in children under 2 years (respiratory depression with promethazine).

5. Prochlorperazine – phenothiazine D2 antagonist; vertigo, Ménière's disease, vomiting; extrapyramidal effects and sedation.

6. Hyoscine – transdermal patch behind the ear for motion sickness; dry mouth, blurred vision, drowsiness.

D. Emetics (brief) Drugs that induce vomiting (apomorphine, ipecac) are rarely used now; gastric lavage and activated charcoal are preferred in poisoning. Emesis is contraindicated in corrosive and kerosene poisoning, unconscious or convulsing patients.

E. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Assess the cause, frequency, amount and character of vomiting; hydration status (skin turgor, urine output), electrolytes and weight.
  2. Timing – give antiemetics before the trigger: 30 minutes before chemotherapy, 30–60 minutes before travel, before meals in gastroparesis; give regularly rather than "as needed" in chemotherapy.
  3. Route – IV/IM/rectal/orally dissolving tablets when the patient cannot keep tablets down.
  4. Observe for adverse effects
    • Extrapyramidal reactions with metoclopramide/prochlorperazine – report immediately (treated with promethazine/diphenhydramine or anticholinergics).
    • Sedation and fall risk with antihistamines; ECG monitoring for QT-prolonging drugs in high-risk patients.
  5. Safety – position the patient on the side or upright to prevent aspiration; keep a vomit bowl and suction ready; side rails as needed.
  6. Supportive care – mouth care after vomiting, fresh air, remove odours, small frequent bland meals, cold fluids, ginger, relaxation techniques; correct fluid and electrolyte losses (ORS/IV).
  7. Record intake–output and response to drugs.
  8. Educate – avoid driving after sedating antiemetics; in pregnancy use only prescribed drugs.

Conclusion Antiemetics act at different receptors – 5-HT3, D2, H1, muscarinic and NK1 – so the choice depends on the cause of vomiting. Correct timing, monitoring for extrapyramidal and cardiac effects, and good supportive nursing care relieve this distressing symptom safely.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: Classify laxatives and purgatives. Explain their uses, contraindications and nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Definitions

  • Laxatives – drugs that promote soft, formed stools (mild action).
  • Purgatives (cathartics) – drugs that cause more fluid evacuation (strong action). The same drug may act as a laxative in small doses and a purgative in larger doses.

A. Classification 1. Bulk-forming laxatives

  • Dietary fibre, ispaghula (psyllium husk – "isabgol"), methylcellulose, bran.
  • Absorb water, increase stool bulk and stimulate peristalsis; act in 12–72 hours; safest for long-term use; must be taken with plenty of water (else may cause obstruction).

2. Stool softeners and lubricants

  • Docusate sodium – detergent action, softens stool.
  • Liquid paraffin – lubricates and softens stool; long-term use reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); leakage from anus; aspiration lipid pneumonia if given at bedtime to elderly/debilitated patients.

3. Osmotic laxatives

  • Lactulose (synthetic disaccharide) – also used in hepatic encephalopathy (reduces ammonia absorption); acts in 1–3 days; causes flatulence.
  • Polyethylene glycol (PEG) – chronic constipation and bowel preparation before colonoscopy/surgery.
  • Saline purgatives – magnesium sulphate, magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia), sodium phosphate – act in 1–3 hours; risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

4. Stimulant (irritant) purgatives

  • Bisacodyl (oral – acts in 6–8 hours, give at bedtime; suppository – 15–60 minutes), senna (sennosides) – 8–10 hours, sodium picosulfate, castor oil (2–6 hours).
  • Stimulate the myenteric plexus and increase secretion; cause cramps; chronic abuse leads to "cathartic colon" and hypokalaemia.

B. Uses

  1. Constipation – due to low-fibre diet, pregnancy, old age, immobility, opioid therapy, after childbirth.
  2. To avoid straining – after myocardial infarction, hernia repair, anorectal surgery (haemorrhoids, fissure), in raised intracranial pressure.
  3. Bowel preparation before colonoscopy, barium studies and abdominal surgery (PEG, sodium phosphate).
  4. Hepatic encephalopathy (lactulose).
  5. To expel poisons (osmotic purgatives) and worms after anthelmintics (older practice).

C. Contraindications

  • Intestinal obstruction, undiagnosed acute abdominal pain, appendicitis (risk of perforation), inflammatory bowel disease in acute phase.
  • Severe dehydration; strong purgatives in pregnancy (castor oil may induce labour); magnesium salts in kidney failure; phosphate preparations in kidney/heart failure.

D. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Assess bowel habits, abdominal distension, pain and cause of constipation; rule out obstruction.
  2. Encourage non-drug measures first – high-fibre diet (fruits, vegetables, whole grains), 2–3 litres of fluid daily, exercise, regular toilet routine, responding to the urge.
  3. Give bulk laxatives with a full glass of water; bisacodyl tablets whole at bedtime (not with milk or antacids – enteric coat dissolves early); suppositories inserted against the rectal wall.
  4. Do not give liquid paraffin at bedtime or to patients with swallowing difficulty.
  5. Monitor stool frequency and character, fluid and electrolyte balance (especially potassium), and signs of dependence.
  6. Ensure toilet/commode access and privacy when the drug is expected to act.
  7. Educate against chronic self-use of stimulant laxatives.

Conclusion Laxatives range from gentle bulk agents to strong stimulants; the safest approach is fibre and fluids first, with drugs chosen according to cause and urgency.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: Explain the antidiarrhoeal drugs and the principles of treatment of diarrhoea.
answer_html:
Introduction Diarrhoea – passage of three or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours – is a leading cause of illness and death in children under five in India. Most deaths are due to dehydration, not the infection itself. Therefore rehydration is the cornerstone of treatment; antidiarrhoeal drugs play a limited, supportive role.

A. Principles of treatment

  1. Rehydration – ORS for prevention and treatment of mild to moderate dehydration; IV Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration.
  2. Zinc supplementation in children – reduces duration and severity and prevents recurrence (10 mg/day below 6 months, 20 mg/day from 6 months to 5 years, for 14 days).
  3. Continued feeding – breastfeeding and normal diet to prevent malnutrition.
  4. Specific antimicrobials only when indicated.
  5. Symptomatic drugs in selected adults.
  6. Prevention – safe water, sanitation, hand washing, rotavirus vaccine.

B. Classification of drugs used in diarrhoea 1. Fluids and electrolytes – low-osmolarity ORS, IV Ringer's lactate/normal saline, potassium supplements.

2. Antimotility drugs (reduce intestinal movement)

  • Loperamide – opioid agonist acting on gut receptors (does not cross into the brain at usual doses); 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool (maximum 16 mg/day) in adults.
  • Diphenoxylate with atropine (Lomotil).
  • Uses: non-infective acute diarrhoea in adults, travellers' diarrhoea (mild), chronic diarrhoea (e.g., IBS), to reduce output in ileostomy.
  • Contraindications: children (especially under 5 years), bloody diarrhoea/dysentery, high fever, C. difficile colitis – they can cause toxic megacolon and prolong infection.

3. Antisecretory drugs

  • Racecadotril – inhibits enkephalinase; reduces secretion without slowing the gut; can be used in children.
  • Octreotide – secretory diarrhoea due to tumours (carcinoid, VIPoma), AIDS-related diarrhoea.
  • Bismuth subsalicylate.

4. Adsorbents – kaolin, pectin, activated charcoal – of little proven value.

5. Probiotics – Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Saccharomyces boulardii – modest benefit in acute and antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

6. Antimicrobials (only when indicated) | Condition | Drug (as per guidelines) | |---|---| | Cholera (severe) | Doxycycline (adults), azithromycin (children, pregnancy) | | Bacillary dysentery (blood in stool) | Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin/ceftriaxone (as per local sensitivity) | | Amoebic dysentery | Metronidazole/tinidazole + luminal agent | | Giardiasis | Metronidazole, tinidazole | | C. difficile colitis | Oral vancomycin, fidaxomicin (metronidazole in mild cases) | Routine antibiotics for watery diarrhoea are not recommended.

C. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Assess degree of dehydration (WHO plans A, B, C), weigh the child, record intake and output.
  2. Prepare and give ORS correctly; teach mothers; continue breastfeeding.
  3. Give zinc for full 14 days.
  4. Never give antimotility drugs to children or in dysentery; observe adults for abdominal distension.
  5. Collect stool samples before antibiotics; maintain enteric precautions and hand hygiene; disinfect soiled linen.
  6. Perianal skin care; nutrition counselling.

Conclusion "ORS, zinc and feeding" save lives in diarrhoea; drugs that stop motility are useful only in carefully selected adults.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: Explain oral rehydration salts (ORS) – composition, mechanism of action, preparation and uses.
answer_html:
Introduction Oral rehydration salts (ORS) – called "the most important medical advance of the 20th century" (The Lancet) – are a simple, cheap mixture of salts and glucose that can correct dehydration due to diarrhoea in most patients without intravenous fluids. Indian scientists and doctors contributed greatly to its development (e.g., use during the 1971 Bangladesh refugee crisis by Dr Dilip Mahalanabis).

1. Composition – WHO/UNICEF low-osmolarity ORS (per litre) | Ingredient | Grams/litre | Contribution | |---|---|---| | Sodium chloride | 2.6 g | Sodium 75 mmol/l, chloride 65 mmol/l | | Glucose, anhydrous | 13.5 g | Glucose 75 mmol/l | | Potassium chloride | 1.5 g | Potassium 20 mmol/l | | Trisodium citrate, dihydrate | 2.9 g | Citrate 10 mmol/l (corrects acidosis) | | Total osmolarity | | 245 mOsm/l | The low-osmolarity formula (2002) reduces stool output, vomiting and the need for IV fluids compared with the older 311 mOsm/l ORS.

2. Mechanism of action

  • In diarrhoea (even in cholera) the sodium–glucose co-transporter (SGLT1) in the small intestinal cells continues to work.
  • Glucose and sodium are absorbed together; water follows passively by osmosis, along with chloride and potassium.
  • Thus glucose helps the absorption of salt and water; citrate corrects metabolic acidosis; potassium replaces losses.
  • ORS does not stop diarrhoea – it replaces losses and prevents dehydration.

3. Preparation and administration

  1. Wash hands; take one packet in 1 litre of clean drinking water (boiled and cooled).
  2. Stir well; do not boil after mixing; use within 24 hours, then discard.
  3. Give small, frequent sips from a cup or spoon (every 1–2 minutes for small children); if the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and continue more slowly.
  4. Amounts (WHO Plan A – no dehydration, after each loose stool): under 2 years – 50–100 ml; 2–10 years – 100–200 ml; older children and adults – as much as wanted.
  5. Plan B (some dehydration): 75 ml/kg over 4 hours, then reassess.
  6. Plan C (severe dehydration): IV Ringer's lactate (ORS once the patient can drink).

4. Uses

  • Prevention and treatment of dehydration in acute diarrhoea of any cause (cholera, rotavirus, food poisoning).
  • Dehydration due to vomiting, heat exhaustion, fever (as advised).
  • Maintenance after IV rehydration.

5. Precautions

  • Not suitable alone in severe dehydration with shock, persistent vomiting, paralytic ileus or unconscious patients – IV fluids needed.
  • Wrong preparation (too concentrated) may cause hypernatraemia.
  • Home-available fluids (salted rice water, dal water, lemon water with salt and sugar, coconut water, buttermilk) can be used if ORS is not at hand; avoid soft drinks and sweet juices.

Nursing role Teach mothers the correct preparation with a demonstration, observe a feed, check hydration signs, give zinc for 14 days, encourage breastfeeding, and educate on hand washing and safe water.

Conclusion ORS works by the sodium–glucose co-transport mechanism; correctly prepared and given early, it prevents most diarrhoeal deaths.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: Explain the mechanism of action of omeprazole.
answer_html:
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI).

Mechanism of action

  1. It is a prodrug – absorbed and carried to the parietal cells of the stomach.
  2. In the acidic secretory canaliculi it is converted into its active form (sulphenamide).
  3. The active form binds irreversibly (covalently) to H⁺/K⁺-ATPase – the proton pump – the final step of acid secretion.
  4. This blocks both basal and stimulated acid secretion (by more than 90%); the effect lasts 24–48 hours until new pumps are synthesised.

It is given 30–60 minutes before breakfast so that the drug is present when the pumps are activated by food.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: List the fluids and electrolytes used in the treatment of diarrhoea and dehydration.
answer_html:
Fluids and electrolytes used in diarrhoea and dehydration

  1. Low-osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/l) – for prevention and treatment of mild to moderate dehydration.
  2. Ringer's lactate – IV fluid of choice for severe dehydration (contains sodium, potassium, calcium, lactate).
  3. Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) – IV alternative when Ringer's lactate is not available.
  4. Potassium chloride – to correct hypokalaemia (added to IV fluids or orally).
  5. Dextrose-containing saline (e.g., N/2 saline with 5% dextrose) – maintenance fluids as ordered.
  6. Sodium bicarbonate – rarely, for severe metabolic acidosis.
  7. Zinc sulphate/acetate – supplement for children (10–20 mg/day for 14 days).
  8. Home fluids – rice water, dal water, buttermilk, coconut water, lemon water with salt and sugar.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Gastrointestinal System
question: What are emetics? Mention their contraindications.
answer_html:
Emetics are drugs or measures that induce vomiting, formerly used to empty the stomach in poisoning.

Examples: apomorphine (dopamine agonist acting on the CTZ; given SC), ipecac syrup (emetine – local irritant and central action); mechanical stimulation of the throat. They are rarely used now – gastric lavage and activated charcoal are preferred.

Contraindications to induced vomiting

  1. Corrosive poisoning (acids, alkalis) – re-exposure of oesophagus, perforation.
  2. Kerosene and hydrocarbon poisoning – aspiration pneumonitis.
  3. Unconscious, drowsy or convulsing patients – aspiration.
  4. Poisoning by CNS stimulants (risk of convulsions).
  5. Shock, cardiac disease, late pregnancy, infants.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Respiratory System
question: Classify the drugs used in bronchial asthma. Describe the pharmacology of bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids, with nursing responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Sites of action of drugs used in bronchial asthma

answer_html:
Introduction Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways with bronchospasm, mucosal oedema and excess mucus, causing recurrent wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough. Treatment aims to relieve bronchospasm (relievers) and control airway inflammation (controllers/preventers). Most asthma drugs are given by inhalation – this delivers the drug directly to the airways, gives quick action with low doses and fewer systemic side effects.

A. Classification of anti-asthmatic drugs 1. Bronchodilators

  • (a) Beta-2 adrenergic agonists
    • Short-acting (SABA): salbutamol (albuterol), levosalbutamol, terbutaline – relievers.
    • Long-acting (LABA): salmeterol, formoterol, (indacaterol – COPD) – controllers, always with inhaled steroids in asthma.
  • (b) Methylxanthines: theophylline, aminophylline (IV), doxofylline.
  • (c) Anticholinergics (antimuscarinics): ipratropium (short-acting), tiotropium (long-acting).

2. Anti-inflammatory (controller) drugs

  • (a) Corticosteroids
    • Inhaled (ICS): budesonide, beclomethasone, fluticasone, ciclesonide.
    • Systemic: prednisolone (oral), hydrocortisone, methylprednisolone (IV) – for acute severe asthma.
  • (b) Leukotriene modifiers: montelukast, zafirlukast (receptor antagonists); zileuton (synthesis inhibitor).
  • (c) Mast-cell stabilisers: sodium cromoglycate, ketotifen.
  • (d) Biologicals: omalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) – severe asthma.

3. Others – magnesium sulphate IV (acute severe asthma), oxygen, adrenaline (anaphylaxis-related bronchospasm).

B. Pharmacology of bronchodilators 1. Beta-2 agonists (salbutamol as the prototype)

  • Mechanism: stimulate β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle → activate adenylyl cyclase → increase cAMP → relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle (bronchodilation); also inhibit mediator release from mast cells and improve mucociliary clearance.
  • Onset/duration: inhaled salbutamol acts within 5 minutes, lasts 4–6 hours; salmeterol lasts 12 hours (slow onset); formoterol has fast onset and long action.
  • Uses: relief of acute asthma attacks, prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm (before exercise), acute severe asthma (nebulised), COPD; salbutamol also for hyperkalaemia; terbutaline earlier for premature labour.
  • Adverse effects: fine tremor of hands (commonest), palpitations, tachycardia, headache, nervousness, muscle cramps, hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia; tolerance with overuse.
  • Note (current guidelines – GINA): asthma should not be treated with SABA alone; every adult and adolescent with asthma should receive an ICS-containing controller, and low-dose ICS–formoterol may be used as the reliever.

2. Methylxanthines (theophylline, aminophylline)

  • Mechanism: inhibit phosphodiesterase (raise cAMP), block adenosine receptors → bronchodilation; also stimulate the respiratory centre and diaphragm.
  • Uses: add-on in chronic asthma/COPD (oral sustained-release), IV aminophylline in acute severe asthma (now less used), apnoea of prematurity (caffeine).
  • Narrow therapeutic index (10–20 µg/ml): toxicity causes nausea, vomiting, restlessness, insomnia, tachycardia, arrhythmias and seizures.
  • Interactions: levels rise with erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine and fall in smokers and with rifampicin.
  • IV aminophylline must be given slowly (over 20–30 minutes) – rapid injection may cause arrhythmia and death.

3. Anticholinergics (ipratropium, tiotropium)

  • Mechanism: block muscarinic (M3) receptors → prevent vagal bronchoconstriction and reduce secretions.
  • Uses: COPD (first line), acute severe asthma (nebulised ipratropium with salbutamol).
  • Adverse effects: dry mouth, bitter taste, urinary retention, glaucoma risk if sprayed into the eyes.

C. Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)

  • Mechanism: reduce airway inflammation – decrease inflammatory cells (eosinophils, mast cells, T cells) and cytokines, reduce mucosal oedema and mucus, reduce airway hyper-responsiveness and up-regulate β2 receptors.
  • Uses: most effective controllers for persistent asthma – reduce symptoms, attacks, hospital admissions and deaths; COPD with frequent exacerbations (with LABA).
  • Not for immediate relief – benefit appears in days to weeks; must be used daily.
  • Adverse effects: oral thrush (candidiasis), hoarseness (dysphonia), sore throat; high doses – adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, growth slowing in children, cataract.
  • Prevention: use a spacer; rinse mouth and gargle after each use (and spit out).
  • Systemic steroids (prednisolone 40–50 mg for 5–7 days; IV hydrocortisone) for acute exacerbations.

D. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Assessment – respiratory rate, use of accessory muscles, wheeze, ability to speak, SpO₂, peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR); identify triggers.
  2. Inhaler technique – teach and check at every visit (metered-dose inhaler with spacer, dry powder inhaler, nebuliser); most treatment failures are due to poor technique.
  3. Relievers vs controllers – explain clearly: carry the reliever always; use controllers daily even when well.
  4. Sequence – when both are prescribed, use the bronchodilator first, wait a few minutes, then the steroid inhaler.
  5. Rinse mouth after ICS; observe for thrush and hoarseness.
  6. Monitor adverse effects – pulse, tremor, potassium (high-dose β2 agonists), theophylline levels and signs of toxicity; give IV aminophylline slowly by infusion pump.
  7. Acute severe asthma – position upright, give oxygen to keep SpO₂ 93–95%, nebulised salbutamol (with ipratropium), systemic steroids as ordered; monitor closely; avoid sedatives.
  8. Education – written asthma action plan, trigger avoidance (dust, smoke, pollen, cold air), smoking cessation, influenza vaccination, regular follow-up, recognising danger signs (reliever needed more often, night symptoms, falling PEFR).

Conclusion Asthma is controlled by combining anti-inflammatory controllers (especially inhaled corticosteroids) with bronchodilator relievers. Correct inhaler use and patient education, led by the nurse, are as important as the drugs themselves.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Respiratory System
question: Explain how salbutamol helps patients with asthma and list two of its adverse effects. Name two mucolytics and two antitussives.
answer_html:
A. Salbutamol in asthma (3 marks) 1. Mechanism of action

  • Salbutamol is a selective short-acting β2-adrenergic agonist.
  • It stimulates β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle → activates adenylyl cyclase → raises cyclic AMP → relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation.
  • It also inhibits release of histamine and leukotrienes from mast cells and increases mucociliary clearance.

2. How it helps the asthma patient

  • Rapid relief of wheeze, breathlessness and chest tightness – inhaled salbutamol acts within 5 minutes and lasts 4–6 hours; hence it is the main "reliever" drug.
  • Prevents exercise-induced bronchospasm when taken 15 minutes before exercise.
  • Used by nebulisation (2.5–5 mg) in acute severe asthma, along with oxygen and steroids.
  • Being selective for β2 receptors, it causes fewer cardiac effects than older drugs (isoprenaline, adrenaline); inhalation reduces systemic effects further.

3. Adverse effects (any two)

  1. Fine tremor of the hands (commonest).
  2. Palpitations and tachycardia.
  3. Hypokalaemia (with high doses).
  4. Headache, nervousness, muscle cramps, hyperglycaemia.

B. Mucolytics (any two) (1 mark) Drugs that reduce the viscosity of sputum so that it can be coughed out easily:

  1. Bromhexine
  2. Ambroxol
  3. N-acetylcysteine (also antidote for paracetamol poisoning)
  4. Carbocisteine; dornase alfa (in cystic fibrosis)

C. Antitussives (any two) (1 mark) Drugs that suppress cough (used only for dry, irritating, non-productive cough):

  1. Codeine (opioid – centrally acting)
  2. Dextromethorphan (non-opioid, centrally acting)
  3. Noscapine, pholcodine
