  4. Antihistamines with cough-suppressant effect (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine)

Nursing points

  • Teach correct inhaler technique and to carry the reliever inhaler always.
  • Do not use antitussives in productive cough (they cause retention of secretions); encourage fluids and steam inhalation with mucolytics.
  • Codeine causes constipation and drowsiness; avoid in children below 12 years.

D. Routes and preparations of salbutamol

  • Metered-dose inhaler (100 µg per puff; 1–2 puffs as needed), with a spacer for children and the elderly.
  • Rotacaps/dry powder inhaler, nebuliser solution (5 mg/ml), tablets and syrup (more side effects, slower action – less preferred), injection in special situations.
  • Overuse warning: needing the reliever more than twice a week means asthma is poorly controlled – the patient must see the doctor for controller (inhaled steroid) therapy.

Conclusion Salbutamol is the fastest-acting reliever in asthma; mucolytics loosen sputum, while antitussives suppress dry cough.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Respiratory System
question: Name two first-generation and two second-generation antihistamines. Describe the advantages of second-generation over first-generation antihistamines. List two antibiotics used in eye infections.
answer_html:
Introduction Antihistamines (H1-receptor antagonists) block the actions of histamine at H1 receptors – vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, itching, sneezing and bronchoconstriction. They are widely used in allergic conditions.

A. Examples (1 mark)

  • First-generation (sedating): chlorpheniramine (CPM), diphenhydramine, promethazine, pheniramine, hydroxyzine, cyproheptadine, dimenhydrinate.
  • Second-generation (non-sedating): cetirizine, levocetirizine, loratadine, desloratadine, fexofenadine, bilastine, ebastine.

B. Advantages of second-generation antihistamines (3 marks) | Feature | First-generation | Second-generation (advantage) | |---|---|---| | Sedation | Marked drowsiness – cross the blood–brain barrier | Little or no sedation – poorly cross BBB; safe for students, drivers, machine operators | | Psychomotor impairment | Impair concentration and performance | No significant impairment | | Anticholinergic effects | Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation | Absent – safe in glaucoma, prostate enlargement, elderly | | Duration | Short – 3–4 times daily | Long – once daily (better adherence) | | Interaction with alcohol/sedatives | Additive CNS depression | Minimal | | Appetite/weight gain | Some (cyproheptadine) | Minimal | Hence second-generation drugs are preferred for allergic rhinitis, urticaria and allergic conjunctivitis. First-generation drugs are still useful when sedation, antiemetic or anti-motion-sickness effects are desired (e.g., promethazine, dimenhydrinate), and by injection in acute allergic reactions (pheniramine, chlorpheniramine).

C. Antibiotics used in eye infections (1 mark)

  1. Moxifloxacin eye drops (fluoroquinolone – conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer).
  2. Ciprofloxacin / ofloxacin eye drops.
  3. Chloramphenicol eye drops/ointment.
  4. Tobramycin / gentamicin eye drops.
  5. Erythromycin ointment (prophylaxis of ophthalmia neonatorum), azithromycin (oral) for trachoma.

Nursing points

  • Warn about drowsiness with first-generation antihistamines; avoid driving and alcohol.
  • For eye drops: hand hygiene, do not touch the dropper to the eye, press the inner canthus for 1–2 minutes after instillation, separate bottles for each patient, discard after the recommended period.

D. Mechanism and uses of H1 antihistamines (in brief)

  • Mechanism: they act as inverse agonists/competitive blockers at H1 receptors, preventing histamine-induced vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, itching, sneezing and bronchial and intestinal smooth-muscle contraction.
  • Uses: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, allergic conjunctivitis, insect-bite reactions, pruritus, drug and transfusion allergies (with adrenaline in anaphylaxis – never instead of it), motion sickness and vomiting (first-generation), common cold (symptomatic), as sedatives (promethazine, hydroxyzine).

Conclusion Second-generation antihistamines give relief from allergy without sedation or anticholinergic effects, making them the drugs of choice for most allergic conditions.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Respiratory System
question: Explain the pharmacology of nasal decongestants.
answer_html:
Definition Nasal decongestants are drugs that reduce swelling (congestion) of the nasal mucosa, opening the nasal passages and improving drainage of sinuses and Eustachian tubes.

1. Classification

  • Topical (nasal drops/sprays): oxymetazoline 0.05%, xylometazoline 0.1% (0.05% for children), naphazoline, phenylephrine.
  • Oral: pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine (often in "cold" combination tablets).

2. Mechanism of action

  • They are α-adrenergic agonists – stimulate α receptors on blood vessels of the nasal mucosa → vasoconstriction → reduced blood flow, oedema and secretions → nasal passages open.

3. Uses

  • Common cold and acute rhinitis.
  • Allergic rhinitis (short-term, with antihistamines/nasal steroids).
  • Acute sinusitis – to improve drainage.
  • Otitis media / Eustachian tube blockage, air travel with blocked ears.
  • Before nasal examination, endoscopy or nasal surgery; to control epistaxis (on cotton packs).

4. Adverse effects

  • Local: stinging, burning, dryness of nasal mucosa, sneezing.
  • Rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) – when topical drops are used for more than 3–5 days, the nose becomes more blocked as the effect wears off, leading to overuse and dependence.
  • Systemic (especially oral or excessive topical use): raised blood pressure, palpitations, restlessness, insomnia, headache, urinary retention.
  • Infants: naphazoline and excessive xylometazoline can cause CNS depression, bradycardia and hypothermia.

5. Contraindications/precautions Hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, prostate enlargement, patients on MAO inhibitors, infants and young children (use saline drops), pregnancy (oral forms).

6. Nursing responsibilities and patient teaching

  1. Use for not more than 3–5 days.
  2. Technique: blow the nose gently; tilt the head back (or lie with head tilted back/sideways); instil drops without touching the dropper to the nose; keep position for 1–2 minutes.
  3. Use the paediatric strength for children; saline nasal drops and suction for infants.
  4. Do not share bottles; check expiry.
  5. Monitor BP in hypertensive patients; avoid evening doses of oral decongestants (insomnia).

7. Safer alternatives Steam inhalation, saline nasal sprays/drops, intranasal corticosteroids for allergic rhinitis and adequate fluids – advise these for prolonged symptoms.

8. Treatment of rebound congestion Stop the decongestant (one nostril at a time if needed), use saline sprays and an intranasal corticosteroid for a few weeks under medical advice.

Conclusion Nasal decongestants give quick relief by vasoconstriction, but must be used briefly to avoid rebound congestion and systemic effects.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Respiratory System
question: Write the mechanism of action and uses of montelukast.
answer_html:
Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist.

Mechanism: it blocks cysteinyl-leukotriene (CysLT1) receptors in the airways, preventing the actions of leukotrienes (LTD4) – bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, mucosal oedema and eosinophilic inflammation.

Uses

  1. Prophylaxis (prevention) of mild persistent asthma; add-on to inhaled steroids.
  2. Exercise-induced and aspirin-induced asthma.
  3. Allergic rhinitis.

Points: given orally once daily (in the evening); not for acute attacks; side effects – headache, GI upset; rarely mood changes and sleep disturbances (report to doctor).

It is especially useful in children who cannot use inhalers properly.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Acting on the Respiratory System
question: Name two mast-cell stabilisers and state their use.
answer_html:
Mast-cell stabilisers prevent degranulation of mast cells and release of histamine and other mediators.

Examples

  1. Sodium cromoglycate (inhaler, nasal spray, eye drops)
  2. Ketotifen (oral; also has H1-blocking action) (Also nedocromil.)

Uses

  • Prophylaxis of bronchial asthma (especially exercise- and allergen-induced, in children).
  • Allergic rhinitis and allergic conjunctivitis (eye drops).
  • Food allergy (oral cromoglycate), urticaria.

Points: preventive only – not effective in an acute attack; must be used regularly before exposure.

Eye drops are used several times a day during the allergy season.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Classify adrenergic drugs. Write their mode of action, therapeutic uses, contraindications and adverse effects.

diagram.caption: Adrenergic receptors and their actions
labels: alpha-1 vasoconstriction and mydriasis; alpha-2 reduced noradrenaline release; beta-1 increased heart rate and force; beta-2 bronchodilation
uterine relaxation; dopamine D1 renal vasodilation

answer_html:
Introduction Adrenergic (sympathomimetic) drugs mimic the effects of stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system – the "fight or flight" system – by acting on adrenergic receptors (α and β) directly or by releasing noradrenaline. They are life-saving drugs in anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, shock and asthma, but are also high-alert medicines because small errors can cause dangerous arrhythmias and hypertension.

A. Adrenergic receptors and their main actions | Receptor | Location | Effect of stimulation | |---|---|---| | α1 | Blood vessels, radial muscle of iris, bladder sphincter | Vasoconstriction (↑BP), mydriasis, urinary retention | | α2 | Presynaptic nerve endings, CNS | ↓ noradrenaline release, ↓ sympathetic outflow, ↓ BP (central) | | β1 | Heart, kidney (JG cells) | ↑ heart rate, ↑ force of contraction, ↑ AV conduction, renin release | | β2 | Bronchi, skeletal-muscle vessels, uterus, liver | Bronchodilation, vasodilation, uterine relaxation, glycogenolysis, tremor, ↓ K⁺ | | D1 (dopamine) | Renal and mesenteric vessels | Vasodilation |

B. Classification of adrenergic drugs 1. According to chemical nature

  • Catecholamines – adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, dobutamine, isoprenaline (not effective orally, short action, given IV/IM/SC).
  • Non-catecholamines – ephedrine, phenylephrine, amphetamine, salbutamol, terbutaline (orally effective, longer action).

2. According to mode of action

  • Directly acting – act on receptors: adrenaline, noradrenaline, isoprenaline, dobutamine, phenylephrine, salbutamol.
  • Indirectly acting – release stored noradrenaline: tyramine, amphetamine.
  • Mixed action – ephedrine, dopamine.

3. According to receptor selectivity

  • α and β agonists – adrenaline, noradrenaline (mainly α1, β1).
  • α1 agonists – phenylephrine, midodrine, (oxymetazoline/xylometazoline – topical decongestants).
  • α2 agonists – clonidine, methyldopa (central antihypertensives), brimonidine (glaucoma), dexmedetomidine (sedation).
  • β1 agonist – dobutamine.
  • β1 + β2 agonist – isoprenaline.
  • β2 agonists – salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol, ritodrine, isoxsuprine.
  • Dopamine – D1, β1 and α1 depending on dose.

4. According to therapeutic use

  • Pressor agents / vasopressors – noradrenaline, phenylephrine, ephedrine, dopamine.
  • Cardiac stimulants – adrenaline, dobutamine, isoprenaline, dopamine.
  • Bronchodilators – salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol.
  • Nasal decongestants – oxymetazoline, xylometazoline, pseudoephedrine.
  • Uterine relaxants – ritodrine, isoxsuprine.
  • CNS stimulants – amphetamine, methylphenidate (ADHD, narcolepsy).
  • Mydriatics – phenylephrine eye drops.

C. Mode of action

  • Adrenergic drugs bind to G-protein-coupled α or β receptors:
    • β receptors → activate adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cyclic AMP → increased heart rate and force (β1), smooth-muscle relaxation (β2).
    • α1 receptors → activate phospholipase C → ↑ intracellular calcium → smooth-muscle contraction (vasoconstriction).
    • α2 receptors → inhibit adenylyl cyclase → reduced noradrenaline release.
  • Indirect agents enter nerve endings and displace noradrenaline from storage vesicles.

D. Therapeutic uses 1. Adrenaline (epinephrine)

  • Anaphylaxis – drug of choice: 0.5 mg IM (0.5 ml of 1:1000 solution) in the anterolateral thigh for adults (0.01 mg/kg in children, maximum 0.5 mg), repeated every 5 minutes if needed.
  • Cardiac arrest: 1 mg IV/IO (10 ml of 1:10,000) every 3–5 minutes during CPR.
  • With local anaesthetics (1:100,000–1:200,000) to prolong action and reduce bleeding – never in fingers, toes, nose tip, ear lobes or penis (end arteries – gangrene).
  • Local haemostatic – cotton soaked in 1:10,000 for epistaxis, tooth socket bleeding.
  • Acute severe asthma (rarely, when other drugs are unavailable).

2. Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) – vasopressor of first choice in septic shock and other hypotensive states (IV infusion via central line).

3. Dopamine – cardiogenic shock, symptomatic bradycardia; dose-dependent effects (moderate doses β1 – inotropic; high doses α1 – vasoconstriction).

4. Dobutamine – acute heart failure and cardiogenic shock (increases contractility); cardiac stress testing.

5. Isoprenaline – heart block and severe bradycardia (temporarily, until pacing).

6. Ephedrine – hypotension during spinal anaesthesia (IV bolus 3–6 mg), nasal decongestant.

7. Phenylephrine – hypotension during anaesthesia, nasal decongestion, mydriasis for fundus examination (without cycloplegia).

8. β2 agonists – bronchial asthma and COPD (salbutamol, formoterol); threatened preterm labour (isoxsuprine/terbutaline – limited use).

9. Others – amphetamine/methylphenidate in narcolepsy and ADHD; clonidine in hypertension.

E. Contraindications and precautions

  1. Hypertension, especially with α agonists.
  2. Ischaemic heart disease, angina, recent myocardial infarction and tachyarrhythmias (β1 stimulation increases oxygen demand).
  3. Hyperthyroidism (increased sensitivity).
  4. Narrow-angle glaucoma (mydriasis), prostate enlargement (urinary retention).
  5. Patients receiving MAO inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants (hypertensive crisis).
  6. During halothane anaesthesia (adrenaline may cause ventricular arrhythmias).
  7. Pregnancy – vasoconstrictors may reduce uterine blood flow.
  8. Local anaesthetic with adrenaline in end-artery areas.
  9. Note: in anaphylaxis there is no absolute contraindication to adrenaline – it must not be withheld.

F. Adverse effects

  • CNS: anxiety, restlessness, tremor, headache, insomnia.
  • CVS: palpitations, tachycardia, arrhythmias (including ventricular fibrillation), hypertension, angina, cerebral haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema.
  • Local: tissue necrosis and gangrene on extravasation of noradrenaline/dopamine; pallor at injection site.
  • Metabolic: hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia (β2), lactic acidosis.
  • Others: urinary retention, dependence and abuse (amphetamine).

G. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Check concentration carefully – confusion between 1:1000 (1 mg/ml, for IM) and 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/ml, for IV) adrenaline is a common, dangerous error; double-check high-alert drugs.
  2. Correct route – IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis; IV adrenaline only in cardiac arrest or by specialists with monitoring.
  3. Give vasopressor infusions through a central line using an infusion pump, label lines clearly; never give bolus flushes through the vasopressor line.
  4. Monitor continuously – BP, heart rate, ECG, urine output, peripheral perfusion, blood glucose and potassium.
  5. Watch the IV site – if extravasation of noradrenaline/dopamine occurs, stop the infusion and inform the doctor (phentolamine infiltration as ordered).
  6. Never stop vasopressors abruptly – taper as ordered.
  7. Keep anaphylaxis and emergency trays ready in every ward and immunisation session.
  8. Protect solutions from light; discard discoloured (pink/brown) adrenaline.
  9. Educate patients with severe allergy about adrenaline auto-injectors and carrying an allergy card.

Conclusion Adrenergic drugs act through α and β receptors to raise blood pressure, stimulate the heart and dilate bronchi. Used correctly – right drug, dose, concentration and route with close monitoring – they save lives in anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest and shock.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Classify antihypertensive drugs. Explain the mechanism of action, adverse effects and nursing responsibilities of commonly used antihypertensives.
answer_html:
Introduction Hypertension (BP ≥140/90 mmHg) affects about one in four Indian adults and is a major cause of stroke, heart attack, heart failure and kidney failure – yet it is often silent. Lifelong antihypertensive drugs, together with lifestyle changes, reduce these complications. The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) uses simple standard protocols with drugs such as amlodipine, telmisartan and chlorthalidone.

A. Classification 1. Diuretics

  • Thiazide and thiazide-like: hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide.
  • Loop diuretics: furosemide, torsemide (in kidney failure, heart failure).

  • Potassium-sparing: spironolactone, amiloride. 2. Drugs acting on the renin–angiotensin system

  • ACE inhibitors: enalapril, ramipril, lisinopril, captopril.

  • Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs): losartan, telmisartan, olmesartan.

  • Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren. 3. Calcium channel blockers (CCBs)

  • Dihydropyridines: amlodipine, nifedipine (long-acting), cilnidipine.

  • Non-dihydropyridines: verapamil, diltiazem. 4. Sympatholytics

  • β-blockers: atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, propranolol; α + β blockers: labetalol, carvedilol.

  • α1-blockers: prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin.

  • Central sympatholytics: clonidine, methyldopa, moxonidine. 5. Direct vasodilators

  • Hydralazine, minoxidil (arteriolar); sodium nitroprusside (arteriolar + venous – emergencies).

First-line drugs for most patients: ACE inhibitor or ARB, CCB, thiazide-like diuretic – often in combination.

B. Mechanism of action, uses and adverse effects of common groups 1. ACE inhibitors (e.g., enalapril)

  • Mechanism: inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme → ↓ angiotensin II (a powerful vasoconstrictor) and ↓ aldosterone → vasodilation and less salt/water retention; also ↑ bradykinin.
  • Special benefits: heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy (reduce proteinuria).
  • Adverse effects: dry cough (bradykinin – commonest), angioedema (rare, dangerous), hyperkalaemia, first-dose hypotension, rise in creatinine (especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis), rash, taste disturbance; contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal damage).

2. ARBs (e.g., telmisartan, losartan)

  • Mechanism: block AT1 receptors of angiotensin II.
  • Similar benefits to ACE inhibitors without cough; hyperkalaemia; contraindicated in pregnancy.

3. Calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine)

  • Mechanism: block L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle → arteriolar dilation → ↓ peripheral resistance; verapamil/diltiazem also slow the heart.
  • Adverse effects: ankle oedema, flushing, headache, palpitations (reflex tachycardia with short-acting nifedipine – avoided), gum hyperplasia; constipation, bradycardia and heart block with verapamil.
  • Safe in elderly, diabetics, asthmatics; nifedipine (long-acting) is used in pregnancy.

4. Thiazide diuretics (e.g., chlorthalidone)

  • Mechanism: inhibit Na⁺/Cl⁻ reabsorption in the distal tubule → initial ↓ blood volume, later ↓ peripheral resistance.
  • Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia (gout), hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidaemia, erectile dysfunction.

5. β-blockers (e.g., atenolol, metoprolol)

  • Mechanism: block β1 receptors → ↓ heart rate and cardiac output, ↓ renin release.
  • Preferred when hypertension coexists with angina, post-MI, heart failure (specific drugs), arrhythmias.
  • Adverse effects: bradycardia, fatigue, cold extremities, bronchospasm (avoid in asthma), masking of hypoglycaemia symptoms in diabetics, erectile dysfunction; rebound hypertension/angina if stopped suddenly.

6. α1-blockers (e.g., prazosin)

  • Dilate arterioles and veins; useful with benign prostatic hyperplasia.
  • "First-dose phenomenon" – sudden postural hypotension and syncope → give the first dose at bedtime.

7. Central sympatholytics

  • Clonidine – rebound hypertensive crisis on sudden withdrawal, dry mouth, sedation.
  • Methyldopa – safe in pregnancy; sedation, positive Coombs test, haemolytic anaemia, hepatitis.

8. Vasodilators

  • Hydralazine – pregnancy-induced hypertension; reflex tachycardia, lupus-like syndrome.
  • Sodium nitroprusside – hypertensive emergencies; continuous IV infusion protected from light; cyanide toxicity with prolonged use.

C. Drugs in special situations | Situation | Preferred drugs | |---|---| | Pregnancy | Methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine (avoid ACEI/ARB) | | Diabetes with proteinuria | ACE inhibitor or ARB | | Heart failure | ACEI/ARB, β-blocker (bisoprolol/carvedilol/metoprolol), diuretic | | Angina/post-MI | β-blocker, ACEI | | Asthma | Avoid β-blockers; CCB, ACEI/ARB | | Elderly | CCB, thiazide-like diuretic | | Hypertensive emergency | IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroglycerin, sodium nitroprusside |

Captopril – drug profile (often asked as "discuss captopril in detail")

  • Group: the first orally active ACE inhibitor; contains a sulfhydryl (–SH) group, short acting (given 2–3 times a day).
  • Mechanism: blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme → ↓ angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction, less aldosterone → less Na⁺ and water retention) and ↑ bradykinin (vasodilation, but also cough).
  • Dose: 12.5–25 mg orally two to three times daily, increased gradually (usual maximum about 150 mg/day); give 1 hour before meals because food reduces absorption; 25 mg chewed/sublingual was once used in urgency (no longer preferred).
  • Uses: hypertension, heart failure, post-MI left ventricular dysfunction, diabetic nephropathy (reduces proteinuria), scleroderma renal crisis.
  • Adverse effects: first-dose hypotension, dry cough, hyperkalaemia, angioedema, rise in creatinine (especially in bilateral renal artery stenosis), loss or alteration of taste (dysgeusia), rashes, neutropenia and proteinuria (–SH group).
  • Contraindications: pregnancy (foetal renal damage, oligohydramnios), bilateral renal artery stenosis, history of angioedema, hyperkalaemia.
  • Nursing points: first dose at bedtime with the patient lying down; check BP, serum potassium and creatinine; avoid potassium supplements and potassium-sparing diuretics unless ordered; teach to report swelling of lips/face (stop drug, emergency) and persistent cough.

D. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Measure BP accurately – correct cuff size, rested patient, same arm, record before giving antihypertensives; check pulse before β-blockers (withhold and inform if below 60/min or as ordered).
  2. Postural hypotension – teach patients to rise slowly from lying to sitting to standing; first dose of prazosin and ACEI at bedtime; fall precautions in the elderly.
  3. Monitor electrolytes (potassium, sodium), creatinine, blood sugar, uric acid and weight; ankle oedema with CCBs; cough with ACEI.
  4. Give drugs at the same time daily; check for drug interactions (NSAIDs reduce effect; potassium supplements with ACEI → hyperkalaemia).
  5. In hypertensive emergencies – IV infusion via pump, BP every 5–15 minutes; avoid lowering BP too fast (not more than 25% in the first hour).
  6. Patient education
    • Hypertension is usually lifelong; do not stop drugs when BP becomes normal – sudden stopping of clonidine or β-blockers is dangerous.
    • Lifestyle: salt less than 5 g/day, DASH-type diet rich in fruits and vegetables, weight control, 30 minutes of exercise most days, avoid tobacco and limit alcohol, stress management.
    • Home BP monitoring; regular follow-up; report swelling, cough, dizziness, slow pulse.
    • Women of child-bearing age on ACEI/ARB should plan pregnancy with the doctor.

Conclusion Several drug groups lower BP by reducing volume, blocking the renin–angiotensin system, dilating vessels or reducing sympathetic activity. Choosing the right drug for the patient, monitoring for side effects and supporting lifelong adherence with lifestyle change are key nursing contributions to preventing stroke and heart disease.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Classify drugs affecting coagulation (anticoagulants, antiplatelets and thrombolytics). Describe the pharmacology of heparin and warfarin with nursing responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Coagulation cascade and sites of action of anticoagulant, antiplatelet and thrombolytic drugs
labels: X – warfarin; thrombin and factor Xa with antithrombin – heparin; fibrin clot dissolved by plasmin – thrombolytics

answer_html:
Introduction Blood clots in the wrong place cause myocardial infarction, stroke, deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism – leading causes of death. Three groups of drugs act on clotting:

  • Anticoagulants – prevent formation and extension of clots (act on clotting factors).
  • Antiplatelet drugs – prevent platelet aggregation (mainly arterial clots).
  • Thrombolytics (fibrinolytics) – dissolve clots already formed. All of them can cause bleeding, and most are high-alert medicines.

A. Classification 1. Anticoagulants

  • Parenteral: unfractionated heparin (UFH); low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH) – enoxaparin, dalteparin; fondaparinux; direct thrombin inhibitors – bivalirudin, argatroban.

  • Oral: vitamin K antagonists – warfarin, acenocoumarol; direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) – dabigatran (thrombin inhibitor), rivaroxaban, apixaban (factor Xa inhibitors). 2. Antiplatelet drugs

  • Aspirin (low dose 75–150 mg) – irreversible COX-1 inhibitor → ↓ thromboxane A2.

  • P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blockers – clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor.
  • GP IIb/IIIa antagonists – abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban (IV, during PCI).

  • Others – dipyridamole, cilostazol. 3. Thrombolytics (fibrinolytics)

  • Streptokinase, urokinase, alteplase (rt-PA), tenecteplase, reteplase. 4. Antidotes / antifibrinolytics

  • Protamine sulphate (heparin), vitamin K (warfarin), idarucizumab (dabigatran), tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic).

B. Heparin (unfractionated)

  1. Source and nature – sulphated polysaccharide from pig intestinal mucosa or bovine lung; strongly acidic; not absorbed orally.
  2. Mechanism – binds and activates antithrombin III, which rapidly inactivates thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa → prevents fibrin formation. Acts immediately (IV) – both in vivo and in vitro.
  3. Administration and monitoring
    • IV (bolus followed by continuous infusion) or SC (5,000 units 8–12-hourly for prophylaxis); never IM (haematoma).
    • Monitored by activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) – kept at 1.5–2.5 times control.
  4. LMWH (enoxaparin) – mainly anti-Xa; SC once or twice daily, predictable effect, no routine monitoring, less thrombocytopenia; dose reduced in kidney failure.
  5. Uses – treatment and prevention of DVT and pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome, during haemodialysis, cardiac surgery and angioplasty, to keep lines patent (flushes), DIC (selected), bridging therapy when starting warfarin; preferred anticoagulant in pregnancy (does not cross placenta).
  6. Adverse effects – bleeding (most important), heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with paradoxical thrombosis, hypersensitivity, alopecia, osteoporosis with long-term use, hyperkalaemia.
  7. Antidote – protamine sulphate (1 mg neutralises about 100 units of heparin), given slowly IV.

C. Warfarin (oral anticoagulant)

  1. Mechanism – vitamin K antagonist: inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → liver cannot make active clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S).
  2. Onset – slow; full effect in 3–5 days (existing factors must be used up) – hence heparin is overlapped for at least 5 days until INR is therapeutic.
  3. Monitoring – prothrombin time expressed as INR; target 2–3 for most indications (2.5–3.5 for mechanical heart valves).
  4. Uses – long-term prevention and treatment of DVT/PE, atrial fibrillation (stroke prevention), prosthetic heart valves, rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF, mural thrombus after MI.
  5. Adverse effects – bleeding (gums, nose, urine, GI, intracranial), bruising, skin necrosis (rare), purple toe syndrome; teratogenic (fetal warfarin syndrome) – contraindicated in pregnancy (especially first trimester).
  6. Interactions – very many:
    • Increase effect/bleeding: aspirin and NSAIDs, enzyme inhibitors (erythromycin, fluconazole, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, amiodarone), paracetamol in high doses, alcohol binges.
    • Decrease effect: enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine), vitamin K-rich foods (green leafy vegetables) in large amounts, oral contraceptives.
  7. Antidote – vitamin K1 (phytonadione) orally/IV; for serious bleeding – fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate for immediate reversal.

D. Antiplatelet and thrombolytic drugs (in brief)

  • Aspirin and clopidogrel – prevention of MI, stroke, after stents (dual antiplatelet therapy); adverse effects – bleeding, GI ulcers (aspirin).
  • Thrombolytics – convert plasminogen to plasmin, which dissolves fibrin clots.
    • Uses: acute ST-elevation MI (best within 3 hours, up to 12 hours – "time is muscle"), acute ischaemic stroke (alteplase within 4.5 hours), massive pulmonary embolism, blocked catheters.
    • Contraindications: active bleeding, previous haemorrhagic stroke, recent surgery/trauma, severe uncontrolled hypertension, bleeding disorders.
    • Adverse effects: bleeding (including intracranial), allergy and hypotension with streptokinase (antigenic – not repeated within months), reperfusion arrhythmias.

E. Nursing responsibilities 1. Before therapy

  • Baseline CBC, platelet count, aPTT, PT/INR, kidney and liver function; history of bleeding, ulcers, recent surgery, pregnancy, current drugs. 2. Administration

  • Double-check doses (high-alert); use infusion pumps for heparin; label lines.

  • SC heparin/LMWH: inject into the abdomen at least 5 cm away from the umbilicus, do not aspirate, do not rub or massage, rotate sites; do not expel the air bubble from prefilled enoxaparin syringes.

  • Give warfarin at the same time every day (usually evening) so dose changes can be made after INR results. 3. Monitoring

  • aPTT for heparin infusion (usually 6-hourly till stable), INR for warfarin, platelet count (HIT), Hb.

  • Watch for bleeding: gums, nose, haematuria, black stools, haematemesis, bruises, prolonged bleeding from puncture sites, headache or confusion (intracranial bleed), back pain (retroperitoneal bleed); vital signs. 4. Bleeding precautions

  • Avoid IM injections; apply firm pressure on puncture sites for 5–10 minutes; soft toothbrush, electric razor; prevent falls.

  • Keep antidotes ready – protamine sulphate, vitamin K. 5. Thrombolysis

  • Rapid administration ("door-to-needle" within 30 minutes for STEMI), continuous ECG and BP monitoring, neurological checks, minimise invasive procedures for 24 hours. 6. Patient education (warfarin)

  • Regular INR tests; never double a missed dose; carry an anticoagulant card.

  • Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs and herbal products without advice; inform every doctor and dentist.
  • Keep intake of green leafy vegetables consistent (not avoided completely); limit alcohol.
  • Report bleeding signs immediately; use contraception (teratogenic).

Conclusion Anticoagulants, antiplatelets and thrombolytics prevent or dissolve life-threatening clots but share the risk of bleeding. Accurate dosing, laboratory monitoring, bleeding precautions, ready antidotes and patient education allow nurses to give these drugs safely.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Classify the drugs used in congestive heart failure. Describe the pharmacology of digoxin and the nurse's responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Mechanism of action of digoxin on the cardiac muscle cell
labels: stronger contraction; vagal slowing of AV node

answer_html:
Introduction Congestive heart failure (CHF) is a condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, leading to breathlessness, fatigue, oedema and congestion of lungs and organs. Drug therapy aims to relieve symptoms, reduce hospital admissions and prolong life. Modern treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction rests on four groups of life-prolonging drugs ("four pillars") plus diuretics for symptom relief.

A. Classification of drugs used in heart failure 1. Drugs that improve survival (disease-modifying)

  • ACE inhibitors (enalapril, ramipril) or ARBs (losartan, valsartan) or ARNI – sacubitril/valsartan.
  • β-blockers – bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (started at low doses when stable).
  • Mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) antagonists – spironolactone, eplerenone.

  • SGLT2 inhibitors – dapagliflozin, empagliflozin. 2. Drugs mainly for symptom relief

  • Diuretics – loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide) for congestion and oedema; thiazides as add-on.

  • Digoxin – improves symptoms, reduces hospitalisation; rate control in atrial fibrillation.
  • Vasodilators – nitrates and hydralazine (especially if ACEI not tolerated).

  • Ivabradine – slows heart rate in selected patients. 3. Drugs for acute (decompensated) heart failure

  • IV furosemide, nitroglycerin, oxygen/non-invasive ventilation, inotropes (dobutamine, dopamine, milrinone), morphine (cautiously).

B. Digoxin 1. Source – a cardiac glycoside obtained from the leaves of Digitalis lanata (foxglove). 2. Mechanism of action

  • Positive inotropic effect: digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump of cardiac muscle → intracellular sodium rises → less sodium–calcium exchange → more calcium inside the cell → stronger contraction.
  • Negative chronotropic and dromotropic effects: increases vagal tone → slows heart rate and slows conduction through the AV node.

  • Result: better cardiac output, reduced congestion, slower ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation. 3. Pharmacokinetics

  • Oral bioavailability about 70%; long half-life (about 36–40 hours) – once-daily dosing; excreted mainly by the kidneys (dose reduction in kidney disease and elderly).

  • Narrow therapeutic index – therapeutic serum level about 0.5–0.9 ng/ml in heart failure; toxicity common above 2 ng/ml.

  • Dose: usually 0.125–0.25 mg once daily (0.0625–0.125 mg in elderly). 4. Uses

  • Heart failure with persistent symptoms despite other drugs, especially with atrial fibrillation.

  • Atrial fibrillation and flutter – to control ventricular rate.

  • Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (rarely now). 5. Adverse effects and digitalis toxicity

  • GI (earliest): anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea.

  • CNS: fatigue, headache, confusion, delirium (elderly), drowsiness.
  • Visual: blurred vision, yellow-green colour vision (xanthopsia), haloes around lights.
  • Cardiac (most dangerous): almost any arrhythmia – ventricular ectopics (bigeminy), AV block, bradycardia, atrial tachycardia with block, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation.

  • Others: gynaecomastia, rash. 6. Factors that increase toxicity

  • Hypokalaemia (e.g., due to diuretics) – the most important; hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia.

  • Kidney failure, old age, hypothyroidism, hypoxia.

  • Drugs – amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine (raise digoxin level), diuretics (lower K⁺), IV calcium. 7. Management of toxicity

  • Stop digoxin; check serum digoxin and potassium; ECG monitoring.

  • Correct hypokalaemia with potassium (unless hyperkalaemia from severe toxicity).
  • Atropine for bradycardia/heart block; lignocaine or phenytoin for ventricular arrhythmias; temporary pacing.
  • Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind/DigiFab) for life-threatening toxicity. 8. Contraindications – heart block, WPW syndrome with AF, ventricular tachycardia, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

C. Nursing responsibilities 1. Before giving digoxin

  • Count the apical pulse for one full minute; withhold the dose and inform the doctor if the rate is below 60/min in adults (below about 70 in children and 90 in infants) or if the rhythm becomes irregular when previously regular.

  • Check recent serum potassium, creatinine and digoxin level; ask about nausea, vomiting, visual changes. 2. Administration

  • Give at the same time each day; measure paediatric elixir with a calibrated syringe (doses are tiny – double-check calculations); IV digoxin slowly over at least 5 minutes. 3. Monitoring in heart failure

  • Daily weight (same time, same scale) – gain of more than 1–2 kg in 2 days suggests fluid retention.

  • Intake–output, oedema, breath sounds, JVP, BP, ECG; electrolytes with diuretics (potassium, sodium, creatinine).

  • Postural hypotension and hyperkalaemia with ACEI/ARB and spironolactone; bradycardia with β-blockers. 4. Supportive care

  • Propped-up (Fowler's) position, oxygen as ordered, rest and gradual activity, salt restriction (2–3 g/day) and fluid restriction if advised. 5. Patient education

  • How to check pulse; signs of toxicity to report; not to double missed doses; avoid over-the-counter antacids and herbal remedies without advice; take potassium-rich foods if on diuretics (unless contraindicated); daily weight chart; regular follow-up.

Conclusion Heart failure is treated with drugs that prolong life (ACEI/ARB/ARNI, β-blockers, aldosterone antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors) and drugs that relieve symptoms (diuretics, digoxin). Digoxin strengthens and slows the heart but has a narrow margin of safety – careful pulse checking, potassium monitoring and early recognition of toxicity are essential nursing duties.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Classify antianginal drugs. Describe the pharmacology of nitrates with nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Angina pectoris is chest pain caused by temporary myocardial ischaemia, when the heart's oxygen demand exceeds the supply through narrowed coronary arteries. It warns of coronary artery disease and the risk of myocardial infarction. Antianginal drugs either reduce the heart's oxygen demand (by lowering heart rate, preload, afterload or contractility) or increase oxygen supply (by dilating coronary arteries).

A. Classification of antianginal drugs 1. Nitrates

  • Short-acting: glyceryl trinitrate (GTN, nitroglycerin) – sublingual tablet/spray, IV; isosorbide dinitrate – sublingual.
  • Long-acting: isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN) – oral; isosorbide dinitrate oral; GTN transdermal patch/ointment. 2. β-adrenergic blockers – atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, propranolol. 3. Calcium channel blockers – amlodipine, nifedipine (long-acting), diltiazem, verapamil. 4. Potassium channel opener – nicorandil. 5. Others – ranolazine, ivabradine (slows heart rate), trimetazidine. 6. Drugs that prevent MI and death in coronary disease – antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel), statins, ACE inhibitors.

B. Pharmacology of nitrates 1. Mechanism of action

  • Nitrates release nitric oxide (NO) in vascular smooth muscle → activates guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cyclic GMP → relaxation of smooth muscle.
  • Venodilation (main effect) → blood pools in veins → ↓ venous return (preload) → smaller heart size and ↓ oxygen demand.
  • Arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload.

  • Coronary vasodilation – relieves coronary spasm and redistributes blood to ischaemic areas. 2. Pharmacokinetics

  • GTN undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism if swallowed – hence given sublingually (acts in 1–3 minutes, lasts 20–30 minutes), as spray, transdermally or IV.

  • ISMN is well absorbed orally and acts for 8–12 hours (or longer with sustained-release forms). 3. Uses

  • Acute attack of angina – sublingual GTN 0.3–0.6 mg (or 0.4 mg spray); can be repeated every 5 minutes up to 3 doses.

  • Prophylaxis – before exertion (sublingual) and chronic prevention (ISMN, patches).
  • Unstable angina / acute coronary syndrome – IV nitroglycerin infusion.
  • Acute left ventricular failure and pulmonary oedema – IV nitroglycerin.

  • Hypertensive emergency with myocardial ischaemia; oesophageal spasm, biliary colic; cyanide poisoning (amyl nitrite – historical). 4. Adverse effects

  • Throbbing headache (commonest – due to dilation of meningeal vessels), flushing, dizziness.

  • Postural hypotension, syncope, reflex tachycardia.
  • Tolerance with continuous use – prevented by a nitrate-free interval of 8–12 hours each day (e.g., remove patch at night; asymmetric ISMN dosing).

  • Rarely methaemoglobinaemia, rash. 5. Contraindications and interactions

  • Hypotension, hypovolaemia, raised intracranial pressure, right ventricular infarction, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

  • Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) taken within 24–48 hours – severe, possibly fatal hypotension.

C. Brief notes on other antianginal drugs

  • β-blockers – ↓ heart rate, contractility and BP → ↓ oxygen demand; drugs of choice for chronic stable angina and after MI; avoid in vasospastic angina, asthma.
  • CCBs – vasodilate (↓ afterload), relieve coronary spasm; diltiazem/verapamil also slow the heart; useful in vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina.
  • Nicorandil, ranolazine, ivabradine – add-on therapy.

D. Nursing responsibilities 1. During an attack

  • Ask the patient to stop activity and sit or lie down (prevents fainting from hypotension).
  • Give sublingual GTN; check BP before and 5 minutes after; repeat as ordered (maximum 3 doses in 15 minutes).
  • If pain persists after 3 doses or lasts more than 15–20 minutes – suspect myocardial infarction: call the doctor/emergency team, give oxygen if SpO₂ is low, obtain ECG, give aspirin as per protocol.

  • Record time, character and severity of pain and response. 2. Storage and handling of GTN

  • Keep tablets in the original airtight glass bottle, away from heat, light and moisture; do not mix with other tablets; replace the bottle as per manufacturer's advice after opening (potency falls).

  • A slight tingling or burning under the tongue indicates potent tablets. 3. Transdermal patches and ointment

  • Apply to a clean, dry, hairless area (chest, upper arm); rotate sites; remove the old patch; wear gloves while applying ointment; remove patches before defibrillation and MRI. 4. IV nitroglycerin

  • Use a glass bottle or non-PVC tubing as per policy (drug binds to PVC), infusion pump, frequent BP monitoring; titrate as ordered. 5. Monitoring – BP (postural), heart rate, headache (paracetamol may help; headache usually decreases with continued use). 6. Patient education

  • Carry GTN at all times; take it before activities that cause angina; sit down when taking it.

  • Avoid sildenafil/tadalafil with nitrates; avoid alcohol.
  • Lifestyle: stop smoking, healthy diet, weight control, regular graded exercise, control of BP, diabetes and cholesterol; take antiplatelets and statins regularly.
  • Know warning signs of heart attack and how to call for help (108 ambulance).

Conclusion Nitrates relieve angina quickly by dilating veins and coronary arteries, while β-blockers and CCBs prevent attacks. Correct use and storage of nitrates, prompt recognition of a possible heart attack and patient education are key nursing responsibilities.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Explain the antiarrhythmic drugs and the nurse's role in administering them.
answer_html:
Introduction Arrhythmias are abnormalities of the rate, rhythm or conduction of the heartbeat – e.g., atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. Antiarrhythmic drugs restore or control normal rhythm, but almost all can also cause arrhythmias (proarrhythmia), so they need close monitoring.

1. Classification (Vaughan Williams) | Class | Action | Examples | Main uses | |---|---|---|---| | I – Sodium channel blockers | Slow conduction | IA: quinidine, procainamide; IB: lignocaine (lidocaine), mexiletine; IC: flecainide, propafenone | Ventricular arrhythmias (lignocaine); AF (flecainide) | | II – β-blockers | ↓ sympathetic effects, slow AV conduction | Metoprolol, esmolol, propranolol | Sinus tachycardia, AF rate control, post-MI | | III – Potassium channel blockers | Prolong repolarisation and refractory period | Amiodarone, sotalol, dronedarone | VT/VF, AF | | IV – Calcium channel blockers | Slow AV node conduction | Verapamil, diltiazem | PSVT, AF rate control | | Others | — | Adenosine (PSVT), digoxin (AF), atropine (bradycardia), magnesium sulphate (torsades de pointes) | — |

2. Important drugs

  • Adenosine – drug of choice to terminate PSVT; 6 mg rapid IV push followed by a 20 ml saline flush through a large vein, then 12 mg if needed; causes brief flushing, chest discomfort and a few seconds of asystole – warn the patient.
  • Amiodarone – broad-spectrum; 300 mg IV in shock-resistant VF/pulseless VT; infusion in stable VT and AF; long-term adverse effects on thyroid, lungs, liver, eyes and skin (photosensitivity).
  • Lignocaine – ventricular arrhythmias; toxicity – drowsiness, numbness, confusion, seizures.
  • Verapamil – PSVT, AF rate control; may cause hypotension and heart block; never give IV with β-blockers.
  • β-blockers – bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm.

3. Nurse's role in administering antiarrhythmics

  1. Baseline assessment – ECG (rhythm, PR, QRS, QT intervals), heart rate, BP, electrolytes (potassium, magnesium), kidney and liver function, thyroid function (amiodarone).
  2. Continuous cardiac monitoring during IV therapy; keep a defibrillator, emergency drugs and airway equipment ready.
  3. Correct preparation – check concentration and dilution (e.g., amiodarone in 5% dextrose), use infusion pumps, label lines, double-check high-alert doses.
  4. Monitor for effects and side effects – conversion to sinus rhythm, rate control, bradycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation, new arrhythmias, phlebitis (amiodarone – use a large vein or central line for prolonged infusion).
  5. Oral therapy – check apical pulse and BP before doses; give at regular intervals.
  6. Maintain normal potassium and magnesium.
  7. Patient education – report palpitations, dizziness, fainting, breathlessness; regular follow-up tests; with amiodarone use sunscreen and get eye, thyroid, lung and liver checks.

Conclusion Antiarrhythmic drugs are powerful but potentially dangerous; continuous monitoring, correct dosing and readiness for emergencies are essential nursing responsibilities.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Explain cholinergic and anticholinergic drugs with their uses. Add a note on the management of organophosphate poisoning.
answer_html:
Introduction Cholinergic (parasympathomimetic) drugs mimic acetylcholine; anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) drugs block its muscarinic actions. They are widely used in anaesthesia, ophthalmology, myasthenia gravis and poisoning.

A. Cholinergic drugs 1. Directly acting – bethanechol (post-operative urinary retention, paralytic ileus), pilocarpine (glaucoma eye drops, dry mouth), carbachol. 2. Indirectly acting – anticholinesterases (prevent breakdown of acetylcholine)

  • Reversible: neostigmine (myasthenia gravis, reversal of non-depolarising muscle relaxants after surgery, urinary retention), pyridostigmine (myasthenia gravis), physostigmine (atropine poisoning), donepezil, rivastigmine (Alzheimer's disease).
  • Irreversible: organophosphates (insecticides – malathion, parathion, chlorpyrifos; nerve gases) – cause poisoning. Muscarinic effects: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchoconstriction, increased secretions (salivation, sweating, lacrimation), miosis, increased gut motility, urination.

B. Anticholinergic drugs

  • Natural: atropine, hyoscine (scopolamine).
  • Synthetic: glycopyrrolate (pre-anaesthetic), hyoscine butylbromide and dicyclomine (antispasmodics), ipratropium, tiotropium (bronchodilators), tropicamide, cyclopentolate (mydriatics), oxybutynin (overactive bladder), trihexyphenidyl (parkinsonism, drug-induced extrapyramidal effects). Uses of atropine
  1. Pre-anaesthetic – reduce secretions, prevent vagal bradycardia.
  2. Symptomatic bradycardia and heart block (0.5–1 mg IV).
  3. Antidote in organophosphate and mushroom (muscarine) poisoning.
  4. Antispasmodic in intestinal, biliary and renal colic.
  5. Mydriatic–cycloplegic for refraction in children and in iritis (prevents adhesions). Adverse effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, photophobia, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, hot dry skin and hyperthermia (especially children), confusion and delirium in elderly ("dry as a bone, red as a beet, hot as a hare, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter"). Contraindications: narrow-angle glaucoma, prostate enlargement, paralytic ileus, tachyarrhythmias.

C. Management of organophosphate poisoning (common in rural India)

  • Features: pinpoint pupils, excessive salivation and sweating, bronchorrhoea and wheeze, vomiting, diarrhoea, bradycardia, muscle fasciculations and weakness, confusion, coma; smell of pesticide. 1. Decontamination – remove contaminated clothes, wash skin with soap and water (staff wear gloves); gastric lavage only if early and airway protected. 2. Airway and breathing – suction secretions, oxygen, intubation and ventilation if needed. 3. Atropine – 1.8–3 mg IV bolus, doubling the dose every 5 minutes until atropinisation: clear chest on auscultation, heart rate above 80/min, systolic BP above 80 mmHg, dry axillae, pupils no longer pinpoint; then maintenance infusion. 4. Pralidoxime (PAM) – reactivates cholinesterase, given early as per protocol. 5. Diazepam for seizures; monitor for "intermediate syndrome" (weakness of neck and respiratory muscles 1–4 days later). 6. Psychiatric evaluation after recovery where poisoning was intentional, with safe storage of pesticides at home.

Nursing points Monitor pulse, temperature, urine output and pupils with these drugs; mouth care; protect eyes from light; watch for atropine toxicity (fever, delirium, tachycardia) during treatment of poisoning.

Conclusion Cholinergic and anticholinergic drugs have opposite effects on the parasympathetic system; atropine is a life-saving antidote in organophosphate poisoning when given in adequate, titrated doses.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Write a note on haematinics.
answer_html:
Definition Haematinics are substances required for the formation of red blood cells and used in the treatment and prevention of anaemia – mainly iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 (also erythropoietin). Iron-deficiency anaemia is the commonest nutritional problem in India, especially among children, adolescent girls and pregnant women (target of Anaemia Mukt Bharat).

1. Iron preparations (a) Oral iron (first choice)

  • Ferrous sulphate (200 mg contains about 60–65 mg elemental iron), ferrous fumarate, ferrous gluconate, ferrous ascorbate, carbonyl iron.
  • Dose: therapeutic – about 100–200 mg elemental iron daily for adults (as prescribed); prophylaxis – IFA tablets (60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid) daily in pregnancy and weekly for adolescents under national programmes.
  • Absorption is increased by vitamin C and empty stomach; reduced by tea, coffee, milk, calcium, antacids, tetracyclines.
  • Adverse effects: epigastric pain, nausea, constipation or diarrhoea, black stools (harmless), metallic taste, staining of teeth with liquid iron.

  • Response: reticulocytes rise in 5–10 days; Hb rises about 1–2 g/dl in 3–4 weeks; continue for 3 months after Hb normalises to refill stores. (b) Parenteral iron

  • Iron sucrose (IV, 100–200 mg per dose), ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) – large single IV doses (up to 1,000 mg) over 15 minutes, used in moderate–severe anaemia in pregnancy; iron dextran (IM/IV – higher anaphylaxis risk).

  • Indications: intolerance or non-compliance with oral iron, malabsorption, severe anaemia in late pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, continuous blood loss.
  • Adverse effects: anaphylaxis (keep adrenaline ready), hypotension, headache, phlebitis; pain and staining with IM injection (Z-track).
  • Acute iron poisoning in children (accidental overdose of tablets) – antidote desferrioxamine.

2. Folic acid

  • Uses: megaloblastic anaemia (5 mg/day), pregnancy and periconceptional period to prevent neural tube defects (400 µg/day), haemolytic anaemias, patients on antiepileptics/methotrexate (as advised).
  • Never give folic acid alone in vitamin B12 deficiency – it corrects anaemia but neurological damage progresses.

3. Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin, hydroxocobalamin)

  • Uses: pernicious anaemia (lifelong IM injections, e.g., 1,000 µg), B12 deficiency in strict vegetarians, after gastrectomy, ileal disease, long-term metformin/PPI use, neuropathy.

4. Erythropoietin – anaemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy.

Nursing responsibilities

  1. Give oral iron between meals with water or lemon juice; with meals if GI upset; avoid tea/milk/antacids within 1–2 hours.
  2. Liquid iron through a straw; brush teeth after.
  3. Warn about black stools; manage constipation with fibre and fluids.
  4. Parenteral iron: test dose/observe as per policy, infuse at the correct rate, monitor vital signs, keep emergency drugs ready.
  5. Monitor Hb; diet education – green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses, meat, fruits rich in vitamin C; deworming; keep iron tablets out of reach of children.

Conclusion Iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 correct most anaemias; correct administration and education ensure good response and safety.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Classify hypolipidaemic drugs. Explain the pharmacology of statins.
answer_html:
Introduction High levels of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides promote atherosclerosis, leading to coronary artery disease and stroke. Hypolipidaemic (lipid-lowering) drugs reduce blood lipids and, especially statins, reduce heart attacks, strokes and deaths.

1. Classification | Group | Examples | Main effect | |---|---|---| | HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) | Atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin | ↓ LDL (most powerful), ↓ TG, ↑ HDL slightly | | Cholesterol absorption inhibitor | Ezetimibe | ↓ LDL (add-on to statin) | | Bile acid sequestrants | Cholestyramine, colesevelam | ↓ LDL | | Fibrates | Fenofibrate, gemfibrozil | ↓ Triglycerides, ↑ HDL | | Nicotinic acid (niacin) | Niacin | ↓ TG, ↓ LDL, ↑ HDL | | Omega-3 fatty acids | Fish oil (EPA, DHA) | ↓ TG | | PCSK9 inhibitors | Evolocumab, alirocumab (injections); inclisiran | Marked ↓ LDL | | Others | Bempedoic acid | ↓ LDL |

2. Statins (a) Mechanism of action

  • Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis in the liver.
  • Fall in liver cholesterol increases LDL receptors on liver cells → more LDL removed from blood → LDL falls by 30–60%.

  • Pleiotropic effects – stabilise atherosclerotic plaques, reduce inflammation, improve endothelial function, antithrombotic. (b) Uses

  • Primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia.

  • Secondary prevention – after MI, angina, stroke, peripheral vascular disease (high-intensity statin regardless of LDL).
  • Primary prevention in high-risk people – diabetes, chronic kidney disease, multiple risk factors.

  • Familial hypercholesterolaemia. (c) Adverse effects

  • Myalgia (muscle pain) and myopathy; rarely rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown → dark urine, kidney failure) – risk higher with gemfibrozil, macrolides, azole antifungals, high doses, elderly, hypothyroidism.

  • Raised liver enzymes; GI upset, headache.
  • Slight increase in risk of diabetes.

  • Contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation and active liver disease. (d) Dosing

  • Simvastatin (short-acting) is given at bedtime because cholesterol synthesis is highest at night; atorvastatin and rosuvastatin (long-acting) can be taken any time.

3. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Baseline and periodic lipid profile, liver enzymes; CK if muscle symptoms.
  2. Teach patients to report unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine.
  3. Emphasise lifelong therapy – benefits are lost on stopping.
  4. Lifestyle: reduce saturated and trans fats (vanaspati, fried foods), increase fibre, fruits, vegetables, whole grains; regular exercise; weight control; stop smoking; limit alcohol (raises TG).
  5. Advise women of child-bearing age about contraception.

Conclusion Statins are the cornerstone of lipid-lowering therapy; with diet and exercise they markedly reduce cardiovascular events.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Explain plasma expanders and the drugs used in the treatment of shock.
answer_html:
Introduction Shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion. Treatment aims to restore circulating volume, cardiac output and blood pressure. Plasma expanders restore volume; vasopressors and inotropes support blood pressure and the heart; other drugs treat the cause.

A. Plasma expanders Definition: high-molecular-weight substances which, when infused IV, remain in the circulation and hold water by colloid osmotic pressure, thus expanding plasma volume. Properties of an ideal plasma expander: stays in circulation for a reasonable time, iso-oncotic, non-antigenic, non-toxic, no interference with blood grouping or clotting, stable, easily sterilised and cheap. 1. Natural colloids

  • Human albumin (5%, 20–25%) – hypoalbuminaemia, burns (after the first 24 hours), large-volume paracentesis in cirrhosis, hypovolaemia; expensive.

  • Fresh frozen plasma – mainly for clotting factor replacement, not as a volume expander. 2. Synthetic colloids

  • Dextrans (dextran 40, dextran 70) – may cause anaphylaxis, bleeding, kidney injury, and interfere with blood grouping and cross-matching (draw the sample before infusion).

  • Gelatin polymers – polygeline (Haemaccel), succinylated gelatin; allergic reactions.
  • Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) – use is now restricted because of kidney injury and increased mortality in sepsis and critically ill patients. 3. Crystalloids – normal saline, Ringer's lactate – first-line fluids for resuscitation in most types of shock; cheaper and safer, though larger volumes are needed. 4. Blood and blood components – for haemorrhagic shock.

B. Drugs used in shock 1. Vasopressors

  • Noradrenaline – first choice in septic shock; raises BP by vasoconstriction (target mean arterial pressure ≥65 mmHg).
  • Adrenaline – anaphylactic shock (IM first); refractory shock.

  • Vasopressin – add-on in septic shock; phenylephrine – vasodilatory hypotension. 2. Inotropes

  • Dobutamine – cardiogenic shock (improves contractility); dopamine; milrinone. 3. Corticosteroids

  • Hydrocortisone – adrenal crisis; refractory septic shock; adjunct in anaphylaxis. 4. Others

  • Antibiotics within the first hour in septic shock (after blood cultures).

  • Sodium bicarbonate only in severe acidosis; oxygen; analgesics; specific antidotes.

C. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Insert two large-bore IV cannulas; give fluids rapidly as ordered (warm fluids in massive resuscitation).
  2. Monitor BP, pulse, respiration, SpO₂, CVP, urine output (≥0.5 ml/kg/hour), level of consciousness, skin colour and capillary refill every 15 minutes initially.
  3. Watch for fluid overload (crepitations, raised JVP) and allergic reactions to colloids.
  4. Give vasopressors through a central line with infusion pump; check the site for extravasation; never stop suddenly.
  5. Keep the patient warm and flat with legs raised (unless contraindicated); record intake–output accurately.

Conclusion Prompt volume replacement with crystalloids, colloids or blood, supported by vasopressors and inotropes when needed, restores perfusion and saves lives in shock.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Classify β-adrenergic blockers. Explain their uses, adverse effects and nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction β-adrenergic blockers competitively block the effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline at β receptors. They are among the most widely used cardiovascular drugs and have proved to save lives after myocardial infarction and in heart failure.

1. Classification | Type | Examples | |---|---| | Non-selective (β1 + β2) | Propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol | | Cardioselective (β1) | Atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, esmolol (ultra-short IV), nebivolol | | With α1-blocking action | Labetalol, carvedilol | | With partial agonist activity | Pindolol |

2. Actions

  • Heart (β1): ↓ heart rate, ↓ force of contraction, ↓ AV conduction → ↓ cardiac output and oxygen demand.
  • ↓ renin release → ↓ BP.
  • Eye: ↓ aqueous humour production (timolol eye drops in glaucoma).
  • Non-selective drugs (β2 block): bronchoconstriction, block tremor and some anxiety symptoms.

3. Uses

  1. Hypertension (with other drugs; labetalol in pregnancy).
  2. Angina pectoris (chronic stable) – drugs of choice.
  3. After myocardial infarction – reduce re-infarction and death.
  4. Chronic heart failure – bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (started in low dose when stable).
  5. Arrhythmias – sinus tachycardia, AF rate control, PSVT; esmolol in acute settings.
  6. Thyrotoxicosis – control of palpitations and tremor (propranolol).
  7. Migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, performance anxiety (propranolol).
  8. Glaucoma – timolol eye drops.
  9. Portal hypertension – prevention of variceal bleeding (propranolol).

4. Adverse effects

  • Bradycardia, heart block, hypotension, worsening of acute heart failure.
  • Bronchospasm – dangerous in asthma (especially non-selective drugs).
  • Cold extremities, worsening of peripheral vascular disease.
  • Fatigue, sleep disturbances, nightmares (propranolol), depression, erectile dysfunction.
  • Masks the warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia (tremor, palpitations) in diabetics on insulin.
  • Withdrawal syndrome – rebound tachycardia, hypertension and angina/MI if stopped suddenly.

5. Contraindications Bronchial asthma, bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, acute decompensated heart failure, severe peripheral vascular disease.

6. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Check apical pulse and BP before each dose – withhold and inform if pulse is below 60/min or systolic BP below the ordered limit.
  2. Ask about wheeze/breathlessness; avoid non-selective drugs in asthmatics.
  3. Monitor diabetics' blood glucose closely – teach that sweating may be the only warning of hypoglycaemia.
  4. Never stop suddenly – taper over 1–2 weeks as ordered.
  5. Teach patients to rise slowly, report dizziness, fainting, swelling of feet or breathlessness.

Conclusion β-blockers protect the heart by reducing its workload; careful monitoring of pulse, BP, breathing and blood sugar ensures their safe use.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: List two uses and two adverse effects of warfarin.
answer_html:
Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant (vitamin K antagonist).

Uses (any two)

  1. Treatment and long-term prevention of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
  2. Atrial fibrillation – prevention of stroke.
  3. Prosthetic (mechanical) heart valves – prevention of valve thrombosis.
  4. Rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation; mural thrombus after MI.

Adverse effects (any two)

  1. Bleeding – gums, nose, urine, GI tract, intracranial (most important).
  2. Teratogenicity – fetal warfarin syndrome (contraindicated in pregnancy).
  3. Skin necrosis, purple toe syndrome, alopecia.

Monitored by INR (target 2–3); antidote vitamin K.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Write a note on injection amiodarone.
answer_html:
Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug (also has class I, II and IV actions); it blocks potassium channels, prolonging the action potential and refractory period.

Uses of IV amiodarone

  • Shock-resistant ventricular fibrillation / pulseless VT in cardiac arrest – 300 mg IV bolus (after the third shock), then 150 mg.
  • Stable ventricular tachycardia; atrial fibrillation/flutter (rate or rhythm control).

Administration: infusion of 150 mg over 10 minutes, then maintenance infusion (e.g., 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min) – diluted in 5% dextrose, through a large vein or central line, using an infusion pump.

Adverse effects: hypotension, bradycardia, QT prolongation, phlebitis; long-term – thyroid dysfunction, pulmonary fibrosis, liver injury, corneal deposits, photosensitivity. Nursing: continuous ECG and BP monitoring; inspect IV site.

subject: Pharmacology I
unit_title: Drugs Used in Cardiovascular and Blood Disorders
question: Define angina pectoris and name two drugs used in its treatment.
answer_html:
Angina pectoris is a clinical syndrome of chest pain or discomfort (retrosternal, pressing or squeezing, often radiating to the left arm, neck or jaw) caused by transient myocardial ischaemia – when the heart's oxygen demand exceeds supply through narrowed coronary arteries. It is typically brought on by exertion, emotion, cold or heavy meals, lasts a few minutes and is relieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin.

Drugs used (any two)

  1. Glyceryl trinitrate (nitroglycerin) – sublingual, for the acute attack.
  2. Isosorbide mononitrate – oral, for prevention.
  3. β-blockers – atenolol, metoprolol.
  4. Calcium channel blockers – amlodipine, diltiazem. (Also aspirin and statins to prevent MI.)

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Describe the types of insulin preparations, mechanism of action, uses, adverse effects and nursing responsibilities in insulin therapy.

diagram.caption: Onset, peak and duration of insulin preparations (graph)

answer_html:
Introduction Insulin, a hormone secreted by the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans, is essential for life in type 1 diabetes and is needed by many people with type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes and diabetic emergencies. It was discovered by Banting and Best in 1921. Insulin is a high-alert medicine – wrong type, dose or timing can cause severe hypoglycaemia or ketoacidosis – so nurses must handle it with special care.

A. Sources

  • Animal (bovine, porcine) – older, more allergic.
  • Human insulin – made by recombinant DNA technology.
  • Insulin analogues – modified human insulin with faster or longer action.

B. Types of insulin preparations (by onset and duration) | Type | Examples | Onset | Peak | Duration | Appearance / timing | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Rapid-acting analogues | Lispro, aspart, glulisine | 5–15 min | 1–2 h | 3–5 h | Clear; just before (or with) meals | | Short-acting (regular/soluble) | Regular human insulin | 30–60 min | 2–4 h | 6–8 h | Clear; 30 minutes before meals; only type routinely given IV | | Intermediate-acting | NPH (isophane) | 1–2 h | 4–12 h | 12–18 h | Cloudy; twice daily | | Long-acting analogues | Glargine, detemir, degludec | 1–2 h | No marked peak | 24 h (degludec >40 h) | Clear; once daily, same time ("basal") | | Premixed | 30/70 (30% regular + 70% NPH), analogue mixes | — | Dual | — | Cloudy; before breakfast and dinner |

  • Concentrations: U-40 (40 units/ml) and U-100 (100 units/ml) are both available in India – the syringe must match the vial (U-40 syringe for U-40 vial); insulin pens use U-100 cartridges.

C. Mechanism of action

  • Insulin binds to the insulin receptor (tyrosine kinase) on cell membranes, triggering intracellular signals.
  • Liver: ↑ glycogen synthesis; ↓ glycogen breakdown, ↓ gluconeogenesis, ↓ ketone formation.
  • Muscle and fat: ↑ glucose uptake (via GLUT-4 transporters), ↑ protein and fat synthesis; ↓ breakdown of fat (lipolysis) and protein.
  • Potassium – drives K⁺ into cells (↓ serum potassium).
  • Net effect: lowers blood glucose and promotes storage of fuel.

D. Uses

  1. Type 1 diabetes mellitus – essential, lifelong (basal–bolus regimen or pump).
  2. Type 2 diabetes – when oral drugs fail, in pregnancy, severe hyperglycaemia, kidney or liver failure, acute illness and surgery.
  3. Gestational diabetes not controlled by diet.
  4. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state – IV regular insulin infusion (0.1 unit/kg/hour) with fluids and potassium.
  5. Hyperkalaemia – regular insulin 10 units with 25 g glucose (50 ml of 50% dextrose) IV.
  6. Hyperglycaemia during total parenteral nutrition, critical illness, steroid therapy.

E. Adverse effects

  1. Hypoglycaemia – the commonest and most dangerous effect.
    • Causes: excess dose, missed or delayed meal, unusual exercise, alcohol, kidney failure, wrong insulin type/syringe.
    • Features: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety, headache, blurred vision, confusion, abnormal behaviour, convulsions, coma.
    • Treatment: conscious patient – 15–20 g fast-acting sugar (3–4 teaspoons glucose/sugar, glucose tablets, fruit juice), recheck after 15 minutes ("rule of 15"), then a snack; unconscious – IV 25–50 ml of 50% dextrose (or 10% dextrose) or glucagon 1 mg IM/SC.
  2. Lipodystrophy – lipohypertrophy (lumps due to repeated injection at the same site; erratic absorption) or lipoatrophy.
  3. Local and systemic allergy (rare with human insulin).
  4. Weight gain, hypokalaemia (IV therapy), insulin oedema.
  5. Somogyi effect (rebound morning hyperglycaemia after night hypoglycaemia) – needs dose adjustment.

F. Nursing responsibilities in insulin therapy 1. Checking the order and preparation

  • Verify type, dose (in units), time and route; two-nurse independent double-check (high-alert drug).
  • Never use abbreviations like "U" (may be misread as 0) – write "units".
  • Match the syringe with the vial strength (U-40/U-100); use insulin syringes only.
  • Check expiry date, appearance (clear insulin must be clear; cloudy NPH uniformly cloudy after mixing).
  • Roll cloudy insulin gently between palms – do not shake (froth gives inaccurate dose).
  • Mixing regular and NPH: inject air into NPH first, then regular; draw clear (regular) before cloudy (NPH); never mix glargine/detemir with other insulins.

2. Administration

  • Subcutaneous route (IV only regular insulin, by infusion pump with frequent glucose checks).
  • Sites: abdomen (fastest, most consistent absorption; 5 cm away from the umbilicus), outer thighs, back of upper arms, upper outer buttocks.
  • Rotate sites systematically within an area to prevent lipohypertrophy; avoid injecting into lumps, scars or bruises.
  • Pinch the skin, insert at 90° (45° in thin persons/children), inject slowly, wait 5–10 seconds (pens 10 seconds) before withdrawing; do not massage.
  • Pen technique – attach new needle, prime with 2 units, dial dose, inject, hold 10 seconds.
  • Timing with meals – regular insulin 30 minutes before meals; rapid analogues just before eating; ensure food is available.

3. Monitoring

  • Capillary blood glucose before meals and at bedtime (more often in DKA/illness); HbA1c every 3 months.
  • Watch for signs of hypoglycaemia, especially at night, after exercise or when meals are missed; keep glucose/50% dextrose and glucagon ready.
  • In DKA – hourly glucose, electrolytes (especially potassium), fluid balance.

4. Storage

  • Unopened vials/pens – in the refrigerator at 2–8 °C; never freeze (discard frozen insulin); not in the door shelf.
  • In-use vial/pen – at room temperature (below about 25–30 °C) for up to 28 days (some products longer), away from direct sunlight and heat; label with date of opening.
  • During travel – carry in insulated bags; never in the checked baggage.

5. Patient education

  • Self-injection technique, site rotation, dose adjustment as advised, self-monitoring of blood glucose.
  • Recognition and treatment of hypoglycaemia; always carry sugar/glucose and a diabetes identity card.
  • Sick-day rules – never stop insulin during illness; check sugar more often; drink fluids; seek help if vomiting or ketones.
  • Diet, exercise, foot care, regular follow-up; safe disposal of needles in a hard container.

Conclusion Insulin preparations differ in onset and duration, allowing basal and mealtime control of blood sugar. Because errors are common and dangerous, careful checking, correct technique and storage, monitoring for hypoglycaemia and thorough patient education are central nursing responsibilities.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the pharmacology of thyroid hormone preparations and antithyroid drugs, with nursing responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Thyroid hormone synthesis and sites of action of antithyroid drugs
labels: oxidation and coupling by thyroid peroxidase (blocked by carbimazole/PTU)

answer_html:
Introduction The thyroid gland produces thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which regulate metabolism, growth and development. Hypothyroidism (underactivity) is treated with thyroid hormone replacement, while hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis), commonly due to Graves' disease or toxic nodular goitre, is treated with antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine or surgery. Thyroid disorders are common in India, especially among women.

A. Thyroid hormone preparations 1. Drugs

  • Levothyroxine sodium (L-T4) – drug of choice for replacement.

  • Liothyronine (T3) – rapid action; used in myxoedema coma and special situations. 2. Mechanism – thyroid hormones enter cells, bind to nuclear receptors and alter gene expression → increase metabolic rate, oxygen consumption, heat production, heart rate, growth and brain development. 3. Uses

  • Primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, after thyroidectomy or radioiodine) – lifelong.

  • Congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism) – start as early as possible after birth to prevent intellectual disability (newborn screening).
  • Myxoedema coma – IV levothyroxine/liothyronine with steroids and supportive care.

  • Simple non-toxic goitre, TSH suppression after surgery for thyroid cancer. 4. Dose and administration

  • About 1.6 µg/kg/day in adults; start low (12.5–25 µg) in elderly and heart patients and increase slowly.

  • Take on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, with water; separate from calcium, iron, antacids, soy by 4 hours.

  • Check TSH 6–8 weeks after each dose change. 5. Adverse effects (overdose → iatrogenic hyperthyroidism)

  • Palpitations, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, angina (elderly), tremor, nervousness, insomnia, heat intolerance, weight loss, diarrhoea; long-term – osteoporosis.

B. Antithyroid drugs – classification | Group | Drugs | Action | |---|---|---| | 1. Thioamides (inhibit hormone synthesis) | Carbimazole (converted to methimazole), methimazole, propylthiouracil (PTU) | Inhibit thyroid peroxidase – block iodination and coupling | | 2. Iodides (inhibit hormone release) | Lugol's iodine (5% iodine + 10% KI), potassium iodide | Rapidly inhibit release; reduce gland size and vascularity | | 3. Radioactive iodine | I-131 | Destroys thyroid tissue by β-radiation | | 4. β-blockers (symptomatic) | Propranolol | Control tachycardia, tremor, anxiety; reduce T4→T3 conversion | | 5. Others | Corticosteroids, cholestyramine | Thyroid storm (reduce conversion and absorption) |

C. Thioamides – carbimazole and PTU

  • Mechanism: inhibit thyroid peroxidase → block oxidation of iodide, iodination of tyrosine and coupling → ↓ synthesis of T4 and T3. PTU also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
  • Onset: slow – clinical improvement in 3–6 weeks (stored hormone must be used up); β-blockers control symptoms meanwhile.
  • Uses: Graves' disease (12–18 months course), preparation for surgery or radioiodine, thyroid storm (PTU preferred), first trimester of pregnancy (PTU preferred); carbimazole in later pregnancy and in most other patients.
  • Adverse effects
    • Agranulocytosis (rare but serious) – presents with sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers – stop the drug and check WBC count immediately.
    • Skin rash, itching, joint pains, altered taste.
    • Hepatotoxicity – especially severe with PTU.
    • Hypothyroidism and goitre with overdose; carbimazole in early pregnancy may cause scalp defects in the baby.

D. Iodides

  • Uses: pre-operative preparation for thyroidectomy (7–10 days – makes the gland firm and less vascular), thyroid storm (given 1 hour after thioamide), protection of the thyroid in radiation emergencies (potassium iodide).
  • Adverse effects: iodism – metallic taste, burning mouth, excessive salivation, rash, sore gums; effect "escapes" after 2–3 weeks, so used short term.

E. Radioactive iodine (I-131)

  • Taken orally; concentrated in the thyroid, where its β-rays destroy thyroid cells over 2–3 months.
  • Uses: Graves' disease (adults, relapses), toxic nodular goitre, thyroid cancer (higher doses).
  • Adverse effects: late hypothyroidism (needs lifelong levothyroxine), radiation thyroiditis.
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding; pregnancy to be avoided for at least 6 months after.
  • Radiation precautions for some days – distance from children and pregnant women, separate utensils, flushing toilet twice, good hand washing.

F. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Monitoring – pulse, BP, weight, sleep, bowel habits, temperature; TSH and T4 levels; WBC count on thioamides if infection symptoms appear.
  2. Teach warning signs: report sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers (agranulocytosis) and jaundice immediately; report palpitations, chest pain (overdose of levothyroxine).
  3. Administration: levothyroxine before breakfast on empty stomach; do not change brands without advice; iodine drops diluted in milk or juice and taken through a straw (prevents staining of teeth, masks taste).
  4. Pregnancy – inform the doctor if planning or pregnant (drug change and dose adjustment needed).
  5. Thyroid storm – cool environment, fluids, antipyretics (paracetamol, not aspirin), monitor cardiac rhythm, give drugs in correct sequence (thioamide, then iodide), steroids, β-blockers.
  6. Radioiodine – explain radiation safety at home; follow-up for hypothyroidism.
  7. Education – lifelong therapy in hypothyroidism; regular tests; iodised salt for prevention of iodine deficiency goitre in the community (National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme).

Conclusion Levothyroxine replaces deficient hormone, while thioamides, iodides, radioactive iodine and β-blockers control excess. Correct timing, monitoring of thyroid function and blood counts, and education about warning signs make thyroid drug therapy safe.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Write a note on oral hypoglycaemic drugs – classification, indications and nursing implications.
answer_html:
