Introduction Oral hypoglycaemic agents (OHAs) – more correctly oral antidiabetic drugs – lower blood glucose in type 2 diabetes mellitus by increasing insulin secretion, improving insulin sensitivity or reducing glucose absorption/reabsorption. They are not useful in type 1 diabetes.

1. Classification | Group | Examples | Mechanism | |---|---|---| | Biguanides | Metformin | ↓ hepatic glucose production, ↑ insulin sensitivity | | Sulphonylureas | Glimepiride, gliclazide, glipizide, glibenclamide | ↑ insulin release from β-cells | | Meglitinides | Repaglinide, nateglinide | Short-acting insulin secretagogues | | Thiazolidinediones | Pioglitazone | ↑ insulin sensitivity (PPAR-γ agonist) | | α-Glucosidase inhibitors | Acarbose, voglibose | ↓ carbohydrate digestion in gut | | DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) | Sitagliptin, vildagliptin, teneligliptin, linagliptin | Prolong incretin (GLP-1) action | | SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins) | Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin | ↑ urinary glucose excretion | | GLP-1 receptor agonists | Oral semaglutide (others injectable) | ↑ insulin, ↓ glucagon, slow gastric emptying, ↓ appetite |

2. Indications

  • Type 2 diabetes not controlled by diet and exercise – metformin is first-line (unless contraindicated), with other drugs added as needed.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors also protect the heart and kidneys (heart failure, chronic kidney disease).
  • Metformin – prediabetes in high-risk persons, polycystic ovary syndrome.

3. Contraindications

  • Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe infections, major surgery (switch to insulin), pregnancy (insulin preferred), severe kidney or liver disease (dose adjustments; metformin avoided when eGFR is very low).

4. Important adverse effects

  • Sulphonylureas: hypoglycaemia (especially glibenclamide in the elderly), weight gain.
  • Metformin: GI upset (diarrhoea, metallic taste), vitamin B12 deficiency, rare lactic acidosis (kidney failure, iodinated contrast, alcohol).
  • Pioglitazone: weight gain, oedema, heart failure, fractures.
  • Acarbose: flatulence, bloating.
  • DPP-4 inhibitors: nasopharyngitis, rarely pancreatitis.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: genital fungal infections, UTI, dehydration, rare euglycaemic ketoacidosis.

5. Nursing implications

  1. Timing: sulphonylureas 15–30 minutes before breakfast; metformin with or after meals; acarbose with the first bite of the meal.
  2. Monitor blood glucose and HbA1c; watch for hypoglycaemia, especially in the elderly, kidney disease and missed meals – teach recognition and treatment (glucose/sugar; with acarbose use glucose, not table sugar).
  3. Hold metformin before iodinated contrast studies and major surgery as ordered; monitor kidney function.
  4. With SGLT2 inhibitors – good genital hygiene, adequate fluids; stop during acute illness with vomiting as advised.
  5. Education: diet, exercise, weight control, regular meals, foot care, eye checks, adherence; do not stop drugs when sugar becomes normal; avoid alcohol.

Conclusion OHAs control blood glucose in type 2 diabetes through different mechanisms; correct timing, monitoring for hypoglycaemia and lifestyle support are key nursing roles.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Write a note on corticosteroid drugs.
answer_html:
Introduction Corticosteroids are hormones of the adrenal cortex and their synthetic analogues. Glucocorticoids (cortisol-like) have powerful anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects; mineralocorticoids (aldosterone-like) regulate salt and water. They are life-saving in many diseases but cause serious adverse effects with long-term use.

1. Classification (glucocorticoids by duration) | Duration | Drug | Equivalent dose | Mineralocorticoid effect | |---|---|---|---| | Short-acting | Hydrocortisone | 20 mg | Present | | Intermediate | Prednisolone, methylprednisolone, triamcinolone | 5 mg / 4 mg | Low | | Long-acting | Dexamethasone, betamethasone | 0.75 mg | Nil | - Mineralocorticoid: fludrocortisone. - Topical/local: inhaled (budesonide), intranasal, eye drops, skin creams (clobetasol, betamethasone), intra-articular injections.

2. Mechanism of action Glucocorticoids enter cells and bind cytoplasmic receptors; the complex alters gene transcription → ↓ synthesis of inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, leukotrienes – via inhibition of phospholipase A2 – and cytokines), ↓ migration of white cells, ↓ capillary permeability, suppression of lymphocytes and antibody formation; stabilisation of membranes.

3. Uses

  • Replacement therapy: Addison's disease, adrenal crisis (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg), congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
  • Allergic and inflammatory conditions: acute severe asthma, COPD exacerbation, anaphylaxis (adjunct to adrenaline), urticaria, angioedema, allergic rhinitis.
  • Autoimmune/inflammatory diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, nephrotic syndrome, ulcerative colitis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, ITP, vasculitis.
  • Skin diseases: eczema, psoriasis, pemphigus.
  • Organ transplantation – prevention and treatment of rejection.
  • Malignancies: leukaemias, lymphomas (with chemotherapy); cerebral oedema around tumours (dexamethasone).
  • Antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone/betamethasone) to mature fetal lungs in threatened preterm labour.
  • Severe COVID-19 needing oxygen (dexamethasone), TB meningitis, septic shock (refractory), chemotherapy-induced vomiting.

4. Adverse effects (long-term, high dose)

  • Cushing's syndrome – moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, thin skin, striae, easy bruising, acne.
  • Hyperglycaemia (steroid diabetes), hypertension, salt and water retention, hypokalaemia.
  • Osteoporosis and fractures, avascular necrosis of femoral head, muscle wasting.
  • Increased susceptibility to infections (reactivation of TB, fungal infections) and masking of infection signs; delayed wound healing.
  • Peptic ulcer (especially with NSAIDs), cataract, glaucoma, growth retardation in children, mood changes, psychosis, insomnia.
  • HPA-axis suppression → adrenal crisis if stopped suddenly.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Give oral steroids in the morning (single dose) with food or milk – mimics the natural rhythm and reduces gastric irritation.
  2. Never stop abruptly after more than 2–3 weeks of therapy – taper as ordered; patient to carry a steroid card; extra dose during illness or surgery as advised.
  3. Monitor BP, weight, blood sugar, electrolytes, signs of infection (fever may be masked), black stools, mood changes, eye problems.
  4. Encourage diet rich in protein, calcium and potassium, low in salt and sugar; calcium and vitamin D supplements; exercise.
  5. Protect from infection – hand hygiene, avoid contact with chickenpox/measles; no live vaccines on high-dose steroids.
  6. Inhaled steroids – rinse mouth; topical steroids – thin layer, avoid face unless advised.

Conclusion Corticosteroids are powerful anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive drugs; the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, careful monitoring and gradual withdrawal minimise their harm.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the drugs used in disorders of calcium metabolism.
answer_html:
Introduction Calcium is needed for bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve conduction, blood clotting and heart function. Its level is controlled by parathyroid hormone (PTH), vitamin D and calcitonin. Disorders include hypocalcaemia (tetany), hypercalcaemia, osteoporosis, rickets/osteomalacia and Paget's disease.

1. Calcium salts

  • Oral: calcium carbonate (40% elemental calcium – take with food), calcium citrate (can be taken any time).
  • Injectable: calcium gluconate 10% (10 ml contains about 90 mg elemental calcium), calcium chloride (more irritant).
  • Uses: osteoporosis (with vitamin D), pregnancy and lactation supplements (as per national guidelines), rickets/osteomalacia, hypocalcaemic tetany (e.g., after thyroidectomy – 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly over 10 minutes), hyperkalaemia (protects the heart), antidote for magnesium sulphate toxicity in eclampsia, calcium channel blocker overdose.
  • Adverse effects: constipation, hypercalcaemia, kidney stones; IV – bradycardia and arrhythmias if given fast, tissue necrosis on extravasation.

2. Vitamin D preparations

  • Cholecalciferol (D3) – e.g., 60,000 IU weekly for deficiency (as prescribed); ergocalciferol (D2).
  • Active forms – calcitriol, alfacalcidol – for chronic kidney disease and hypoparathyroidism (do not need kidney activation).
  • Uses: rickets, osteomalacia, vitamin D deficiency, osteoporosis, hypoparathyroidism.
  • Toxicity: hypercalcaemia – nausea, constipation, thirst, polyuria, confusion, kidney stones.

3. Bisphosphonates

  • Alendronate (70 mg weekly), risedronate, ibandronate; zoledronic acid (IV once yearly).
  • Mechanism: bind to bone and inhibit osteoclastic bone resorption.
  • Uses: osteoporosis, Paget's disease, hypercalcaemia of malignancy, bone metastases.
  • Administration (oral): take first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water, remain upright for 30 minutes, no food, drinks or other drugs for 30 minutes.
  • Adverse effects: oesophagitis/ulcers, flu-like reaction (IV), osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare), atypical femoral fractures.

4. Other drugs

  • Calcitonin (salmon – injection/nasal spray) – hypercalcaemia, Paget's disease, pain of osteoporotic fractures.
  • Teriparatide (PTH analogue) – builds bone in severe osteoporosis.
  • Denosumab (RANKL antibody), raloxifene (selective oestrogen receptor modulator) – osteoporosis.
  • Cinacalcet – hyperparathyroidism.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Give IV calcium slowly with ECG monitoring; check the IV site; avoid in digoxin-treated patients unless ordered (arrhythmias); do not mix with bicarbonate or phosphate.
  2. Watch for signs of hypocalcaemia (tingling, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs) and hypercalcaemia (constipation, polyuria, confusion).
  3. Separate oral calcium from iron, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and levothyroxine by 2–4 hours.
  4. Teach correct bisphosphonate administration.
  5. Advise sunlight exposure, calcium-rich diet (milk, ragi, green leafy vegetables), weight-bearing exercise and fall prevention for osteoporosis.

Conclusion Calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates and related drugs maintain calcium balance and bone strength when used correctly.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: List the oral hypoglycaemic agents.
answer_html:
Oral hypoglycaemic (antidiabetic) agents

  1. Biguanides – metformin.
  2. Sulphonylureas – glimepiride, gliclazide, glipizide, glibenclamide.
  3. Meglitinides – repaglinide, nateglinide.
  4. Thiazolidinediones – pioglitazone.
  5. α-Glucosidase inhibitors – acarbose, voglibose, miglitol.
  6. DPP-4 inhibitors – sitagliptin, vildagliptin, teneligliptin, linagliptin.
  7. SGLT2 inhibitors – dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin.
  8. Oral GLP-1 agonist – semaglutide. Metformin is the first-line drug for type 2 diabetes.

Note: sulphonylureas can cause hypoglycaemia; metformin and gliptins rarely do when used alone. They are not used in type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis – insulin is needed.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Write the uses and adverse effects of anabolic steroids.
answer_html:
Anabolic steroids are synthetic derivatives of testosterone with increased anabolic (protein-building) and reduced androgenic effects – e.g., nandrolone decanoate, oxandrolone, stanozolol, oxymetholone.

Uses

  • Catabolic states – after major surgery, severe burns, chronic illness, wasting in HIV/cancer.
  • Aplastic anaemia and anaemia of chronic kidney disease (older use – stimulate red cell production).
  • Hereditary angioedema (danazol/stanozolol).

Adverse effects

  • Virilisation in women (hirsutism, deep voice, menstrual irregularity), acne.
  • Liver damage (cholestatic jaundice, tumours), adverse lipid profile, heart disease.
  • Testicular atrophy, infertility, gynaecomastia; premature closure of epiphyses in children; aggression. They are misused by athletes and body-builders and banned in sports.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Describe the topical drugs used in skin disorders – scabicides, antifungals and silver sulphadiazine – with the nurse's responsibilities in topical application.

diagram.caption: Topical drug application – fingertip unit and correct technique
labels: cream squeezed from fingertip to first crease (one fingertip unit)
thin layer in direction of hair growth

answer_html:
Introduction Skin diseases – scabies, fungal infections (ringworm), bacterial infections, eczema and burns – are very common in India, especially in crowded, hot and humid conditions. Topical drugs applied directly to the skin act at the site with minimal systemic effects. The nurse's correct application technique and health teaching are as important as the drug.

A. Dosage forms used on skin

  • Lotions – liquid; for hairy and large areas, acute oozing lesions.
  • Creams – oil-in-water; for moist lesions and flexures; cosmetically acceptable.
  • Ointments – greasy; for dry, scaly, chronic lesions; better penetration.
  • Gels, pastes, powders, shampoos, solutions.

B. Scabicides and pediculicides Scabies is caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei; it causes intense night-time itching and spreads by close contact within families and hostels. 1. Permethrin 5% cream (drug of choice)

  • Mechanism: synthetic pyrethroid; blocks sodium channels in the nerve membranes of the mite → paralysis and death.
  • Application: after a bath, dry the skin; apply a thin layer to the entire body from the neck down (including between fingers and toes, under nails, genitals, buttocks) – include the scalp and face in infants and the elderly; leave for 8–14 hours (overnight), then wash off; repeat after 7 days.
  • 1% lotion – head lice (apply to washed hair for 10 minutes, then rinse).

  • Adverse effects: mild burning, itching, rash; safe in children above 2 months and in pregnancy. 2. Benzyl benzoate 25% emulsion

  • Cheap and effective; applied to the whole body below the neck; repeated applications as directed.

  • Irritant – burning sensation; dilute for children; avoid eyes and mucosa. 3. Gamma benzene hexachloride (lindane) 1%

  • Effective but neurotoxic (seizures) – avoid in infants, pregnant and lactating women, and on broken skin; now rarely used. 4. Others

  • Crotamiton 10% (also antipruritic), sulphur ointment 5–10% (safe in infants and pregnancy; messy, smelly).

  • Oral ivermectin (200 µg/kg, two doses one week apart) – crusted scabies, outbreaks in institutions. Important: treat all family members/close contacts at the same time, even without symptoms; itching may persist for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment.

C. Topical antifungal drugs 1. Imidazoles – clotrimazole 1%, miconazole 2%, ketoconazole 2%, econazole, luliconazole, sertaconazole.

  • Mechanism: inhibit fungal ergosterol synthesis (lanosterol demethylase) → damaged fungal cell membrane.
  • Uses: tinea (ringworm) of body, groin, feet; cutaneous candidiasis (intertrigo, nappy rash, paronychia); pityriasis versicolor; oral thrush (clotrimazole mouth paint, miconazole oral gel); vaginal candidiasis (clotrimazole pessary); otomycosis (ear drops); ketoconazole shampoo for dandruff.

  • Adverse effects: local irritation, burning, allergy (rare). 2. Allylamines – terbinafine 1% cream – fungicidal for dermatophytes. 3. Others – Whitfield's ointment (benzoic acid + salicylic acid), nystatin (Candida only), tolnaftate, amorolfine and ciclopirox nail lacquers. Points:

  • Apply twice daily to the lesion and 2–3 cm of surrounding normal skin, and continue for 2 weeks after the lesion clears (usually 4 weeks in total).

  • Avoid steroid–antifungal–antibiotic combination creams sold over the counter – steroids worsen and spread fungal infection ("tinea incognito"), a growing problem in India.
  • Extensive or nail and scalp infections need oral antifungals (terbinafine, itraconazole, griseofulvin).

D. Silver sulphadiazine 1% cream

  • Mechanism: releases silver ions (bind bacterial DNA and cell membrane) and sulphadiazine – broad-spectrum activity against Gram-negative bacteria including Pseudomonas, Gram-positive bacteria and Candida.
  • Uses: prevention and treatment of infection in burn wounds (partial- and full-thickness), sometimes in chronic wounds and ulcers.
  • Application: clean the wound, then apply with a sterile gloved hand or spatula as a layer about 2–3 mm thick, once or twice daily; cover with sterile dressing or leave open as ordered; remove old cream before reapplying.
  • Adverse effects: burning, rash (sulpha allergy), transient leucopenia, skin discolouration; may delay epithelialisation on long use.
  • Avoid in sulphonamide allergy, late pregnancy and newborns under 2 months (risk of kernicterus), and caution in G6PD deficiency.

E. Other topical agents (in brief)

  • Antibacterials: mupirocin, fusidic acid (impetigo, infected wounds).
  • Keratolytics: salicylic acid (warts, psoriasis); emollients: liquid paraffin, petroleum jelly, urea.
  • Acne: benzoyl peroxide, adapalene, clindamycin gel; psoriasis: coal tar, calcipotriol; sunscreens.

F. Nurse's responsibilities in topical application

  1. Hand hygiene; wear gloves (protects the nurse and prevents contamination).
  2. Explain the procedure; ensure privacy.
  3. Clean the skin gently, remove previous application, pat dry (unless instructed otherwise).
  4. Use a sterile spatula/gloved hand; never put used fingers or swabs back into the container.
  5. Apply a thin, even layer in the direction of hair growth (prevents folliculitis); use the fingertip unit to measure creams.
  6. Avoid eyes, mouth and mucous membranes unless the preparation is meant for them.
  7. Cover with dressing only if ordered – occlusion increases absorption (and side effects).
  8. Observe for irritation, allergy and response; document.
  9. Children absorb more through the skin – use correct strength and area.
  10. Health education
    • In scabies: wash clothes, bedding and towels in hot water and dry in the sun, or seal them in a bag for 72 hours; treat all contacts; trim nails.
    • In fungal infections: keep skin dry, loose cotton clothing, separate towels, dry between toes, change socks daily; do not stop treatment early.
    • Do not buy steroid-containing creams without prescription.

Conclusion Scabicides, antifungals and silver sulphadiazine are effective when applied correctly, for the full duration, with treatment of contacts and good hygiene – areas where the nurse's skill and teaching make the difference.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the antipruritic agents and the management of itching.
answer_html:
Introduction Pruritus (itching) is the most common skin symptom. It may be due to skin diseases (eczema, urticaria, scabies, fungal infection, dry skin), systemic diseases (jaundice/cholestasis, kidney failure, thyroid disease, diabetes, iron deficiency, lymphoma), drugs or pregnancy. Scratching damages skin, causes infection and disturbs sleep. Antipruritics are drugs that relieve itching.

1. Topical antipruritics

  • Calamine lotion (zinc oxide with ferric oxide) – cooling and mildly astringent; chickenpox, insect bites, sunburn, urticaria; shake well, dab on, allow to dry.
  • Menthol (0.25–1%) and camphor – produce a cooling sensation, counter-irritants.
  • Crotamiton 10% – antipruritic and scabicide.
  • Local anaesthetics – pramoxine, lidocaine (short-term; benzocaine may sensitise).
  • Topical corticosteroids – for itching due to inflammatory dermatoses (eczema, contact dermatitis, lichen planus).
  • Emollients/moisturisers – liquid paraffin, petroleum jelly, urea creams – most important for dry skin (xerosis) itching in the elderly.
  • Doxepin cream, capsaicin (localised neuropathic itch).

2. Systemic antipruritics

  • H1 antihistamines
    • Sedating (hydroxyzine, chlorpheniramine, promethazine) – at night, helpful when itching disturbs sleep.
    • Non-sedating (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine) – urticaria, allergic itch during the day.
  • Cholestatic pruritus – cholestyramine, rifampicin, naltrexone, sertraline.
  • Uraemic pruritus – gabapentin, UVB phototherapy, adequate dialysis.
  • Treat the underlying cause (antiscabies, antifungal, thyroid treatment, iron).

3. Nursing management of itching

  1. Identify the cause and pattern; examine skin for lesions and scratch marks.
  2. Keep the room cool and well ventilated; avoid overheating and woollen clothing – use loose cotton clothes.
  3. Lukewarm baths (not hot) with mild soap or soap substitutes; oatmeal or baking soda baths; pat dry.
  4. Apply moisturisers within 3 minutes of bathing to trap moisture.
  5. Keep nails short; cotton mittens for children; gentle pressure or cold compress instead of scratching.
  6. Give antihistamines as ordered; warn about drowsiness; avoid driving.
  7. Distraction, relaxation, adequate fluids.
  8. Observe for secondary infection.

4. When to refer Generalised itching without a rash, itching with jaundice, weight loss, night sweats or pale stools/dark urine, or itching that does not improve in 2 weeks needs medical evaluation for systemic disease.

Conclusion Itching is relieved by treating the cause, using topical and systemic antipruritics, and simple nursing measures that keep the skin cool, moist and protected.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the potency classes, uses, adverse effects and guidelines for the safe use of topical corticosteroids.
answer_html:
Introduction Topical corticosteroids are the most widely used drugs in dermatology because of their anti-inflammatory, antipruritic and immunosuppressive effects. Their misuse – especially of potent steroids in over-the-counter combination creams and as "fairness creams" – is a major problem in India.

1. Potency classes (examples) | Potency | Examples | |---|---| | Very potent (super-potent) | Clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol | | Potent | Betamethasone valerate 0.1%, betamethasone dipropionate 0.05%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05% | | Moderately potent | Clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone acetonide (low strength) | | Mild | Hydrocortisone 0.5–1% | Potency increases with ointment base, occlusion and application on thin skin.

2. Uses

  • Eczema/dermatitis (atopic, contact, seborrhoeic), psoriasis (localised plaques), lichen planus, discoid lupus, insect-bite reactions, alopecia areata and keloids (intralesional), vitiligo (selected), itching of inflammatory origin.

3. Adverse effects Local

  • Skin atrophy (thinning), striae, telangiectasia, easy bruising.
  • Steroid acne, rosacea and perioral dermatitis on the face.
  • Hypopigmentation, excess hair growth.
  • Masking and spread of infections – "tinea incognito" (fungal infection treated with steroid creams), worsening of scabies and bacterial infections.

  • Allergic contact dermatitis; tachyphylaxis; rebound flare on sudden stopping. Systemic (with potent steroids on large areas, under occlusion, or in children)

  • Adrenal suppression, Cushing's syndrome, growth retardation, hyperglycaemia.

4. Guidelines for safe use

  1. Use the lowest potency that controls the disease, for the shortest time.
  2. Mild steroids for the face, flexures (axilla, groin), genitals and infants; potent steroids for thick skin (palms, soles) and chronic plaques.
  3. Apply once or twice daily as a thin layer; measure by fingertip unit (cream from the tip of an adult index finger to the first crease ≈ 0.5 g, enough for an area equal to two adult palms).
  4. Limit very potent steroids (clobetasol) to about 2 weeks continuously; taper (reduce frequency/potency) rather than stop abruptly.
  5. Avoid fixed-dose combinations of steroid + antifungal + antibiotic for ringworm; never use steroid creams as fairness creams.
  6. Do not apply on infected or ulcerated skin unless prescribed with antimicrobials.
  7. Use occlusion only under medical advice.

5. Nursing responsibilities Teach correct quantity and technique, wash hands after application, observe for thinning and infection, keep records of tube consumption in chronic use, and counsel against self-medication.

Conclusion Topical corticosteroids are safe and effective when the right potency is used on the right site for the right duration; misuse causes serious, sometimes permanent skin damage.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Write the uses and precautions of silver sulphadiazine.
answer_html:
Silver sulphadiazine 1% cream is a topical antibacterial combining silver ions and sulphadiazine; active against Gram-negative (including Pseudomonas) and Gram-positive bacteria and Candida.

Uses

  1. Prevention and treatment of infection in burn wounds (main use).
  2. Infected chronic ulcers and skin graft donor sites (selected cases).

Precautions

  • Apply with a sterile gloved hand/spatula as a 2–3 mm layer once or twice daily after cleaning the wound.
  • Avoid in sulphonamide allergy, late pregnancy and newborns below 2 months (kernicterus); caution in G6PD deficiency and kidney/liver impairment.
  • Watch for rash, burning and leucopenia (check blood counts in extensive burns).

subject: Pharmacology I
question: (a) Classify antimicrobial drugs (4 marks). (b) Explain the principles of antimicrobial therapy (6 marks).

diagram.caption: Sites of action of antimicrobial drugs on the bacterial cell

answer_html:
Introduction Antimicrobial agents are drugs that kill or inhibit microorganisms – bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths – with selective toxicity (harming the microbe more than the host). Since the discovery of penicillin (1928), they have saved millions of lives. But their misuse has led to antimicrobial resistance, so they must be used according to sound principles.

(a) Classification of antimicrobial drugs (4 marks)

1. According to chemical structure | Group | Examples | |---|---| | β-lactams | Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems (meropenem), monobactams (aztreonam) | | Aminoglycosides | Gentamicin, amikacin, streptomycin | | Macrolides | Erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin | | Tetracyclines | Doxycycline, minocycline | | Fluoroquinolones | Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin | | Sulphonamides and diaminopyrimidines | Sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim (cotrimoxazole) | | Glycopeptides | Vancomycin, teicoplanin | | Nitroimidazoles | Metronidazole, tinidazole | | Oxazolidinones | Linezolid | | Polypeptides | Polymyxin B, colistin | | Others | Chloramphenicol, clindamycin, nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin |

2. According to mechanism of action

  1. Inhibit cell-wall synthesis – penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, vancomycin, bacitracin.
  2. Damage the cell membrane – polymyxins (colistin); antifungals – amphotericin B, azoles.
  3. Inhibit protein synthesis
    • On 30S ribosome – aminoglycosides, tetracyclines.
    • On 50S ribosome – macrolides, chloramphenicol, clindamycin, linezolid.
  4. Inhibit nucleic acid synthesis – fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase), rifampicin (RNA polymerase), metronidazole (DNA damage).
  5. Antimetabolites (inhibit folate synthesis) – sulphonamides, trimethoprim, dapsone, pyrimethamine.
  6. Inhibit mycolic acid synthesis – isoniazid, ethambutol (antitubercular).

3. According to type of action

  • Bactericidal (kill bacteria) – penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, vancomycin, rifampicin, metronidazole, cotrimoxazole.
  • Bacteriostatic (inhibit growth) – tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides (usually), sulphonamides, clindamycin, linezolid.

4. According to spectrum

  • Narrow-spectrum – penicillin G, cloxacillin, vancomycin (Gram-positive); aminoglycosides (aerobic Gram-negative); isoniazid (mycobacteria).
  • Broad-spectrum – tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, third-generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones.

5. According to type of organism – antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, antiprotozoal (antimalarial, antiamoebic), anthelmintic.

6. According to source – natural (penicillin G, streptomycin), semi-synthetic (ampicillin, amoxicillin), synthetic (sulphonamides, fluoroquinolones).

(b) Principles of antimicrobial therapy (6 marks) 1. Confirm that an antimicrobial is needed

  • Treat only bacterial (or other susceptible) infections – not viral colds, most sore throats, acute watery diarrhoea or fever without a focus.
  • Make a clinical diagnosis of the likely site and organism.

2. Collect specimens before starting therapy

  • Culture and sensitivity (blood, urine, pus, sputum, CSF) and Gram stain before the first dose, without delaying treatment in serious infections.

3. Choose the right drug

  • Empirical therapy – based on the likely organism, site of infection, severity and the local antibiogram/hospital antibiotic policy.
  • Definitive (targeted) therapy – once culture results are available, de-escalate to the narrowest effective drug.
  • Consider drug penetration to the site (CSF – ceftriaxone; urine – nitrofurantoin; bone; abscesses need drainage).

4. Consider patient factors

  • Age (neonates – avoid chloramphenicol, sulphonamides; children – avoid tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones), pregnancy and lactation (avoid tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones), kidney and liver function (dose adjustment), allergy (penicillin), immune status, genetic factors (G6PD deficiency), drug interactions.

5. Correct dose, route, frequency and duration

  • Adequate dose to reach effective levels; IV route for serious infections, switch to oral when the patient improves.
  • Time-dependent drugs (β-lactams) need regular intervals or extended infusion; concentration-dependent drugs (aminoglycosides) can be given once daily.
  • Adequate but not excessive duration – e.g., uncomplicated UTI 3–5 days, pneumonia 5–7 days, typhoid 10–14 days, tuberculosis 6 months, endocarditis 4–6 weeks.

6. Combination therapy only when indicated

  • To prevent resistance (tuberculosis, HIV, leprosy), for synergism (penicillin + gentamicin in enterococcal endocarditis), broad empirical cover in severe sepsis, polymicrobial infections (intra-abdominal).
  • Avoid irrational fixed-dose combinations.

7. Prophylactic use – limited and specific

  • Surgical prophylaxis – single dose within 60 minutes before incision, not beyond 24 hours; prevention of rheumatic fever, meningococcal contacts, HIV-related opportunistic infections, PEP.

8. Monitor the patient

  • Clinical response (fever, WBC), adverse effects (allergy, kidney and liver function, hearing), drug levels (vancomycin, aminoglycosides); review at 48–72 hours ("antibiotic time-out").

9. Prevent resistance and superinfection

  • Antimicrobial stewardship, infection control, patient education on adherence and avoiding self-medication.

Problems with antimicrobial therapy – resistance, superinfection, toxicity, allergy, masking of infections (e.g., partially treated meningitis, TB treated with fluoroquinolones).

Nursing responsibilities Collect cultures first, check allergies, give doses on time, monitor for adverse effects, remind about review and de-escalation, educate patients to complete the course exactly as prescribed and never share or self-start antibiotics.

Conclusion Antimicrobials are classified by structure, mechanism, action and spectrum. Using them on sound principles – right diagnosis, right drug, dose, route and duration, with monitoring – cures infections and protects these precious drugs from resistance.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Describe the first-line antitubercular drugs – mechanism of action, adverse effects, treatment regimen under NTEP and nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Tuberculosis needs combination therapy for several months because Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, lives inside macrophages and in caseous lesions, and quickly develops resistance to single drugs. Under India's National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), drugs are given free, daily, as weight-band fixed-dose combinations (FDCs), with treatment support and digital monitoring through Ni-kshay.

A. First-line antitubercular drugs | Drug | Mechanism | Action | Daily dose (adult) | Major adverse effects | |---|---|---|---|---| | Isoniazid (H) | Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis | Bactericidal (rapidly dividing bacilli) | 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg) | Peripheral neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine), hepatitis, rash, rarely psychosis, seizures | | Rifampicin (R) | Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase | Bactericidal; sterilising (kills slow and intermittent multipliers) | 10 mg/kg (max 600 mg) | Hepatitis, orange-red urine, sweat, tears (stains contact lenses), flu-like syndrome, thrombocytopenia; enzyme inducer – reduces effect of oral contraceptives, warfarin, ARVs | | Pyrazinamide (Z) | Active in acidic environment inside macrophages | Sterilising (intracellular bacilli) | 25 mg/kg | Hepatotoxicity (most hepatotoxic), hyperuricaemia, arthralgia/gout, GI upset | | Ethambutol (E) | Inhibits arabinosyl transferase (cell wall arabinogalactan) | Bacteriostatic; prevents resistance | 15 mg/kg | Optic neuritis – reduced visual acuity, red–green colour blindness (dose-related, usually reversible) | | Streptomycin (S) | Aminoglycoside (30S ribosome) | Bactericidal (extracellular) | 15 mg/kg IM | Ototoxicity (vertigo, deafness), nephrotoxicity; avoid in pregnancy (rarely used now) |

B. Treatment regimen for drug-sensitive TB (NTEP)

  • Intensive phase (IP): 2 months – HRZE daily.
  • Continuation phase (CP): 4 months – HRE daily.
  • Total 6 months for new and previously treated drug-sensitive TB; the continuation phase may be extended in some forms (e.g., TB meningitis, bone/spinal TB) as per guidelines.
  • Weight-band FDC tablets (e.g., 4-drug FDC – H 75 mg, R 150 mg, Z 400 mg, E 275 mg per tablet; number of tablets according to weight) for adults; dispersible paediatric FDCs for children.
  • Pyridoxine for patients at risk of neuropathy (diabetes, alcohol use, HIV, malnutrition, pregnancy).
  • Universal drug-susceptibility testing (CBNAAT/Truenat) at diagnosis to detect rifampicin resistance.
  • Drug-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) is treated with all-oral regimens containing newer drugs such as bedaquiline, delamanid, pretomanid, linezolid and fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin); shorter 6–11-month regimens (e.g., BPaLM) are being introduced.

C. Why combination and long treatment?

  • Different drugs act on different bacterial populations (rapidly dividing, slowly dividing, intracellular dormant).
  • Prevents emergence of resistance (spontaneous mutants resistant to one drug are killed by the others).
  • Sterilises lesions and prevents relapse.

D. Nursing responsibilities 1. Before starting

  • Baseline weight, liver function tests, kidney function, visual acuity and colour vision (ethambutol), HIV and blood sugar testing; pregnancy status.
  • Counselling of patient and family about the disease, long duration and the importance of not stopping treatment.

2. Administration and adherence

  • Give drugs daily, at the same time, on an empty stomach (or with a light meal if GI upset – as advised); all FDC tablets together.
  • Treatment supporter (ASHA, family member, health worker) and digital adherence tools (Ni-kshay, 99DOTS); follow up missed doses immediately.
  • Never give single drugs alone; adjust doses as weight changes.

3. Monitoring for adverse effects

  • Hepatotoxicity: loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine – stop drugs and inform the doctor immediately.
  • Vision (ethambutol) – ask about blurring and colour vision monthly; children who cannot report need careful use.
  • Numbness/tingling (isoniazid) – pyridoxine.
  • Joint pain (pyrazinamide); hearing and balance (streptomycin).
  • Skin rash – may need drug withdrawal.

4. Patient education

  • Explain the harmless orange-red colour of urine and tears due to rifampicin.
  • Women on oral contraceptives need alternative or additional contraception (rifampicin reduces effect).
  • Avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic self-medication.
  • Cough etiquette, masks, ventilation; sputum disposal.
  • Nutrition – balanced diet; nutritional support is provided through the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (direct benefit transfer).
  • Follow-up sputum tests (end of IP and end of treatment); complete the full course even when feeling well.

5. Public health role

  • Notification of every TB case (mandatory), contact tracing and screening of household contacts, TB preventive treatment for eligible contacts and PLHIV, reducing stigma.

E. Management of drug-induced hepatitis (in brief) If jaundice or raised liver enzymes (more than 3 times normal with symptoms, or 5 times without) occur, all hepatotoxic drugs are stopped; once liver function recovers, drugs are reintroduced one by one under supervision (as per NTEP guidelines), while a safer interim regimen may be used.

Conclusion Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol given together for six months cure most patients with drug-sensitive TB. The nurse's role in counselling, ensuring adherence, monitoring for hepatotoxicity and visual problems, and public health follow-up is central to India's goal of ending TB.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Classify penicillins and cephalosporins. Describe their mechanism of action, uses, adverse effects and nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Penicillins and cephalosporins belong to the β-lactam group of antibiotics – the most widely used antibiotics in the world. They are bactericidal, relatively safe and effective against many infections; their main danger is hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis.

A. Classification of penicillins

  1. Natural penicillins
    • Penicillin G (benzylpenicillin) – crystalline (aqueous) IV/IM; procaine penicillin (IM); benzathine penicillin (long-acting IM – 1.2 or 2.4 million units).
    • Penicillin V – oral (acid-stable).
  2. Semi-synthetic penicillins
    • Penicillinase-resistant: cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin (methicillin, oxacillin).
    • Extended-spectrum (aminopenicillins): ampicillin, amoxicillin.
    • Antipseudomonal: piperacillin, ticarcillin.
  3. β-lactamase inhibitor combinations
    • Amoxicillin–clavulanic acid, ampicillin–sulbactam, piperacillin–tazobactam.

B. Classification of cephalosporins (generations) | Generation | Examples | Spectrum/uses | |---|---|---| | First | Cefazolin (IV), cephalexin, cefadroxil (oral) | Gram-positive; surgical prophylaxis, skin infections | | Second | Cefuroxime, cefaclor, cefoxitin | Some Gram-negative; respiratory infections; cefoxitin – anaerobes | | Third | Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ceftazidime (anti-Pseudomonas), cefoperazone, cefixime, cefpodoxime (oral) | Gram-negative; meningitis, typhoid, gonorrhoea, sepsis, hospital infections | | Fourth | Cefepime | Broad; Gram-negative incl. Pseudomonas | | Fifth | Ceftaroline | MRSA | | With β-lactamase inhibitor | Ceftazidime–avibactam, cefoperazone–sulbactam | Resistant Gram-negatives |

C. Mechanism of action

  • β-lactams bind to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs – transpeptidases) in the bacterial cell wall and inhibit cross-linking of peptidoglycan.
  • The weakened wall cannot withstand osmotic pressure; autolytic enzymes are activated → cell lysis – bactericidal, acting mainly on actively growing bacteria.
  • Human cells have no cell wall – hence low toxicity.
  • Resistance: β-lactamase enzymes (penicillinase, ESBL, carbapenemase), altered PBPs (MRSA), reduced permeability.

D. Uses Penicillins

  • Penicillin G: streptococcal infections (pharyngitis, cellulitis, erysipelas), pneumococcal and meningococcal infections, syphilis (benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU), rheumatic fever prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks), diphtheria, tetanus, gas gangrene, leptospirosis, anthrax.
  • Amoxicillin: otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis, community-acquired pneumonia, UTI (sensitive organisms), H. pylori eradication, dental infections; with clavulanate – bites, mixed infections.
  • Cloxacillin: staphylococcal skin and soft-tissue infections, osteomyelitis (non-MRSA).

  • Piperacillin–tazobactam: serious hospital infections, Pseudomonas, febrile neutropenia. Cephalosporins

  • Ceftriaxone: bacterial meningitis, enteric fever (typhoid), gonorrhoea, community-acquired pneumonia, sepsis, pyelonephritis.

  • Cefazolin: surgical prophylaxis.
  • Ceftazidime/cefepime: Pseudomonas infections, febrile neutropenia.
  • Cefixime: oral step-down therapy (typhoid, UTI).

E. Adverse effects

  1. Hypersensitivity (most important) – rash, urticaria, fever, serum sickness, angioedema, bronchospasm and anaphylaxis (rare but fatal); cross-sensitivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is low (about 1–2%), but cephalosporins are avoided after penicillin anaphylaxis.
  2. GI upset, diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis, superinfection (thrush).
  3. Ampicillin/amoxicillin rash in infectious mononucleosis (non-allergic).
  4. Neurotoxicity with very high doses (seizures), especially in kidney failure; never given intrathecally.
  5. Local – pain at IM site, sterile abscess; benzathine penicillin given accidentally IV can cause cardiac arrest; procaine reaction.
  6. Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction in syphilis.
  7. Cephalosporin-specific – ceftriaxone biliary sludge; ceftriaxone must not be given with IV calcium in neonates; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (cefoperazone); bleeding (cefoperazone); thrombophlebitis.

F. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Allergy history – ask specifically about previous reactions to penicillin or any antibiotic; record and flag allergies.
  2. Sensitivity test / test dose before parenteral penicillins as per hospital policy (many Indian hospitals require it), and keep adrenaline and resuscitation equipment ready; observe the patient for at least 30 minutes after the first dose.
  3. Reconstitution – use the correct diluent and volume; give promptly (β-lactams are unstable in solution); check compatibility – do not mix with aminoglycosides in the same syringe/infusion.
  4. Benzathine penicillin – shake well, give deep IM into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (or ventrogluteal site) with a wide-bore needle, aspirate to avoid IV injection, inject slowly; never IV.
  5. Give doses at exact intervals; IV infusion over the recommended time.
  6. Monitor for rash, breathlessness, diarrhoea, thrush, phlebitis; kidney function and dose adjustment.
  7. Educate to complete the course exactly as prescribed; report rash or swelling; inform all doctors about penicillin allergy (carry an allergy card).

G. Management of anaphylaxis (summary for the nurse)

  1. Stop the drug; call for help; lay the patient flat with legs raised (sit up if breathless).
  2. Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (0.5 ml of 1:1000) in the anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5 minutes if needed.
  3. Oxygen, airway support, IV fluids (normal saline) for hypotension.
  4. Adjuncts – antihistamine, hydrocortisone, nebulised salbutamol for wheeze.
  5. Monitor vital signs; record the reaction and label the patient as allergic; report under pharmacovigilance.

Conclusion Penicillins and cephalosporins kill bacteria by blocking cell-wall synthesis and remain the backbone of antibiotic therapy. Careful allergy assessment, readiness for anaphylaxis, correct reconstitution and administration, and monitoring make their use safe.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Classify antimalarial drugs. Describe the pharmacology of chloroquine, primaquine and artemisinin derivatives, and the treatment of malaria as per national guidelines.
answer_html:
Introduction Malaria, caused by Plasmodium species and transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito, is still a public health problem in many parts of India, though cases have fallen greatly and the country aims at elimination by 2030. Antimalarial drugs act on different stages of the parasite's life cycle; correct choice and complete treatment cure the patient and stop transmission.

A. Classification of antimalarial drugs 1. According to the stage of the life cycle acted upon | Action | Drugs | |---|---| | Blood schizonticides (kill erythrocytic forms – clinical cure) | Chloroquine, artemisinins (artesunate, artemether, arteether), quinine, mefloquine, lumefantrine, amodiaquine, piperaquine; slow-acting – pyrimethamine, sulfadoxine, proguanil, doxycycline | | Tissue schizonticides – causal prophylaxis (liver stage) and anti-relapse (hypnozoites) | Primaquine, tafenoquine (anti-relapse); proguanil (causal) | | Gametocides (kill gametocytes – stop transmission) | Primaquine (P. falciparum); chloroquine, quinine (P. vivax) | | Sporontocides (prevent development in mosquito) | Primaquine, proguanil |

2. According to chemical structure

  • 4-aminoquinolines: chloroquine, amodiaquine.
  • 8-aminoquinolines: primaquine, tafenoquine.
  • Cinchona alkaloids: quinine, quinidine.
  • Artemisinin derivatives: artesunate, artemether, arteether, dihydroartemisinin.
  • Others: mefloquine, lumefantrine, piperaquine, pyrimethamine, sulfadoxine, proguanil, atovaquone; antibiotics – doxycycline, clindamycin.

B. Chloroquine

  • Mechanism: concentrates in the parasite's food vacuole and inhibits haem polymerase – toxic haem accumulates and kills the parasite.
  • Uses: treatment of P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae (and sensitive P. falciparum – resistance is widespread in India); extra-intestinal amoebiasis (amoebic liver abscess); rheumatoid arthritis and lupus (hydroxychloroquine).
  • Dose (vivax): 25 mg/kg over 3 days (10 mg/kg on days 1 and 2, 5 mg/kg on day 3).
  • Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, headache, itching, blurred vision; long-term – retinopathy (eye checks), ototoxicity, cardiomyopathy, QT prolongation; overdose is very dangerous, especially in children (cardiac collapse) – keep out of reach.

C. Primaquine

  • Mechanism: interferes with parasite mitochondrial function (oxidant damage).
  • Uses:
    • Radical cure of P. vivax/ovale – kills hypnozoites and prevents relapse: 0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days.
    • Gametocidal for P. falciparum – single dose 0.75 mg/kg to stop transmission.
  • Adverse effects: abdominal pain, nausea; haemolytic anaemia in G6PD-deficient persons (dark urine, jaundice, pallor – stop immediately); methaemoglobinaemia.
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy, infants below 6 months (and in severe G6PD deficiency); test for G6PD where possible.

D. Artemisinin derivatives (artesunate, artemether, arteether)

  • Derived from the Chinese herb Artemisia annua (discovery honoured with the Nobel Prize to Tu Youyou, 2015).
  • Mechanism: the endoperoxide bridge is activated by iron in haem to release free radicals that damage parasite proteins.
  • Most rapidly acting blood schizonticides; also reduce gametocytes.
  • Always given as Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) – never alone (to prevent resistance) – e.g., artesunate + sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (AS+SP), artemether–lumefantrine (AL).
  • Injectable artesunate is the drug of choice for severe malaria.
  • Adverse effects: generally safe – nausea, dizziness, delayed haemolysis after IV artesunate; caution in the first trimester (as per guidelines).

E. Quinine (in brief)

  • Used in severe malaria when artesunate is unavailable and in certain situations of pregnancy as per guidelines; given as slow IV infusion in 5% dextrose.
  • Adverse effects: cinchonism (tinnitus, deafness, headache, nausea, blurred vision), hypoglycaemia (stimulates insulin), hypotension and arrhythmia if given rapidly.

F. Treatment of malaria as per national guidelines (NCVBDC) – in brief | Type | Treatment | |---|---| | P. vivax | Chloroquine for 3 days + primaquine 0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days | | P. falciparum (uncomplicated) | ACT – artesunate for 3 days + sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine on day 1 (AS+SP); artemether–lumefantrine in north-eastern states; + single dose primaquine 0.75 mg/kg on day 2 | | Mixed infection | ACT + primaquine for 14 days | | Severe malaria | Injectable artesunate (or artemether/arteether/quinine), then full oral ACT course | (Doses are given by age/weight bands; pregnancy and infants have special rules.)

  • Prophylaxis for travellers (short stays in high-risk areas): doxycycline daily or mefloquine weekly as advised.

G. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Collect a blood smear/RDT before starting treatment.
  2. Give drugs after food to reduce nausea; observe the patient swallowing (directly observed therapy); repeat the dose if vomited within 30 minutes.
  3. Ensure completion of primaquine for 14 days – the commonest cause of vivax relapse is incomplete treatment.
  4. Watch for dark urine, jaundice, breathlessness (haemolysis with primaquine); check G6PD if possible.
  5. Severe malaria – monitor consciousness, blood glucose (hypoglycaemia), urine output, temperature, fluid balance, convulsions; give IV artesunate as per protocol.
  6. Record temperature chart and follow-up smears.
  7. Health education – mosquito nets (LLINs), repellents, full-sleeved clothing, elimination of breeding sites, early testing for fever, safe storage of tablets.

Conclusion Antimalarials act at different stages of the parasite's life cycle; chloroquine and primaquine provide radical cure of vivax malaria, and artemisinin-based combinations treat falciparum malaria. Complete, supervised treatment and vector control, supported by nurses, are the keys to eliminating malaria.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Classify antiretroviral drugs. Describe the principles of antiretroviral therapy, first-line regimen as per NACO, adverse effects and nursing responsibilities.

diagram.caption: HIV life cycle and targets of antiretroviral drugs

answer_html:
Introduction Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has changed HIV infection from a fatal illness into a chronic, manageable condition. ART does not cure HIV, but suppresses viral replication, allows recovery of CD4 cells, prevents opportunistic infections and prevents transmission (a person with an undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV sexually – "U = U"). India's National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) provides free ART through ART centres and Link ART centres.

A. Classification of antiretroviral drugs | Class | Drugs | Mechanism | |---|---|---| | Nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) | Tenofovir (TDF/TAF), lamivudine (3TC), emtricitabine (FTC), zidovudine (AZT), abacavir (ABC) | Incorporated into viral DNA → chain termination | | Non-nucleoside RT inhibitors (NNRTIs) | Efavirenz (EFV), nevirapine (NVP), rilpivirine, etravirine, doravirine | Bind directly to reverse transcriptase → inhibit it | | Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) | Dolutegravir (DTG), raltegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir | Block integration of viral DNA into host DNA | | Protease inhibitors (PIs) | Atazanavir, lopinavir, darunavir (boosted with ritonavir – "/r") | Block viral protease → immature, non-infectious virions | | Entry/fusion inhibitors | Enfuvirtide (fusion), maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist) | Prevent entry into CD4 cells | | Newer agents | Lenacapavir (capsid inhibitor) | Long-acting options |

B. Principles of ART

  1. Combination therapy – at least three active drugs from two classes (usually 2 NRTIs + 1 INSTI/NNRTI/PI) to suppress the virus completely and prevent resistance.
  2. "Treat All" – ART is offered to every person diagnosed with HIV, irrespective of CD4 count or clinical stage, as early as possible (same day or within 7 days, after readiness assessment).
  3. Lifelong therapy with very high adherence (above 95%).
  4. Monitoring with viral load (at 6 and 12 months, then yearly) and CD4 count; treatment failure → second-line regimen after adherence counselling.
  5. Prevention and treatment of opportunistic infections (cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, TB preventive therapy) and management of co-infections (TB, hepatitis B).

C. First-line ART as per NACO

  • Adults and adolescents: TLD – tenofovir (TDF) 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg, as a single fixed-dose tablet once daily.
  • Children: dolutegravir-based regimens (e.g., abacavir + lamivudine + paediatric dolutegravir) according to weight.
  • Pregnant women: TLD is preferred; ART continues lifelong (prevention of parent-to-child transmission).
  • With rifampicin-based TB treatment: dolutegravir dose increased to 50 mg twice daily (drug interaction).
  • Second-line: boosted PI-based regimens (e.g., atazanavir/r or darunavir/r with zidovudine + lamivudine) depending on the first-line regimen.

D. Adverse effects

  • Tenofovir (TDF): kidney toxicity (rising creatinine, proteinuria), bone loss.
  • Zidovudine: anaemia, neutropenia, nausea, headache, myopathy, lactic acidosis.
  • Abacavir: hypersensitivity reaction (fever, rash, GI and respiratory symptoms) – never re-challenge.
  • Nevirapine: severe skin rash (Stevens–Johnson syndrome), hepatotoxicity.
  • Efavirenz: CNS effects – dizziness, vivid dreams, insomnia, depression (give at bedtime), rash.
  • Dolutegravir: insomnia, headache, weight gain; interacts with antacids, iron and calcium (give 2 hours before or 6 hours after).
  • Protease inhibitors: GI upset, dyslipidaemia, hyperglycaemia, lipodystrophy, jaundice (atazanavir); many drug interactions (ritonavir).
  • Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) – worsening of an existing infection (TB, cryptococcal) in the first weeks of ART as immunity recovers.

E. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Pre-ART counselling – explain lifelong therapy, adherence, side effects, disclosure and support; assess readiness; ensure confidentiality and non-discriminatory care (HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017).
  2. Baseline tests – CD4, creatinine, Hb, hepatitis B, TB screening, pregnancy test.
  3. Adherence support – same time daily, pill boxes, mobile reminders, treatment supporters; missed dose – take as soon as remembered unless close to the next dose; never double.
  4. Monitor for side effects – rash, jaundice, anaemia, kidney function, mood changes; report promptly.
  5. Drug interactions – check all medicines (rifampicin, antacids, iron, calcium, antiepileptics, herbal products).
  6. OI prophylaxis – cotrimoxazole, TB preventive therapy; vaccination as per guidelines.
  7. Prevention – condom use, partner testing, PPTCT for pregnant women (ART for mother, nevirapine prophylaxis for the baby, safe infant feeding), PEP after exposures, PrEP for high-risk persons where available.
  8. Nutrition and psychosocial support; linkage to community support groups.

F. Post-exposure and pre-exposure prophylaxis (in brief)

  • PEP – TLD for 28 days, started within 72 hours (ideally 2 hours) after occupational or sexual exposure.
  • PrEP – daily tenofovir + emtricitabine for HIV-negative persons at high risk, with regular testing.

Conclusion Combination ART with drugs from different classes – most commonly TLD in India – suppresses HIV, restores immunity and prevents transmission. Lifelong adherence, monitoring for side effects and compassionate, confidential care are the nurse's key contributions to its success.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the antileprotic drugs, with the dosage and side effects of dapsone.
answer_html:
Introduction Leprosy (Hansen's disease), caused by Mycobacterium leprae, affects skin and peripheral nerves. India has achieved elimination as a public health problem but still reports the largest number of new cases in the world. Leprosy is curable with multidrug therapy (MDT), provided free under the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP).

1. Antileprotic drugs

  • First-line: dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine.
  • Second-line/alternative: ofloxacin or moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin.

2. Multidrug therapy (MDT)

  • Adult multibacillary (MB) regimen (12 months):
    • Once monthly (supervised): rifampicin 600 mg + clofazimine 300 mg + dapsone 100 mg.
    • Daily (self-administered): clofazimine 50 mg + dapsone 100 mg.
  • Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy: 6 months – the WHO now recommends the same three drugs for PB leprosy (follow current NLEP guidelines).
  • Given in blister calendar packs; child doses are reduced.
  • Single-dose rifampicin is given as post-exposure prophylaxis to eligible contacts under NLEP.

3. Dapsone (diaminodiphenyl sulphone, DDS)

  • Mechanism: like sulphonamides, it inhibits folate synthesis (competes with PABA) in M. leprae – bacteriostatic.
  • Dosage: 100 mg once daily for adults (about 1–2 mg/kg/day for children), orally, as part of MDT.
  • Other uses: dermatitis herpetiformis, Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis/treatment (with trimethoprim), toxoplasmosis.
  • Side effects:
    • Haemolytic anaemia – especially in G6PD deficiency; mild haemolysis is common.
    • Methaemoglobinaemia – bluish lips and nails, breathlessness.
    • GI upset, headache, skin rash.
    • "Dapsone syndrome" – a serious hypersensitivity reaction appearing 4–6 weeks after starting: fever, rash (exfoliative dermatitis), lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, jaundice – stop the drug immediately.
    • Agranulocytosis (rare), peripheral neuropathy, psychosis.

4. Other drugs (side effects in brief)

  • Clofazimine – reddish-brown to black skin discolouration (reversible after stopping), dry skin, abdominal pain; also useful in lepra reactions.
  • Rifampicin – orange-red urine, hepatitis.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Ensure the monthly supervised dose and regular daily doses; follow up defaulters.
  • Explain that skin darkening with clofazimine is temporary.
  • Monitor Hb and signs of haemolysis; report rash, fever, jaundice early.
  • Teach self-care of anaesthetic hands and feet (daily inspection, soaking, oiling, protective footwear) to prevent ulcers and deformity.
  • Explain lepra reactions (sudden redness of patches, painful nerves, nodules) – report at once.
  • Reduce stigma – leprosy is curable and patients on MDT quickly become non-infectious.

Conclusion Dapsone, rifampicin and clofazimine in MDT cure leprosy; regular supervised treatment, monitoring of dapsone's side effects and self-care teaching prevent disability.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Write a note on metronidazole – indications, dose, adverse effects and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole drug active against anaerobic bacteria and several protozoa. It is cheap, well absorbed orally and widely used in India.

1. Mechanism of action

  • It is a prodrug; inside anaerobic organisms its nitro group is reduced to toxic free radicals, which damage DNA → death of the organism (cidal).
  • Aerobic human cells do not reduce it significantly – hence selective toxicity.

2. Indications (a) Protozoal infections

  • Amoebiasis – amoebic dysentery and amoebic liver abscess (followed by a luminal agent).
  • Giardiasis.

  • Trichomonas vaginitis – treat the sexual partner too. (b) Anaerobic bacterial infections

  • Intra-abdominal infections (peritonitis, appendicular abscess), pelvic infections, dental infections, lung and brain abscess, aspiration pneumonia, diabetic foot.

  • Surgical prophylaxis in colorectal and gynaecological surgery.

  • Bacterial vaginosis. (c) Others

  • Helicobacter pylori eradication (in combination), mild C. difficile colitis, tetanus (adjunct), Vincent's angina.

3. Dose

  • Adults: 400 mg orally three times daily (5–10 days depending on the condition); amoebic liver abscess 400–800 mg three times daily; trichomoniasis 2 g single dose or 400 mg twice daily for 7 days.
  • IV: 500 mg 8-hourly, infused over 20–30 minutes.
  • Children: about 7.5 mg/kg three times daily.

4. Adverse effects

  • Metallic taste, nausea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, dry mouth, furred tongue.
  • Dark (reddish-brown) urine – harmless.
  • Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol – flushing, headache, vomiting, palpitations.
  • Headache, dizziness; peripheral neuropathy and seizures with high doses or long use.
  • Rash, transient leucopenia.
  • Interactions: increases the effect of warfarin (bleeding) and lithium.

5. Nursing implications

  1. Give with or after food to reduce GI upset.
  2. Advise strict avoidance of alcohol during treatment and for 48–72 hours after the last dose (including alcohol-containing syrups and mouthwashes).
  3. Explain the metallic taste and dark urine.
  4. IV infusion – use ready-to-use bottles, give over the recommended time, do not mix with other drugs in the same line.
  5. Ask about pregnancy (avoid high single doses in early pregnancy unless advised) and breastfeeding.
  6. Report numbness or tingling of hands and feet.
  7. Complete the course; treat sexual partners in trichomoniasis; hygiene and safe water education in amoebiasis/giardiasis.

Conclusion Metronidazole is the drug of choice for many anaerobic and protozoal infections; avoiding alcohol and completing the course are the key teaching points.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the aminoglycoside antibiotics with special reference to gentamicin.
answer_html:
Introduction Aminoglycosides – gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin, streptomycin, neomycin – are powerful bactericidal antibiotics, mainly against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli. Their use is limited by ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, which need careful monitoring.

1. Mechanism of action

  • They enter bacteria (oxygen-dependent transport) and bind irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit → misreading of mRNA and faulty proteins → membrane damage → cell death.
  • Concentration-dependent killing and a long post-antibiotic effect → once-daily dosing is effective and less toxic.
  • Not active against anaerobes.

2. Pharmacokinetics

  • Not absorbed orally – given IM or IV (neomycin orally only for gut action).
  • Do not cross the blood–brain barrier well; excreted unchanged by the kidneys – dose reduced in kidney disease.

3. Uses

  • Gentamicin: serious Gram-negative infections – sepsis, complicated UTI/pyelonephritis, hospital pneumonia (with β-lactam), neonatal sepsis (ampicillin + gentamicin), endocarditis (synergy with penicillin), peritonitis (with metronidazole); topical eye/ear drops and creams.
  • Amikacin: infections resistant to gentamicin, drug-resistant TB (selected).
  • Streptomycin: tuberculosis (second-line now), plague.
  • Neomycin: bowel preparation, hepatic encephalopathy (oral); topical.

4. Dose (gentamicin)

  • 5–7 mg/kg once daily IV (or 1.5–2 mg/kg 8-hourly in some indications), adjusted for kidney function and drug levels.

5. Adverse effects

  1. Ototoxicity – vestibular damage (vertigo, ataxia, nystagmus – especially streptomycin, gentamicin) and cochlear damage (tinnitus, high-frequency hearing loss – amikacin, neomycin); often irreversible.
  2. Nephrotoxicity – acute tubular damage (rising creatinine, reduced urine output); usually reversible.
  3. Neuromuscular blockade – respiratory paralysis, especially after anaesthesia or in myasthenia gravis (reversed by IV calcium).
  4. Hypersensitivity (rare). - Risk increases with high trough levels, long courses, elderly, dehydration, kidney disease, and with furosemide, vancomycin, amphotericin B, cisplatin. - Contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal deafness – especially streptomycin).

6. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Calculate dose by weight; check kidney function before starting and regularly.
  2. Infuse IV over 30–60 minutes; do not mix with penicillins in the same syringe or infusion (inactivation).
  3. Collect peak and trough levels as ordered (trough level should be low before the next dose).
  4. Monitor urine output, creatinine; ensure good hydration.
  5. Ask daily about tinnitus, hearing loss, dizziness, unsteadiness; audiometry in prolonged therapy.
  6. Observe breathing after surgery in patients receiving aminoglycosides.

Conclusion Aminoglycosides are potent against Gram-negative bacteria but toxic to the ear and kidney; once-daily dosing, drug-level monitoring and vigilant nursing observation keep them safe.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the fluoroquinolones – mechanism of action, uses, adverse effects and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Fluoroquinolones are synthetic, broad-spectrum, bactericidal antibiotics with good oral absorption and tissue penetration. Overuse in India has led to widespread resistance (e.g., in typhoid and gonorrhoea), so they should be reserved for appropriate infections.

1. Examples

  • Ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, norfloxacin (urinary), levofloxacin, moxifloxacin ("respiratory fluoroquinolones"); nalidixic acid is an older non-fluorinated quinolone.

2. Mechanism of action

  • Inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) in Gram-negative bacteria and topoisomerase IV in Gram-positive bacteria → DNA cannot be supercoiled/separated → DNA breaks and cell death.

3. Uses

  • Urinary tract infections (complicated), prostatitis.
  • Gastroenteritis and bacillary dysentery (shigellosis), cholera (alternative), travellers' diarrhoea.
  • Respiratory infections – community-acquired pneumonia, COPD exacerbations (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin).
  • Bone and joint infections, skin and soft-tissue infections, intra-abdominal infections (with metronidazole).
  • Drug-resistant tuberculosis (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin).
  • Eye and ear infections (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, moxifloxacin drops).
  • Typhoid (only if sensitive), gonorrhoea (resistance common), anthrax, plague; meningococcal prophylaxis (single dose ciprofloxacin).

4. Adverse effects

  • GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis.
  • CNS: headache, dizziness, insomnia, confusion, seizures (especially with NSAIDs or theophylline).
  • Tendinitis and tendon rupture (Achilles tendon) – higher risk in elderly, with steroids.
  • Cartilage damage in growing animals – avoided in children and adolescents and in pregnancy/lactation unless benefits outweigh risks.
  • QT prolongation and arrhythmias (moxifloxacin).
  • Photosensitivity, rash.
  • Blood sugar disturbances (hypo- and hyperglycaemia) in diabetics, peripheral neuropathy, aortic aneurysm (rare), worsening of myasthenia gravis.

5. Interactions

  • Antacids, calcium, iron, zinc, milk products reduce absorption (chelation) – separate by at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after.
  • Ciprofloxacin raises theophylline and warfarin levels.

6. Nursing implications

  1. Give with plenty of water; maintain fluid intake (prevents crystalluria).
  2. Space doses away from antacids, iron, calcium and dairy.
  3. Advise avoiding excessive sunlight; use sunscreen.
  4. Ask patients to report tendon pain, palpitations, numbness – stop the drug if tendon pain occurs.
  5. Monitor blood glucose in diabetics and ECG in cardiac patients.
  6. IV infusion slowly over 60 minutes; caution about dizziness when driving.
  7. Avoid in children and pregnancy unless specifically ordered.

Conclusion Fluoroquinolones are effective broad-spectrum drugs, but their serious adverse effects and rising resistance demand careful, limited use.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Classify antifungal drugs. Explain the pharmacology of amphotericin B and fluconazole.
answer_html:
Introduction Fungal infections range from superficial ringworm to life-threatening systemic mycoses (candidaemia, cryptococcal meningitis, aspergillosis, mucormycosis). Antifungal drugs target structures unique to fungi, mainly ergosterol in the cell membrane and glucan in the cell wall.

1. Classification | Group | Drugs | Mechanism | |---|---|---| | Polyene antibiotics | Amphotericin B (conventional, liposomal), nystatin | Bind ergosterol → pores in membrane | | Azoles – imidazoles | Clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole | Inhibit ergosterol synthesis (14α-demethylase) | | Azoles – triazoles | Fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole | Same, more selective, systemic use | | Echinocandins | Caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin | Inhibit β-1,3-glucan synthesis (cell wall) | | Allylamines | Terbinafine | Inhibit squalene epoxidase | | Others | Griseofulvin (dermatophytes), flucytosine (with amphotericin), ciclopirox, tolnaftate | — |

2. Amphotericin B

  • Uses: drug of choice in life-threatening systemic mycoses – mucormycosis (liposomal form), cryptococcal meningitis (with flucytosine), invasive candidiasis, histoplasmosis; visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) – single-dose liposomal amphotericin B is used in India's elimination programme.
  • Administration: IV only – conventional form dissolved in 5% dextrose (not saline), infused slowly over 4–6 hours (liposomal over about 2 hours) through a pump.
  • Adverse effects:
    • Infusion reactions – fever, chills, rigors, headache, nausea, hypotension ("shake and bake") – premedication with paracetamol, antihistamine (± hydrocortisone).
    • Nephrotoxicity – most important (rising creatinine); reduced by saline loading before infusion and use of liposomal formulation.
    • Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia – check daily and replace.
    • Anaemia, thrombophlebitis.
  • Nursing: vital signs every 30 minutes during infusion, daily creatinine and electrolytes, intake–output, IV site care.

3. Fluconazole

  • Mechanism: triazole – inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis; fungistatic.
  • Pharmacokinetics: almost completely absorbed orally (oral = IV), long half-life (once daily), good CSF and urine penetration, excreted by kidneys.
  • Uses: oral and oesophageal candidiasis, vaginal candidiasis (150 mg single dose), candidaemia (sensitive species), cryptococcal meningitis (consolidation and maintenance), prophylaxis in transplant and HIV patients, coccidioidomycosis.
  • Not effective against Aspergillus and Mucorales.
  • Adverse effects: nausea, headache, rash, raised liver enzymes, QT prolongation; enzyme inhibitor – raises levels of warfarin, phenytoin, sulfonylureas, statins; avoid high doses in pregnancy.

4. Others in brief

  • Itraconazole – dermatophytosis (widely used in India), aspergillosis; take capsules with food.
  • Voriconazole – invasive aspergillosis; visual disturbances, photosensitivity.
  • Echinocandins – candidaemia, including Candida auris.
  • Terbinafine/griseofulvin – nail and scalp ringworm.

Nursing responsibilities Correct dilution and slow infusion of amphotericin, premedication, monitoring of kidney function and electrolytes, liver function with azoles, drug-interaction checks, and teaching completion of long courses with hygiene measures.

Conclusion Amphotericin B remains the life-saver in severe mycoses despite its toxicity, while fluconazole is a safe, convenient drug for candidiasis and cryptococcal disease.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the antiviral drugs (other than antiretrovirals) with special reference to acyclovir.
answer_html:
Introduction Viruses multiply inside human cells using the cell's machinery, so few drugs can stop them without harming the host. Antiviral drugs target virus-specific enzymes or steps (attachment, uncoating, nucleic acid synthesis, release). Unlike antibiotics, most are active against only one or a few viruses.

1. Classification | Virus | Drugs | |---|---| | Herpes simplex and varicella-zoster | Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir | | Cytomegalovirus (CMV) | Ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir | | Influenza | Oseltamivir, zanamivir (neuraminidase inhibitors), baloxavir; amantadine (resistance) | | Hepatitis B | Tenofovir, entecavir | | Hepatitis C | Direct-acting antivirals – sofosbuvir with daclatasvir or velpatasvir (free under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme) | | COVID-19 | Remdesivir, molnupiravir, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (as per guidelines) | | Broad/others | Ribavirin, interferons |

2. Acyclovir (a) Mechanism of action

  • Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue; it is phosphorylated by the viral enzyme thymidine kinase (only in infected cells) and then by cellular enzymes to acyclovir triphosphate.
  • This inhibits viral DNA polymerase and causes chain termination → stops viral DNA synthesis.

  • Selective for virus-infected cells → low toxicity. (b) Uses

  • Herpes simplex: genital herpes, herpes labialis (cold sores), herpes keratitis (eye ointment), herpes encephalitis (IV 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for 14–21 days), neonatal herpes.

  • Varicella (chickenpox): in adults, adolescents and high-risk persons – 800 mg five times daily for 5–7 days, started within 24–72 hours.
  • Herpes zoster (shingles): 800 mg five times daily for 7 days, best within 72 hours of rash; reduces pain and complications.
  • Prophylaxis in immunocompromised and transplant patients.

  • Valacyclovir (prodrug) – better absorbed, fewer daily doses. (c) Adverse effects

  • Oral – nausea, diarrhoea, headache (well tolerated).

  • IV – crystalluria and kidney injury (prevent by good hydration and slow infusion over 1 hour), phlebitis (alkaline solution), neurotoxicity (confusion, tremors, seizures) – especially in kidney failure (dose adjustment needed).

3. Oseltamivir (brief)

  • Neuraminidase inhibitor – prevents release of influenza virus from infected cells.
  • 75 mg twice daily for 5 days in adults, started early (preferably within 48 hours) in influenza (including H1N1); prophylaxis of contacts as per guidelines.
  • Nausea, vomiting (take with food).

4. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Start treatment early – antivirals work best in the first days of illness.
  2. IV acyclovir – infuse over at least 1 hour, maintain fluid intake and urine output, monitor creatinine, inspect IV site.
  3. Isolation precautions – airborne and contact for chickenpox/disseminated zoster, droplet for influenza; keep non-immune and pregnant staff away.
  4. Lesion care – keep clean and dry, prevent scratching, calamine for itching.
  5. Education – complete the course; condom use and abstinence during genital herpes outbreaks; antivirals do not cure latent herpes.

Conclusion Antiviral drugs act on specific viral steps; acyclovir is a safe and effective treatment for herpes and varicella infections when started early and given with attention to hydration and kidney function.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Classify anthelmintic drugs. Explain the pharmacology of albendazole.
answer_html:
Introduction Intestinal worm infestations (roundworm, hookworm, whipworm, pinworm) are very common among Indian children and cause anaemia, malnutrition, poor growth and poor school performance. Anthelmintics are drugs that kill or expel worms. India conducts National Deworming Day (10 February and 10 August) for children aged 1–19 years.

1. Classification (according to worm) | Worm | Drugs | |---|---| | Roundworm (Ascaris), hookworm, whipworm (Trichuris) | Albendazole, mebendazole, pyrantel pamoate | | Pinworm/threadworm (Enterobius)* | Albendazole, mebendazole, pyrantel | | Strongyloides | *Ivermectin, albendazole | | Filaria (Wuchereria, Brugia) | Diethylcarbamazine (DEC), albendazole, ivermectin (mass drug administration) | | Tapeworms (Taenia), Hymenolepis | Praziquantel, niclosamide, albendazole | | Neurocysticercosis, hydatid cyst | Albendazole (± praziquantel) | | Flukes (Schistosoma, liver flukes) | Praziquantel, triclabendazole |

2. Albendazole (a) Mechanism of action

  • A benzimidazole that binds to β-tubulin of the worm and inhibits microtubule formation → impaired glucose uptake and depletion of energy (glycogen) → death of the worm (slow, over days); also kills larvae and eggs. (b) Uses

  • Single dose 400 mg (200 mg for children 1–2 years) for roundworm, hookworm, whipworm and pinworm – used in mass deworming (chewable tablet).

  • Strongyloidiasis, cutaneous larva migrans.
  • Neurocysticercosis – 15 mg/kg/day for 8–30 days with steroids and antiepileptics.
  • Hydatid disease – before/after surgery or alone.
  • Lymphatic filariasis – with DEC (and ivermectin) in mass drug administration.

  • Giardiasis (alternative). (c) Adverse effects

  • Single dose – usually well tolerated; mild abdominal pain, nausea, headache, dizziness.

  • Long courses – raised liver enzymes, hair loss, bone-marrow suppression (check blood counts).
  • In neurocysticercosis – headache, seizures due to inflammation around dying cysts (steroids given).
  • Contraindicated in the first trimester of pregnancy (teratogenic in animals); given in the 2nd/3rd trimester under national programmes.

3. Other anthelmintics in brief

  • Mebendazole – 100 mg twice daily for 3 days or 500 mg single dose.
  • Pyrantel pamoate – causes spastic paralysis of worms.
  • Ivermectin – opens chloride channels → paralysis; strongyloidiasis, scabies (oral), filariasis.
  • Praziquantel – increases calcium permeability → spastic paralysis; tapeworms, schistosomiasis.
  • DEC – filariasis; reactions due to dying microfilariae (fever, headache, body ache).

4. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Give albendazole after food (chewed, under supervision in school programmes); observe for adverse events.
  2. Do not give to sick children or in the first trimester; record doses.
  3. Treat all family members in pinworm infection; repeat dose after 2 weeks.
  4. Health education – hand washing with soap before eating and after toilet, wearing footwear (hookworm), trimming nails, safe drinking water, washing vegetables, cooking pork properly (tapeworm), use of toilets (Swachh Bharat).

Conclusion A single dose of albendazole, given twice a year with good hygiene, protects children from the harmful effects of worm infestations.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Explain the sulphonamides and cotrimoxazole – mechanism of action, uses and adverse effects.
answer_html:
Introduction Sulphonamides were the first systemic antibacterial drugs (Domagk's prontosil, 1935). Alone they are now little used because of resistance and toxicity, but in combination with trimethoprim as cotrimoxazole they remain important, especially for Pneumocystis pneumonia and prophylaxis in HIV.

1. Classification of sulphonamides

  • Short/intermediate-acting: sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine.
  • Long-acting: sulfadoxine (with pyrimethamine in malaria).
  • Poorly absorbed (gut action): sulfasalazine (ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis).
  • Topical: silver sulphadiazine (burns), sulfacetamide sodium eye drops, mafenide.

2. Mechanism of action

  • Bacteria must make their own folic acid from para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA).
  • Sulphonamides are structural analogues of PABA and competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase → ↓ folate synthesis → bacteriostatic.
  • Trimethoprim inhibits the next enzyme, dihydrofolate reductase.
  • Cotrimoxazole (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim in 5:1 ratio, e.g., 400 mg + 80 mg) produces sequential blockade of two steps → synergistic and bactericidal action, with less resistance.
  • Human cells use preformed dietary folate – hence selective toxicity.

3. Uses of cotrimoxazole

  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) – drug of choice for treatment and prophylaxis in HIV/AIDS (cotrimoxazole preventive therapy – one double-strength tablet daily as per guidelines).
  • Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis; Nocardia; Isospora/Cyclospora diarrhoea in HIV.
  • Urinary tract infections (where organisms are sensitive), shigellosis, travellers' diarrhoea.
  • Respiratory infections (bronchitis, otitis media – resistance common), community MRSA skin infections, brucellosis (with other drugs).

4. Adverse effects

  • Hypersensitivity – rash, fever, photosensitivity; Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (serious – stop at first sign of rash with mucosal involvement).
  • Crystalluria and kidney stones – ensure good fluid intake.
  • Blood disorders – haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency, megaloblastic anaemia (folate deficiency), leucopenia, thrombocytopenia.
  • Kernicterus in newborns (displace bilirubin) – avoid in late pregnancy and in infants below 2 months.
  • Hyperkalaemia (trimethoprim), GI upset, hepatitis.
  • Interactions – potentiate warfarin, phenytoin and sulphonylureas.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Take an allergy history (sulpha drugs).
  2. Encourage 2–3 litres of fluid daily.
  3. Stop the drug and report any rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or jaundice.
  4. Monitor blood counts and potassium in prolonged or high-dose therapy (e.g., PCP treatment).
  5. Advise sun protection; avoid in late pregnancy and neonates; caution in G6PD deficiency.
  6. Ensure adherence to daily prophylaxis in people living with HIV.

Conclusion Sulphonamides block folate synthesis; combined with trimethoprim as cotrimoxazole they give synergistic, bactericidal action that remains vital for PCP treatment and prophylaxis.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: Give the uses of rifampicin.
answer_html:
Rifampicin – a bactericidal antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

Uses

  1. Tuberculosis – all forms; key first-line, sterilising drug in the 6-month regimen.
  2. Leprosy – monthly supervised dose in MDT; single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis for contacts.
  3. Prophylaxis of meningococcal and H. influenzae meningitis in close contacts.
  4. Brucellosis (with doxycycline).
  5. Serious staphylococcal (including MRSA) infections – prosthetic device infections, in combination.
  6. Cholestatic pruritus (selected cases), Legionella (adjunct).

Note: colours urine, sweat and tears orange-red; enzyme inducer – reduces effect of oral contraceptives, warfarin and some ARVs; hepatotoxic.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: List the first-line antitubercular drugs.
answer_html:
First-line antitubercular drugs (HRZE ± S)

  1. Isoniazid (H) – bactericidal; side effect: peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis.
  2. Rifampicin (R) – bactericidal, sterilising; orange urine, hepatitis.
  3. Pyrazinamide (Z) – sterilising (intracellular); hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia.
  4. Ethambutol (E) – bacteriostatic; optic neuritis.
  5. Streptomycin (S) – injectable aminoglycoside (now rarely used); ototoxicity.

Under NTEP: 2 months HRZE + 4 months HRE, given daily as weight-band fixed-dose combinations.

Pyridoxine is given to prevent isoniazid neuropathy in patients at risk. Drug-resistant TB needs second-line drugs such as bedaquiline, linezolid and fluoroquinolones.

subject: Pharmacology I
question: What is superinfection? Give examples.
answer_html:
Superinfection (suprainfection) is the appearance of a new infection during the course of antimicrobial therapy, caused by organisms resistant to the drug being used, because the drug has suppressed the normal protective flora.

More common with: broad-spectrum antibiotics (tetracyclines, ampicillin, clindamycin, third-generation cephalosporins), prolonged courses, and in immunocompromised, diabetic and elderly patients.

Examples

  1. Oral thrush and vaginal candidiasis (Candida).
  2. Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis (Clostridioides difficile).
  3. Staphylococcal enterocolitis; Pseudomonas or Proteus infections.

Prevention: use narrow-spectrum drugs for the shortest effective time; good oral hygiene; report new diarrhoea or white patches in the mouth.
